blocks.html:
EXPOSÉ I
PRESHEAVESby A. Grothendieck and J.L. Verdier
(with an appendix by N. Bourbaki)

In sections 0 to 5 of this exposé, we present the elementary and, for the most part, well-known properties of the categories of presheaves∗. These properties are used constantly throughout the seminar, and a knowledge of them is essential for understanding the following exposés. The proofs are immediate; they are most often omitted. In sections 6 to 9 we take up a few themes used on various occasions in what follows. The hurried reader may omit them on a first reading. Section 10 fixes the terminology employed. The appendix 11 is due to N. Bourbaki.

footnotes.html: (∗) The reader may also consult SGA 3 I §§ 1 to 3.

blocks.html: 0. Universes
A universe is a non-empty set \(\mathcal{U}\) that enjoys the following properties:

1. (\(\mathcal{U}\) 1)

    If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) and if \(y \in x\) then \(y \in \mathcal{U}\).

  2. (\(\mathcal{U}\) 2)

    If \(x, y \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(\{x,y\} \in \mathcal{U}\).

  3. (\(\mathcal{U}\) 3)

    If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}\).

  4. (\(\mathcal{U}\) 4)

    If \((x_i,\ i \in I \in \mathcal{U})\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), then \(\bigcup_{i\in I} x_i \in \mathcal{U}\).
From the preceding axioms one easily deduces the properties:
— If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), the set \(\{x\}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\).
— If \(x\) is a subset of \(y \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(x \in \mathcal{U}\).
— If \(x,y \in \mathcal{U}\), the ordered pair \((x,y) = \{\{x,y\}, x\}\) (Kuratowski's definition) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).
— If \(x,y \in \mathcal{U}\), the union \(x \cup y\) and the product \(x \times y\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\).
— If \((x_i,\ i \in I \in \mathcal{U})\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), the product \(\prod_{i\in I} x_i\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).
— If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(\mathrm{card}(x) < \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\) (strictly). In particular the relation \(\mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{U}\) does not hold.
One can therefore perform all the usual operations of set theory starting from the elements of a universe without, for all that, the final result ceasing to be an element of the universe.

The primary interest of the notion of universe is that it provides a definition of the usual categories: the category of sets belonging to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (\(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens), the category of topological spaces belonging to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\), the category of commutative groups belonging to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (\(\mathcal{U}\)-Ab), the category of categories belonging to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) ... .

However, the only known universe is the set of symbols of the type \(\{\{\varnothing\}, \{\{\varnothing\}, \varnothing\}\}\) etc. (all the elements of this universe are finite sets and this universe is countable). In particular, one does not know of any universe containing an element of infinite cardinal. One is therefore led to add to the axioms of set theory the axiom:
(\(\mathcal{U}\)A) For every set \(x\) there exists a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(x \in \mathcal{U}\).

Since the intersection of a family of universes is a universe, one deduces immediately that every set is an element of a smallest universe. One can show that the axiom (\(\mathcal{U}\)A) is independent of the axioms of set theory.
One will also add the axiom:
(\(\mathcal{U}\)B) Let \(R\{x\}\) be a relation and \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe. If there exists an element \(y \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(R\{y\}\), then \(\tau_x R\{x\} \in \mathcal{U}\).
The consistency of the axioms (\(\mathcal{U}\)A) and (\(\mathcal{U}\)B) relative to the other axioms of set theory is neither proved nor provable, it seems.

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(c(\mathcal{U})\) the supremum of the cardinals of the elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (\(c(\mathcal{U}) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\)). The cardinal \(c(\mathcal{U})\) enjoys the following properties:

1. (FI)

    If \(a < c(\mathcal{U})\), then \(2^a < c(\mathcal{U})\).

  2. (FII)

    If \((a_i, i \in I)\) is a family of cardinals strictly less than \(c(\mathcal{U})\) and if \(\mathrm{card}(I)\) is strictly less than \(c(\mathcal{U})\), then \(\sum_{i\in I} a_i < c(\mathcal{U})\).
The cardinals that possess the properties (FI) and (FII) are called strongly inaccessible cardinals.
The cardinal 0 and the countable infinite cardinal are strongly inaccessible.
The axiom (\(\mathcal{U}\)A) implies:
(\(\mathcal{U}\)A') Every cardinal is strictly bounded above by a strongly inaccessible cardinal.

One can show (11) that, conversely, the consistency of (\(\mathcal{U}\)A') implies the consistency of (\(\mathcal{U}\)A), and that the consistency of these axioms entails that of the axiom (\(\mathcal{U}\)B).

Let us call artinian set any set \(E\) such that there exists no infinite family \((x_n, n \in \mathbb{N})\) with \(x_0 \in E\), \(x_{n+1} \in x_n\). One can then show [loc. cit.] that there is a one-to-one correspondence between the strongly inaccessible cardinals and the artinian universes, defined as follows: to every strongly inaccessible cardinal \(c\) one associates the unique artinian universe \(\mathcal{U}_c\) such that \[ \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}_c) = c . \] Let \(c < c'\) be two strongly inaccessible cardinals. One has: \[ \mathcal{U}_c \in \mathcal{U}_{c'}, \] In particular the artinian universes of cardinals less than a given cardinal form a well-ordered set (for the membership relation). The axiom (\(\mathcal{U}\)A') is equivalent to the axiom:
(\(\mathcal{U}\)A'') Every artinian set is an element of an artinian universe.
Let us remark that all the usual sets (\(\mathbb{Z}\), \(\mathbb{Q}\), ...) are artinian sets.
1. \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. Presheaves of sets

In the remainder of the seminar, and unless expressly stated otherwise, the universes considered will possess an element of infinite cardinal. Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. A set is said to be \(\mathcal{U}\)-small (or, when no confusion results, small) if it is isomorphic to an element of \(\mathcal{U}\). We also use the terminology: small group, small ring, small category... We will often assume, without explicit mention, that the schemes, topological spaces, index sets... with which we work are \(\in \mathcal{U}\), or at least have a cardinal \(\in \mathcal{U}\); however, many categories with which we will work will not be \(\in \mathcal{U}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.1

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(C\) a category. We say that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category if for every pair \((x,y)\) of objects of \(C\), the set \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(x,y)\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small.
Let \(C\) and \(D\) be two categories and \(\mathrm{Fonct}(C,D)\) the category of functors from \(C\) to \(D\). One verifies immediately the following assertions:
a) If \(C\) and \(D\) are elements of a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. \(\mathcal{U}\)-small), the category \(\mathrm{Fonct}(C,D)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) (resp. is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small).
b) If \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small and if \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, then \(\mathrm{Fonct}(C,D)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 1.1.2

Let \(D\) be a category possessing the following properties:

  1. (C1)

    The set \(\mathrm{ob}(D)\) is contained in the universe \(\mathcal{U}\).

  2. (C2)

    For every pair \((x,y)\) of objects of \(D\), the set \(\mathrm{Hom}_D(x,y)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

(The usual categories constructed from a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) possess these two properties: \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens, \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ab, ... ). Let \(C\) be a category belonging to \(\mathcal{U}\). Then the category \(\mathrm{Fonct}(C,D)\) does not in general possess the properties (C1) and (C2). For example, the category \(\mathrm{Fonct}(C, \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\) possesses neither of the properties (C1) and (C2). This is what justifies the definition adopted for \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, in preference to the more restrictive notion given by the conditions (C1) and (C2) above.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1.2

Let \(C\) be a category. We call category of presheaves of sets on \(C\) relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) (or, when no confusion results, category of presheaves on \(C\)) the category of contravariant functors on \(C\) with values in the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets.

We denote by \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) (or more simply, when no confusion results, by \(\widehat{C}\)) the category of presheaves of sets on \(C\) relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\). The objects of \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) are called \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves (or more simply presheaves) on \(C\). When \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, the category \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. When \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\) is not necessarily a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

blocks.title: Construction-definition
blocks.html:
Construction-definition 1.3

Let \(x\) be an object of a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\). We call \(\mathcal{U}\)-functor represented by \(x\) the functor \(h_{\mathcal{U}}(x) : C^\circ \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) whose construction follows∗. Let \(y\) be an object of \(C\).

a) If \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), then: \[ h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(y) = \mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x) \]

b) Suppose that \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x)\) is not an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), and let \(R(Z,x,y)\) be the relation: "The set \(Z\) is the target of an isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } Z\)". One then sets: \[ h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(y) = \tau_Z\, R(Z) . \] (By virtue of the axiom (\(\mathcal{U}\)B), \(h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(y)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\)). Let \(R'(u,x,y)\) be the relation: "\(u\) is a bijection \(u : \mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(y)\)".

One then sets: \[ \varphi(y,x) = \tau_u\, R'(u) . \]

One will note that, in cases (a) and (b), one has a canonical isomorphism: \[ \varphi(y,x) : \mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(y) . \] (In case a) \(\varphi(y,x)\) is the identity). Now let \(u : y \to y'\) be an arrow of \(C\). The morphism \(u\) defines, by the composition of morphisms, a map: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_C(u,x) : \mathrm{Hom}_C(y',x) \to \mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x) . \]

One then sets \[ h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)(u) = \varphi(y,x)\, \mathrm{Hom}_C(u,x)\, \varphi(y',x)^{-1} . \]

One verifies immediately that \(h_{\mathcal{U}}(x)\), thus defined, is a functor \(C^\circ \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\).

Similarly, one defines, with the help of the isomorphisms \(\varphi\), for every morphism \(y : x \to x'\) a morphism of functors: \[ h_{\mathcal{U}}(y) : h_{\mathcal{U}}(x) \to h_{\mathcal{U}}(x') \] and one verifies immediately that one has thus defined a functor \[ h_{\mathcal{U}} : C \to \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} . \]

Now let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a universe such that \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\). One then has a canonical fully faithful functor: \[ \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{V}\text{-Ens} \] whence a fully faithful functor: \[ \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} . \]

and the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[rr]^-{h_{\mathcal{U}}} \ar[dr]_-{h_{\mathcal{V}}} & & \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \ar[d] \\ & & \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}} } \] is commutative up to canonical isomorphism. When \(C\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), this canonical isomorphism is the identity.

In practice, the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) is fixed once and for all and is not mentioned. One then uses the notations \(\widehat{C}\) (for the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves of sets) and \[ h : C \to \widehat{C} . \] For every object \(x\) of \(C\), the presheaf \(h(x)\) is called the presheaf represented by \(x\) and we will always identify the value at \(y \in \mathrm{ob}(C)\) of the presheaf \(h(x)\) with \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(y,x)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1.4

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(F\) a presheaf on \(C\) and \(X\) an object of \(C\). There exists an isomorphism, functorial in \(X\) and in \(F\): \[ i : \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(h(X),F) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } F(X) , \] the map \(i\) being none other, when \(F\) is of the form \(h(Y)\), than the map: \[ h : \mathrm{Hom}(h(X),h(Y)) \longleftarrow \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y) . \] In particular the functor \(h\) is fully faithful.

This proposition justifies the usual abuses of language identifying an object of \(C\) with the corresponding contravariant functor. A presheaf isomorphic to an object that is the image under \(h\) (or, using the abuse of language noted above, isomorphic to an object of \(C\)) is called a representable presheaf.

Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a universe containing a universe \(\mathcal{U}\). The category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves is a full subcategory of the category of \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves, and consequently a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf is representable if and only if its image in the category of \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaves is a representable \(\mathcal{V}\)-presheaf.

footnotes.html: (∗) \(C^\circ\) will always denote the category opposite to \(C\).

blocks.html: 2. Projective and inductive limits

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and \(I\) a small category. Let us denote by \(\mathrm{Fonct}(I,C)\) the category of functors from \(I\) to \(C\). The category \(\mathrm{Fonct}(I,C)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. To every object \(X\) of \(C\) let us associate the subcategory \(\underline{X}\) of \(C\) having as sole object the object \(X\) and as sole arrow the identity of \(X\). Let us denote by \(i_X : \underline{X} \to C\) the inclusion functor. There exists one and only one functor \(e_X : I \to \underline{X}\), and we will denote by \(k_X : I \to C\) the functor \(i_X \circ e_X\). (One says that \(k_X\) is the constant functor with value \(X\)). The correspondence \(X \mapsto k_X\) is visibly functorial in \(X\), which allows us to define, for every functor \(G : I \to C\), the presheaf \[ X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Fonct}(I,C)}(k_X, G). \]

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.1

One calls projective limit of \(G\) and denotes by \(\varprojlim_I G\) the presheaf: \[ X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Fonct}(I,C)}(k_X, G) . \] When the presheaf \(\varprojlim_I G\) is representable, one denotes again by \(\varprojlim_I G\) an object of \(C\) that represents it. The object \(\varprojlim_I G\) is thus defined only up to isomorphism. When no confusion results, one uses the abbreviated notation \(\varprojlim G\).
For variable \(G\), \(\varprojlim G\) is a functor from the category \(\mathrm{Fonct}(I,C)\) with values in \(\widehat{C}\).

One likewise defines, by symmetry (reversing the direction of the arrows in \(C\)), the inductive limit of a functor: it is a covariant functor on \(C\) with values in the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets. We will use the notations \(\varinjlim_I G\) or else \(\varinjlim G\).
One will note that products, fibre products, and kernels are projective limits. Likewise sums, amalgamated sums, and cokernels are inductive limits.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.2

Let \(I\) and \(C\) be two categories and \(G : I \to C\) a functor. One says that the projective limit of \(G\) is representable if there exists a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that:

1) The category \(I\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small.

2) The category \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

3) The presheaf \(\varprojlim G\) with values in the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets is representable.

It follows from section 1 that the object \(\varprojlim G\) representing the presheaf \(\varprojlim G\) does not depend, up to isomorphism, on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\). Let us also note that there exists a smallest universe \(\mathcal{U}'\) possessing the properties (1) and (2), and that the presheaf \(\varprojlim G\) is necessarily with values in the category of \(\mathcal{U}'\)-sets.

Let \(I\) and \(C\) be two categories. One says that the \(I\)-projective limits in \(C\) are representable if for every functor \(G : I \to C\), the projective limit of \(G\) is representable. Finally, let \(C\) be a category and \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe. One says that the \(\mathcal{U}\)-projective limits in \(C\) are representable if for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category \(I\) and every functor \(G : I \to C\), the projective limit of \(G\) is representable.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3

Let \(C\) be a category and \(\mathcal{U}\) a non-empty universe. The following assertions are equivalent:

i) The \(\mathcal{U}\)-projective limits in \(C\) are representable.

ii) Products indexed by a small set are representable, and the kernels of pairs of arrows are representable.

iii) Products indexed by a small set are representable, and the fibre products are representable.

Proof. It suffices to note that there exists an isomorphism functorial in \(G\) \[ \varprojlim G \simeq \mathrm{Ker}\left( \prod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} G(i) \rightrightarrows \prod_{u\in\mathrm{Fl}(I)} G(\mathrm{but}(u))\right), \] the pair of arrows being defined by the morphisms \[ \prod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} G(i) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{pr}_{\mathrm{but}(u)}\ } G(\mathrm{but}(u)) \] \[ \prod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} G(i) \xrightarrow{\ \mathrm{pr}_{\mathrm{source}(u)}\ } G(\mathrm{source}(u)) \xrightarrow{\ G(u)\ } G(\mathrm{but}(u)) . \] Moreover, it is clear that \(\mathrm{Ker}\bigl(X \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} Y\bigr) = X \underset{X\times Y}{\times} X\), the two morphisms from \(X\) to \(X\times Y\) being \(\mathrm{id}_X\times u\) and \(\mathrm{id}_X\times v\).

There obviously exist analogous definitions and assertions for inductive limits, which we will not make explicit. Likewise for finite projective and inductive limits (i.e. relative to a finite category \(I\)).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.3.2

Let us denote by \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets and by \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ab the category of abelian group objects of \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens. The \(\mathcal{U}\)-projective and inductive limits in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens and in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ab are representable.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.3.3

Let \(I\) be a small category, \(F : I \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) a functor and \(G \subset \mathrm{ob}\, I\) a small set of objects of \(I\) such that for every object \(X\) of \(I\) there exists an object \(Y \in G\) and a morphism \(Y \to X\) (resp. \(X \to Y\)). Then \(\varprojlim_I F\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_I F\)) is representable and one has \(\mathrm{card}(\varprojlim_I F) \leq \prod_{Y\in G} \mathrm{card}(F(Y))\) (resp. \(\mathrm{card}(\varinjlim_I F) \leq \sum_{Y\in G} \mathrm{card}(F(Y))\)).

Proof. One verifies immediately that \(\varprojlim_I F\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_I F\)) is isomorphic to a subobject (resp. a quotient of \(\prod_{Y\in G} F(Y)\) (resp. \(\coprod_{Y\in G} F(Y)\))); whence the proposition.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.4.1

Let \(C\) be a category in which the finite projective (resp. inductive) limits are representable and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor. One says that \(u\) is left exact (resp. right exact) if it "commutes" with finite projective (resp. inductive) limits. A functor that is left and right exact is called an exact functor.

It follows from 2.3 that, for a functor to be exact, it is necessary and sufficient that it transform the final object (= empty product) into the final object, the product of two objects into the product of the two image objects, and the kernel of a pair of two arrows into the kernel of the image pair, or again, that it transform the final object into the final object and the fibre products into fibre products. (One assumes that in \(C\) the finite \(\varprojlim\) are representable.)

Let \(I, J\) and \(C\) be three categories, \(G : I \times J \to C\) a functor (i.e. a functor from \(I\) with values in the category of functors from \(J\) to \(C\)). Suppose that the projective limits of the functors \[ G_i : J \to C \qquad i \in \mathrm{ob}(I) \] \[ j \mapsto G(i \times j) \] are representable, and that the functor: \[ i \mapsto \varprojlim G_i \] admits a representable projective limit. It is clear that then the functor \(G\) admits a representable projective limit and that one has a canonical isomorphism: \[ \varprojlim_{I\times J} G \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_I \varprojlim_J G_i, \] and that consequently one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \varprojlim_I \varprojlim_J G_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_J \varprojlim_I G_j . \] We will say in what follows, more briefly, that projective limits commute with projective limits. One sees likewise that inductive limits commute with inductive limits. But it is not true in general that inductive limits commute with projective limits.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.5

Let \(C\) be a category with representable fibre products, \(I\) a category, \(G : I \to C\) a functor, \(g : G \to X\) a morphism from \(G\) to an object of \(C\) (i.e. a morphism from \(G\) to the constant functor associated with \(X\)), \(m : Y \to X\) a morphism of \(C\). Let \(G \times_X Y : I \to C\) be the functor \[ i \mapsto G(i) \times_X Y . \] One says that the inductive limit of \(G\) is universal if for every object \(X\), every morphism \(g : G \to X\), every morphism \(m : Y \to X\),

a) the inductive limit of the functor \(G \times_X Y\) is representable,

b) the canonical morphism \(\varinjlim(G \times_X Y) \to (\varinjlim G) \times_X Y\) is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.6

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. The inductive limits in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens that are representable (in particular, the \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits (2.2.1) in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens) are universal.
We will also use another commutation result between projective and inductive limits, which we now present.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2.7

A category \(I\) is pseudo-filtered when it possesses the following properties:

PS 1) Every diagram of the form: \[ \xymatrix{ & j \\ i \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & \\ & j' } \] can be inserted into a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ & j \ar[dr] & \\ i \ar[ur] \ar[dr] & & k \\ & j' \ar[ur] & } \]

PS 2) Every diagram of the form: \[ \xymatrix{ i \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{u} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{v} & j } \] can be inserted into a diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ i \ar@<0.6ex>[r]^-{u} \ar@<-0.6ex>[r]_-{v} & j \ar[r]^-{w} & k } \] such that \[ w \circ u = w \circ v . \]

A category \(I\) is said to be filtered if it is pseudo-filtered, non-empty and connected, i.e. if any two objects of \(I\) can be joined by a chain of arrows (one imposes no condition on the direction of the arrows); this also means, in the presence of PS 2, that \(I \neq \varnothing\) and that for two objects \(a, b\) of \(I\), there always exist an object \(c\) of \(I\) and arrows \(a \to c\) and \(b \to c\). One also says that a category \(I\) is cofiltered if \(I^\circ\) is filtered.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 2.7.1

If in \(I\) the amalgamated sums (resp. the sums of two objects) and the cokernels of double arrows are representable, then \(I\) is pseudo-filtered (resp. filtered).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.8

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. The filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens commute with finite projective limits.
One reduces immediately to proving that the filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits commute with fibre products. The proof is left to the reader. One may use the description of the limit given by the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2.8.1

Let \(I\) be a small filtered category, \(i \mapsto X_i\) a functor from \(I\) to \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens. On the sum set \(\coprod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} X_i\), let \(R\) be the relation:

(R) Two elements \(x_i \in X_i\) and \(x_j \in X_j\) are related if there exists an object \(k \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\) and two morphisms \(u : i \to k\) and \(v : j \to k\) such that the images in \(X_k\) of \(x_i\) and of \(x_j\) under the transition maps \(u\) and \(v\) respectively are equal.

Then:

1) \(R\) is an equivalence relation.

2) The quotient \(\coprod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} X_i / R\) is canonically isomorphic to \(\varinjlim_I X_i\).

3) Two elements \(x_i \in X_i\) and \(x_j \in X_j\) are respectively equivalent, under \(R\), to two elements of one and the same \(X_k\).

4) For every \(i \in \mathrm{ob}(I)\), two elements \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) of \(X_i\) are equivalent under \(R\) if and only if there exists a morphism \(u : i \to j\) such that \(u(\alpha) = u(\beta)\).

Assertion 1) follows from (PS 1) (2.7). To prove 2), one verifies that \(\coprod_{i\in\mathrm{ob}(I)} X_i / R\) possesses the universal property of the inductive limit (one uses only (PS 1)). Assertion 3) follows from the fact that \(I\) is connected. Assertion 4) follows from (PS 2).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.9

Let \(\gamma\) be a species of algebraic structure "defined by finite projective limits". (The reader is asked to give a mathematical meaning to the preceding sentence. Let us only note that the structures of groups, abelian groups, rings, modules, etc... are such structures). Let us denote by \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens. The functor that to each object of \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) associates the underlying set commutes with filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits. Consequently the filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) commute with finite projective limits.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2.10

The pseudo-filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ab commute with finite projective limits.
(One reduces to filtered limits by decomposing the index category into connected components).

Let us now note a result that we will use constantly: Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, \(u\) and \(v\) two functors \(C \underset{u}{\overset{v}{\rightleftarrows}} C'\), \(u\) left adjoint of \(v\). Let us recall that this means that there exists an isomorphism between the bifunctors with values in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{C'}(u(X),X') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_C(X,v(X')) . \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.11

The functor \(u\) commutes with representable inductive limits; the functor \(v\) commutes with representable projective limits.

This assertion means that for every category \(I\) and every functor \(G : I \to C'\) such that the projective limit of \(G\) is representable, the functor \(v \circ G\) admits a representable projective limit and one has a canonical isomorphism: \[ v(\varprojlim G) \longrightarrow \varprojlim(v \circ G) . \] The reader will make explicit for himself the assertion concerning the functor \(u\).
Let us finally point out a computation of projective limits in the case where the index category admits products.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2.12

Let \(I\) and \(C\) be two categories, \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe. Suppose that the \(\mathcal{V}\)-projective limits in \(C\) are representable and that there exists in \(I\) a family of objects \((i_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\), where \(A\) is an element of \(\mathcal{V}\), such that:

1) the products \(i_\alpha \times i_\beta\) are representable for every pair \((\alpha,\beta) \in A\times A\),

2) every object of \(I\) maps into at least one of the \(i_\alpha\).

Then for every contra-functor \(F\) from \(I\) to \(C\) \[ F : I^\circ \to C, \] the projective limit of \(F\) exists and there exists an isomorphism functorial in \(F\): \[ \varprojlim F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Ker}\left( \prod_{\alpha\in A} F(i_\alpha) \rightrightarrows \prod_{(\alpha,\beta)\in A\times A} F(i_\alpha \times i_\beta)\right), \] the two arrows being defined by the projections of the products \(i_\alpha \times i_\beta\) onto the factors.

pages.title: 3. Exactness properties of the category of presheaves

blocks.html: 3. Exactness properties of the category of presheaves
Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(\widehat{C}\) the category of presheaves on \(C\). The exactness properties of \(\widehat{C}\) all follow from the following proposition:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.1

The \(\mathcal{U}\)-projective and inductive limits in \(\widehat{C}\) are representable. For every object \(X\) of \(C\), the functor on \(\widehat{C}\): \[ F \mapsto F(X) \qquad F \in \widehat{C} \] commutes with inductive and projective limits.
In other words, "the inductive and projective limits in \(\widehat{C}\) are computed argument by argument". Let us cite a few corollaries.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.2

Let \(\gamma\) be an algebraic structure defined by finite projective limits. The category of contravariant functors with values in \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\) is equivalent to the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\widehat{C}\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.3

A morphism of \(\widehat{C}\) that is both a monomorphism and an epimorphism is an isomorphism. A morphism of \(\widehat{C}\) factors in a unique way as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism. The inductive limits in \(\widehat{C}\) that are representable are universal. The filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-inductive limits in \(\widehat{C}\) commute with finite projective limits. The canonical functor \(C \to \widehat{C}\) commutes with representable projective limits.
More generally, one can say that the category \(\widehat{C}\) inherits all the properties of the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets involving inductive and projective limits.

Let \(F\) be an object of \(\widehat{C}\). One denotes by \(C/F\) the following category: The objects of \(C/F\) are the pairs formed of an object \(X\) of \(C\) and a morphism \(u\) from \(X\) to \(F\). Let \((X,u)\) and \((Y,v)\) be two objects. A morphism from \((X,u)\) to \((Y,v)\) is a morphism \(g\) from \(X\) to \(Y\) such that the diagram below is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ X \ar[rr]^-{g} \ar[dr]_-{u} & & Y \ar[dl]^-{v} \\ & F & } \]

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.4

With the notations of (3.4.0), the source functor \(C/F \to \widehat{C}\) admits a representable inductive limit in \(\widehat{C}\). The canonical morphism: \[ \varinjlim_{C/F} \mathrm{source}(.) \to F \] is an isomorphism.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 3.5

Let \(F\) and \(H\) be two objects of \(\widehat{C}\). There exists a canonical isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(F,H) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{(X,u)\in\mathrm{ob}(C/F)} H(X) . \]
Proof. The corollary follows immediately from 3.4 and from 1.2.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3.6

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(i : \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}} \to \widehat{C}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the natural injection functor of the corresponding categories of presheaves (1.3). The functor \(i\) commutes with inductive and projective limits. Moreover, for every object \(F\) of \(\widehat{C}_{\mathcal{U}}\), every subobject of \(i(F)\) is isomorphic to the image under \(i\) of a unique subobject of \(F\) (so that one obtains a bijection of the set of subobjects of \(F\) with the set of subobjects of \(i(F)\)).
4. Sieves

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4.1

Let \(C\) be a category. One calls sieve of the category \(C\) a full subcategory \(D\) of \(C\) possessing the following property: every object of \(C\) such that there exists a morphism from this object to an object of \(D\) is in \(D\). Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\); one calls (by abuse of language) sieves of \(X\) the sieves of the category \(C/X\).

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe such that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Let \(\widehat{C}\) be the corresponding category of presheaves. To every sieve of \(X\) one associates a subobject of \(X\) in \(\widehat{C}\) in the following manner: To every object \(Y\) of \(C\), one makes correspond the set of morphisms \(f : Y \to X\) such that the object \((Y,f)\) belongs to the sieve.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4.2

The map defined above establishes a bijection between the set of sieves of \(X\) and the set of subobjects of \(X\) in \(\widehat{C}\).

Proof. Let us only show that it is the inverse map. To every subfunctor \(R\) of \(X\) one associates the category \(C/R\) of objects of \(C\) above \(R\) (3.4). One verifies immediately that \(C/R\) is a sieve of \(X\).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 4.2.1

One sees likewise that the sieves of \(C\) are in canonical one-to-one correspondence with the set of subfunctors of the "final functor" on \(C\) ("final" object of \(\widehat{C}\)).

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. By abuse of language we will also call sieves of \(X\) the subobjects of \(X\) in the category \(\widehat{C}\). This abuse of language allows us, for every presheaf \(F\) and every sieve \(R\) of \(X\), to define \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F)\) as being the set of morphisms from the functor \(R\) to \(F\). One has moreover a canonical isomorphism functorial in \(F\) (3.5): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(R,F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C/R} F(.) , \] which allows one to give a direct definition of it. Likewise, proposition 4.2 allows us to transpose to sieves the usual operations on functors. Let us cite:
4.3.1. Base change.

Let \(R\) be a sieve of \(X\) and \(f : Y \to X\) a morphism of objects of \(C\). The fibre product \(R \times_X Y\) is a sieve of \(Y\) which one calls sieve deduced from \(R\) by base change. The corresponding subcategory of \(C/Y\) is the inverse image of the subcategory of \(C/X\) defined by \(R\) under the canonical functor \(C/Y \to C/X\) defined by \(f\).
4.3.2. Order relation, intersection, union.

The inclusion relation on the subfunctors of \(X\) is an order relation. One can define the union and the intersection of a family of sieves indexed by an arbitrary set as being the supremum and the infimum of the corresponding family of subpresheaves.
4.3.3. Image, generated sieve.

Let \((F_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\) be a family of presheaves and, for each \(\alpha \in A\), a morphism \(f_\alpha : F_\alpha \to X\) where \(X\) is an object of \(C\). The union of the images of the \(f_\alpha\) is called the image of this family of morphisms. The image of this family is therefore a sieve of \(X\). In particular, if all the \(F_\alpha\) are objects of \(C\), the image sieve will be called the sieve generated by the morphisms \(f_\alpha\). The category \(C/R\) is the full subcategory of \(C/X\) formed of the objects \(X' \to X\) over \(X\) such that there exists an \(X\)-morphism from \(X'\) into one of the \(F_\alpha\).

The reader may, as an exercise, translate into terms of the categories \(C/R\) the relations and operations defined here on subfunctors. He will then observe that these relations and operations do not depend on the universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and that they are consequently defined for every category, without one being obliged to specify the universe to which the sets of morphisms belong; something which could moreover be foreseen a priori thanks to 3.6.
5. Functoriality of categories of presheaves

Let \(C, C', D\) be three categories and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor. We denote by \(u^*\) the functor: \[ u^* : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C'^\circ,D) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ,D), \qquad G \mapsto G \circ u, \] obtained by composition with the functor \(u\). The functor \(u^*\) commutes with inductive and projective limits.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.1

Suppose that \(C\) is small, and that, in \(D\), the inductive (resp. projective) \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits are representable. The functor \(u^*\) admits a left adjoint \(u_!\) (resp. a right adjoint \(u_*\)). We thus have an isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ,D)}(F, u^*G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C'^\circ,D)}(u_! F, G) \] \[ (\text{resp. } \mathrm{Hom}_{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ,D)}(u^*G, F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C'^\circ,D)}(G, u_* F) ) . \]

Proof. We shall indicate only the proof of the existence of the left adjoint functor. The resp. part of the proposition then follows formally by means of the isomorphisms: \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ,D) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,D^\circ)^\circ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}((C^\circ)^\circ, D^\circ)^\circ . \]

Let \(Y\) be an object of \(C'\). We denote by \(I_u^Y\) the following category: The objects of \(I_u^Y\) are the pairs \((X,m)\) where \(X\) is an object of \(C\) and \(m\) a morphism \(Y \to u(X)\). Let \((X,m)\) and \((X',m')\) be two objects of \(I_u^Y\). A morphism from \((X,m)\) to \((X',m')\) is a morphism \(\xi : X \to X'\) such that \(m' = u(\xi)m\). The composition of morphisms is defined in the obvious manner.
Let \(f : Y \to Y'\) be a morphism of \(C'\). The morphism \(f\) defines by composition a functor \(I_u^f : I_u^Y \to I_u^{Y'}\).

We have moreover a functor \(\mathrm{pr}_Y : I_u^Y \to C\) which associates to the object \((X,m)\) the object \(X\). Note that then the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ I_u^Y \ar[rr]^-{I_u^f} \ar[dr]_-{\mathrm{pr}_Y} & & I_u^{Y'} \ar[dl]^-{\mathrm{pr}_{Y'}} \\ & C & } \tag{\(*\)} \] is commutative.

Now let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\) and set: \[ u_! F(Y) = \varinjlim_{I_u^Y} F\, \mathrm{pr}_Y(.) . \tag{5.1.1} \] The commutativity of the diagram (\(*\)) and the functoriality of the inductive limit make \(u_! F\) a presheaf on \(C'\). Let us show that the functor \(u_!\) is a left adjoint of the functor \(u^*\). To this end let us show that for every presheaf \(G\) on \(C'\), there exists a functorial isomorphism \(\mathrm{Hom}(u_! F,G) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(F,u^*G)\). Let \(\xi \in \mathrm{Hom}(u_! F,G)\). For every object \(X\) of \(C\), we therefore have a morphism: \[ \xi_X : u_! F(u(X)) \to G(u(X)) . \]

But \((u(X), \mathrm{id}_{u(X)})\) is an object of \(I_u^{u(X)}\), and by definition of the inductive limit, we have a canonical morphism: \[ F(X) \to u_! F(u(X)). \] We deduce from this, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), a morphism: \[ \eta_X : F(X) \to G(u(X)) \] which is visibly functorial in \(X\). Whence a morphism \[ \eta : F \to u^*G . \]

Conversely, let \(\eta \in \mathrm{Hom}(F,u^*G)\). We deduce from this, for every object \(Y\) of \(C'\), a morphism of functors: \[ \eta_Y : F\,\mathrm{pr}_Y \to (u^*G)\,\mathrm{pr}_Y , \] whence, by composing with the obvious morphism from the functor \((u^*G)\,\mathrm{pr}_Y\) into the constant functor \(G(Y)\), a morphism: \[ \xi_Y : u_! F(Y) \to G(Y) \] which is functorial in \(Y\). Whence a morphism: \[ \xi : u_! F \to G . \]
The reader will verify that the two maps thus defined are inverse to one another, and will thereby complete the proof.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.2

Suppose that in \(D\), the inductive \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits are representable, the finite projective limits are representable, and that the filtered inductive \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits commute with finite projective limits. Suppose moreover that in \(C\) the finite projective limits are representable and that the functor \(u\) is left exact (2.3.2). Then the finite projective limits are representable in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ,D)\) and in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C'^\circ,D)\), and the functor \(u_!\) is left exact.

Proof. The first assertion is trivial. Let us prove the second. By the proof of 5.1, for every presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) and every object \(Y\) of \(C'\) we have: \[ u_! F(Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{I_u^Y} F\,\mathrm{pr}_Y . \] It therefore suffices to show that the category \((I_u^Y)^\circ\) satisfies the axioms (PS 1) and (PS 2) (2.7) and that this category is connected. The verification is left to the reader.

By specializing these results to the case where \(D\) is the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets, we obtain a sequence of three functors: \[ u_! , \quad u^* , \quad u_* , \] which is a "sequence of adjoint functors" in the sense that for two consecutive functors of the sequence the one on the right is a right adjoint of the other.
Their essential properties are summarized in the following:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.4

Let \(C\) be a small category, \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and \(u : C \to C'\) a functor.

1) The functor \(u^* : \widehat{C'} \to \widehat{C}\) commutes with inductive and projective limits.

2) The functor \(u_* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'}\) commutes with projective limits. For every presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) and every object \(Y\) of \(C'\), we have \[ u_* F(Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(u^*(Y),F) . \]

3) The functor \(u_! : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'}\) commutes with inductive limits. The functor \(u_!\) is defined only up to isomorphism, but it can always be chosen such that the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[rr]^-{u} \ar[d]_-{h} & & C' \ar[d]^-{h'} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]_-{u_!} & & \widehat{C'} } \] (\(h\) and \(h'\) are the canonical inclusion functors) is commutative. For every presheaf \(F\) on \(C\), we have: \[ u_! F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{C/F} h'u . \]

4) If the finite projective limits are representable in \(C\) and if \(u\) is left exact (2.3.2), the functor \(u_!\) is left exact.

Proof. Assertion (1) is trivial. Assertion (2) follows from the fact that \(u_*\) is a right adjoint functor, by (2.11) and (1.4). The same holds for assertion (3), but one applies in addition (3.4). Finally assertion (4) is none other than 5.2, which can be applied thanks to (2.7).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.5

Let \(C\) and \(C'\) be two small categories and \(C \underset{u}{\overset{v}{\rightleftarrows}} C'\) a pair of functors, where \(v\) is a left adjoint of \(u\). Then there exist isomorphisms, compatible with the adjunction isomorphisms: \[ v^* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u_! \] \[ v_* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u^* . \]

Proof. It suffices to exhibit an isomorphism \(v^* \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u_!\); the other isomorphism follows from it by adjunction. Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\) and \(Y\) an object of \(C'\). We then have: \[ v^* F(Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(v(Y),F) . \] Then, using (3.4): \[ \mathrm{Hom}(v(Y),F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C/F} \mathrm{Hom}(v(Y),.) . \] But \(v\) is a left adjoint of \(u\) and consequently: \[ \varprojlim_{C/F} \mathrm{Hom}(v(Y),.) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C/F} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,u(\,.\,)) . \] Then, using 5.4 3), it follows that: \[ \varprojlim_{C/F} \mathrm{Hom}(Y,u(\,.\,)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(Y,u_! F) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u_! F(Y) . \] We have thus determined, for every object \(Y\) of \(C'\), an isomorphism \(v^* F(Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } u_! F(Y)\) which is visibly functorial in \(Y\) and in \(F\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 5.5.1

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a functor that admits a left adjoint. The functor \(u_! : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'}\) commutes with projective limits (recall that it commutes with inductive limits by (1.4, 3)).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.5.2

We thus find a "sequence of four adjoint functors" (cf. 5.3): \[ v_! , \quad v^* = u_! , \quad v_* = u^* , \quad u_* , \] of which the first three (resp. last three) therefore commute with \(\varinjlim\) (resp. \(\varprojlim\)).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.6

The hypotheses are those of 5.4. The following conditions are equivalent:

i) The functor \(u\) is fully faithful.

ii) The functor \(u_!\) is fully faithful.

iii) The adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id}_{\widehat{C}} \to u^*u_!\) is an isomorphism.

iv) The functor \(u_*\) is fully faithful.

v) The adjunction morphism \(u^*u_* \to \mathrm{id}_{\widehat{C}}\) is an isomorphism.

Proof. It is clear that ii) ⟺ iii) and iv) ⟺ v) (general properties of adjoint functors) and that (5.4 3)). Let us show that i) ⟹ iii). The functors \(\mathrm{id}_{\widehat{C}}\), \(u^*\) and \(u_!\) commute with inductive limits. By (3.4), it therefore suffices to prove that \(H \to u^*u_! H\) is an isomorphism when \(H\) is representable, which is obvious. Let us show that iii) is equivalent to v). For every object \(H\) (resp. \(K\)) of \(\widehat{C}\) denote by \(\Phi(H) : H \to u^*u_! H\) (resp. by \(\Psi(K) : u^*u_* \to K\)) the adjunction morphism. We then have a commutative diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(H,u^*u_*K) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{Hom}(H,\Psi(K))} \ar@{-}[d]|-{\wr} & & \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(H,K) \\ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C'}}(u_!H,u_*K) \ar@{-}[d]|-{\wr} & & \\ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(u^*u_!H,K) \ar[uurr]_-{\mathrm{Hom}(\Phi(H),K)} & & } \] Consequently \(\Phi(H)\) is an isomorphism for every \(H\) if and only if \(\Psi(K)\) is an isomorphism for every \(K\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 5.7

a) The equivalences ii) ⟺ iii) ⟺ iv) ⟺ v) are general results on adjoint functors.

b) The explicit form of \(u_!\), resp. \(u_*\), given in the proof of 1.4 shows at once that, under the general hypotheses of 1.1, if \(u\) is fully faithful, then the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id} \to u^*u_!\) (resp. \(u^*u_* \to \mathrm{id}\)) is an isomorphism, i.e. that \(u_!\) (resp. \(u_*\)) is fully faithful.

Let \(\gamma\) be a species of algebraic structure defined by finite projective limits, \(\mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens}\) the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens, \(\mathrm{esj} : \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens} \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) the underlying-set functor (for simplicity we assume that the species of structure under consideration has a single base set). Let \(C\) be a category. Composition with \(\mathrm{esj}\) yields a functor denoted \[ \widehat{\mathrm{esj}} : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens}) \to \widehat{C}. \] Since in \(\widehat{C}\) the projective limits are computed argument by argument, the functor \(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}\) factors through an equivalence. \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens}) \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } \widehat{C}_\gamma , \tag{5.8.1} \] where \(\widehat{C}_\gamma\) is the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\widehat{C}\), and a functor again denoted \[ \widehat{\mathrm{esj}} : \widehat{C}_\gamma \to \widehat{C}, \] and called the "underlying presheaf of sets" functor.

Suppose that the functor \(\mathrm{esj} : \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens} \to \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\) admits a left adjoint \(\mathrm{Lib} : \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens} \to \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens}\)∗ (one can in fact show that this condition is always satisfied). Composition with \(\mathrm{Lib}\) yields a functor \[ \widehat{\mathrm{Lib}} : \widehat{C} \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-}\gamma\text{-Ens}) \] and, by composing with the equivalence (5.8.1), a functor again denoted \[ \widehat{\mathrm{Lib}} : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C}_\gamma , \] and called the "generated presheaf of free \(\gamma\)-objects" functor. The functor \(\widehat{\mathrm{Lib}}\) is a left adjoint of the functor \(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.8.3

Let \(\gamma\) be a species of algebraic structure defined by finite projective limits such that in the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens the inductive \(\mathcal{U}\)-limits are representable∗∗, \(C\) a category belonging to \(\mathcal{U}\), \(C'\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(u : C \to C'\) a functor. Denote by \(\widehat{C}_\gamma\) (resp. \(\widehat{C'}_\gamma\)) the category of \(\gamma\)-objects of \(\widehat{C}\) (resp. \(\widehat{C'}\)) and by \(u^{*\gamma}\) the functor on the \(\gamma\)-objects deduced from the functor \(u^*\). It follows from 5.1 and from the equivalence 5.8.1 that there exists a functor left adjoint (resp. right adjoint) to the functor \(u^{*\gamma}\). This functor is denoted \(u_{!\gamma}\) (resp. \(u_{*\gamma}\)).

1) The functor \(u^{*\gamma}\) commutes with inductive and projective limits. The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C'}_\gamma \ar[rr]^-{u^{*\gamma}} \ar[d]_-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}'}} & & \widehat{C}_\gamma \ar[d]^-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}} \\ \widehat{C'} \ar[rr]_-{u^*} & & \widehat{C} } \tag{\(*\)} \] is commutative (\(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}'}\) and \(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}\) denote the "underlying set" functors).

2) The functor \(u_{*\gamma}\) commutes with projective limits. The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C}_\gamma \ar[rr]^-{u_{*\gamma}} \ar[d]_-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}} & & \widehat{C'}_\gamma \ar[d]^-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}'}} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]_-{u_*} & & \widehat{C'} } \tag{\(**\)} \] is commutative up to isomorphism.

3) The functor \(u_{!\gamma}\) commutes with inductive limits. Suppose that \(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}\) (resp. \(\widehat{\mathrm{esj}'}\)) admits a left adjoint \(\widehat{\mathrm{Lib}}\) (resp. \(\widehat{\mathrm{Lib}'}\)) (5.8.2). The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]^-{u_!} \ar[d]_-{\widehat{\mathrm{Lib}}} & & \widehat{C'} \ar[d]^-{\widehat{\mathrm{Lib}'}} \\ \widehat{C}_\gamma \ar[rr]_-{u_{!\gamma}} & & \widehat{C'}_\gamma } \tag{\(***\)} \] is commutative up to isomorphism.

Suppose that \(u_!\) commutes with finite projective limits (5.4 4) and 5.6). Then the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C}_\gamma \ar[rr]^-{u_{!\gamma}} \ar[d]_-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}}} & & \widehat{C'}_\gamma \ar[d]^-{\widehat{\mathrm{esj}'}} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]_-{u_!} & & \widehat{C'} } \tag{\(****\)} \] is commutative up to isomorphism, and \(u_{!\gamma}\) commutes with finite projective limits.

Proof. Assertion (1) is obvious. Assertion (2) too, since \(u_*\) is a right adjoint and consequently (2.11) commutes with projective limits and, in particular, with finite projective limits; whence the commutativity of diagram (\(**\)). The commutativity of diagram (\(***\)) follows from the uniqueness, up to isomorphism, of the left adjoint functor, and finally the commutativity of diagram (\(****\)) follows immediately from the fact that \(u_!\) commutes with finite projective limits.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.html:
Notation 5.9

By abuse of notation, the functors \(u^{*\gamma}\) and \(u_{*\gamma}\) will often be denoted \(u^*\) and \(u_*\), which cannot give rise to any confusion by virtue of the commutativity of diagrams (\(*\)) and (\(**\)). On the other hand, when \(u_!\) does not commute with finite projective limits, diagram (\(****\)) is not commutative up to isomorphism, and the notations \(u_!\) and \(u_{!\gamma}\) will have to be used in order to avoid confusion.

Let \(C\) be a small category. For every object \(X\) of \(\widehat{C}\), we denote by \(C/X\) the category of arrows with target \(X\) and source an object of \(C\). The source functor defines a functor \(j_X : C/X \to C\). Let \(m : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). The composition of morphisms defines a functor \(j_m : C/Y \to C/X\). The diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ C/Y \ar[rr]^-{j_m} \ar[dr]_-{j_Y} & & C/X \ar[dl]^-{j_X} \\ & C & } \] is commutative. It follows from 5.1 that for every object \(F\) of \(\widehat{C/X}\) and every object \(Y\) of \(C\), we have: \[ j_{X!} F(Y) = \coprod_{u\in\mathrm{Hom}_C(Y,X)} F(u) . \tag{5.10.1} \]

Formula (5.10.1) allows one to define \(j_{X!}\) when \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and one verifies that the functor \(j_{X!}\) thus defined is always a left adjoint of the functor \(j_X^* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C/X}\) (5.0).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.11

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(X\) a presheaf on \(C\).

1) The functor \[ j_{X!} : \widehat{C/X} \to \widehat{C} \] factors through the category \(\widehat{C}/X\): \[ \widehat{C/X} \xrightarrow{\ e_X\ } \widehat{C}/X \to \widehat{C} . \] The functor \(e_X\) is an equivalence of categories.

2) The functor \(e_X \circ j_X^* : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C}/X\) is canonically isomorphic to the functor \(H \mapsto (H\times X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_2} X)\).

Proof. 1) Let \(f\) be the final object of \(\widehat{C/X}\). We have a canonical isomorphism \(f \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{Y\in\mathrm{ob}\,C/X} Y\) and consequently \(j_{X!}(f) = \varinjlim_{Y\in\mathrm{ob}\,C/X} j_X(Y)\) (5.4). But \(j_{X!}(f) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X\); whence the factorization. To show that \(e_X\) is an equivalence we shall content ourselves with exhibiting a quasi-inverse functor: To every object \(H \to X\) of \(\widehat{C}/X\) we associate the presheaf on \(C/X\): \[ (Y \to X) \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}/X}((Y \to X), (H \to X)) . \]

2) The functor \(e_X \circ j_X^*\) is a right adjoint of the forgetful functor and consequently the functor \(e_X \circ j_X^*\) is canonically isomorphic to the functor \(H \mapsto (H\times X \xrightarrow{\mathrm{pr}_2} X)\).

Let \(m : Y \to X\) be a morphism of \(\widehat{C}\). By (5.11), the morphism \(m\) is canonically isomorphic to the image under \(e_X\) of an object of \(\widehat{C/X}\) which we shall denote \([m]\). The functor \(e_X\) defines, by restriction to the subcategories, an equivalence \[ (C/X)/[m] \xrightarrow{\ e_m\ } C/Y . \] The diagram \[ \xymatrix{ (C/X)/[m] \ar[rr]^-{e_m} \ar[dr]_-{j_{[m]}} & & C/Y \ar[dl]^-{j_m} \\ & C/X & } \] is commutative up to canonical isomorphism.

Let us point out a result that will be useful to us in Exp. VI. Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a functor between small categories. For every object \(H\) of \(\widehat{C}\) denote by \(u/H : C/H \to C'/u_! H\) the functor which associates to every morphism \(m : X \to H\) the morphism \(u_! X \xrightarrow{\ u_! m\ } u_! H\) (we know (5.4) that one can always set \(u_! X = uX\)). The diagram below is commutative: \[ \xymatrix{ C/H \ar[rr]^-{u/H} \ar[d]_-{j_H} & & C'/u_! H \ar[d]^-{j_{u_! H}} \\ C \ar[rr]_-{u} & & C' } \tag{5.13.1} \] We thus have a diagram, commutative up to isomorphism: \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C/H} \ar[rr]^-{(u/H)_!} \ar[d]_-{(j_H)_!} & & \widehat{C'/u_! H} \ar[d]^-{(j_{u_! H})_!} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]_-{u_!} & & \widehat{C'} } \tag{5.13.2} \] and since \((u/H)_!\) transforms the final object of \(\widehat{C/H}\) into the final object of \(\widehat{C'/u_! H}\), the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ \widehat{C/H} \ar[rr]^-{(u/H)_!} \ar[d]_-{e_H} & & \widehat{C'/u_! H} \ar[d]^-{e_{u_! H}} \\ \widehat{C}/H \ar[rr]_-{u_!/H} & & \widehat{C'}/u_! H } \tag{5.13.3} \] is commutative up to isomorphism (6.1).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5.14

Let \(u : C \to C'\) be a functor between small categories. Suppose that \(u\) possesses the following property:

(PPF) For every object \(X\) of \(C\) the functor \(u/X : C/X \to C'/uX\) is fully faithful.

Then:

1) Let \(f\) be the final object of \(\widehat{C}\). The functor \(u\) factors as \[ C = C/f \xrightarrow{\ u/f\ } C'/u_! f \xrightarrow{\ \overline{j}_{u_! f}\ } C' . \] The functor \(u/f\) is fully faithful.

2) The functor \(u_! : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'}\) factors as \[ \widehat{C} = \widehat{C/f} \xrightarrow{\ (u/f)_!\ } \widehat{C'/u_! f} \xrightarrow{\ e_{u_! f}\ } \widehat{C'}/u_! f \to \widehat{C'} , \] where the functor \((u/f)_!\) is fully faithful, the functor \(e_{u_! f}\) an equivalence, and the functor \(\widehat{C'}/u_! f \to \widehat{C'}\) the forgetful functor.

3) In particular the functor \(u_!\) is faithful and consequently the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id} \xrightarrow{\ \Phi\ } u^*u_!\) is a monomorphism. Moreover, for every morphism \(\alpha : H \to K\) of \(\widehat{C}\), the diagram: \[ \xymatrix{ H \ar@{^{(}->}[rr]^-{\Phi(H)} \ar[d]_-{\alpha} & & u^*u_! H \ar[d]^-{u^*u_!(\alpha)} \\ K \ar@{^{(}->}[rr]_-{\Phi(K)} & & u^*u_! K } \] is cartesian.

Proof. 1) The factorization comes from the diagram (5.13.1). The functor \(u\) is faithful. Hence \(u/f\) is faithful. Let us show that it is fully faithful. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two objects of \(C\), \(\mathrm{can}_X : uX \to u_! f\) (resp. \(\mathrm{can}_Y : uY \to u_! f\)) the canonical morphisms and \[ \xymatrix{ uX \ar[rr]^-{m} \ar[dr]_-{\mathrm{can}_X} & & uY \ar[dl]^-{\mathrm{can}_Y} \\ & u_! f & } \] a morphism of \(C'/u_! f\). We have \(u_! f = \varinjlim_{Z\in\mathrm{ob}\,C} uZ\) and consequently (3.1): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C'}}(uX, u_! f) = \varinjlim_{Z\in\mathrm{ob}\,C} \mathrm{Hom}_{C'}(uX, uZ) . \] By definition of the inductive limit, to say that \(\mathrm{can}_Y\, m = \mathrm{can}_X\) is equivalent to saying that there exists
a) a finite sequence of objects of \(C\), \(X_i\), \(i \in [0,n]\), \(X_0 = X\), \(X_n = Y\),
b) for every \(i\), a morphism \(m_i : uX \to uX_i\) (\(m_0 = \mathrm{id}_{uX}\), \(m_n = m\)),
c) for every pair \((i,i+1)\) a morphism \(f_i : X_i \to X_{i+1}\) or else \(f_i : X_{i+1} \to X_i\),

such that the diagrams \[ \xymatrix{ & uX \ar[dl]_-{m_i} \ar[dr]^-{m_{i+1}} & \\ uX_i \ar[rr]_-{u(f_i)} & & uX_{i+1} } \qquad \text{or} \qquad \xymatrix{ & uX \ar[dl]_-{m_i} \ar[dr]^-{m_{i+1}} & \\ uX_i & & uX_{i+1} \ar[ll]^-{u(f_i)} } \] are commutative.
One then proves immediately, by induction on \(i\) and using the property (PPF), that \(m_i\) is of the form \(u(p_i)\). In particular \(m = u(p)\) and consequently \(u/f\) is fully faithful.
2) The factorization is immediate. The functor \((u/f)_!\) is fully faithful by virtue of 5.6. The other assertions follow from 5.11.

3) The functor \(u_!\) is composed of the forgetful functor, which is faithful, and of fully faithful functors. It is consequently faithful. It follows, from the general properties of adjoint functors, that the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id} \to u^*u_!\) is a monomorphism. By 2) the functor \(u_!\) appears as the composite of a fully faithful functor \(v : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'}/u_! f\) and the forgetful functor. The functor \(u^*\), right adjoint of \(u_!\), is therefore the composite of the functor "product by \(u_! f\)", right adjoint of the forgetful functor, and of a functor \(w\) right adjoint of \(v\). Moreover, \(v\) being fully faithful, the adjunction morphism \(\mathrm{id} \to wv\) is an isomorphism. The last assertion follows from it easily.

footnotes.html: (∗) The functor Lib is the "generated free \(\gamma\)-objects" functor. Example: free group, free commutative group, free A-module, etc... .
(∗∗) One can show that this condition is always satisfied.

blocks.html: 6. Faithful functors and conservative functors

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 6.1

Let \(E\) be a category, \((\varphi_i : E \to F_i)_{i\in I}\) a family of functors \[ \varphi_i : E \to F_i . \] The family of functors \((\varphi_i)\) is said to be faithful if for every pair of objects \(X, Y\) of \(E\), and every pair of arrows \(u, v : X \rightrightarrows Y\), the relation \(\varphi_i(u) = \varphi_i(v)\) for every \(i \in I\) implies \(u = v\) (in other words, if the map \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,Y) \to \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi_i(X), \varphi_i(Y))\) defined by \((\varphi_i)\) is injective). The family of functors \((\varphi_i)\) is said to be conservative if every arrow \(u\) of \(E\), such that \(\varphi_i(u)\) is an isomorphism for every \(i \in I\), is an isomorphism. One says that \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative for monomorphisms (resp. for epimorphisms, resp. ....) if the preceding condition is satisfied whenever \(u\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism, resp. ....).

If one introduces the unique functor \[ \varphi : E \to F = \prod_{i\in I} F_i \] defined by the family of functors \((\varphi_i)\), it is clear that the latter is faithful (resp. conservative, resp. conservative for monomorphisms, resp. ...) if and only if the functor \(\varphi\) is faithful (resp. conservative, resp. ...) (by which one means that the family reduced to the single object \(\varphi\) is faithful, resp. conservative, resp. ...). One could therefore, without major inconvenience, restrict ourselves in what follows to the case of a family reduced to a single functor. For the convenience of future references, we shall nevertheless give the following statements for families.
The notions of 6.1 are especially useful when the \(\varphi_i\) satisfy suitable exactness properties, and in this case they tend to coincide:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.2

The notations are those of 6.1.

(i) If the kernels of double arrows, or the cokernels of double arrows, are representable in \(E\), and if the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them, then one has the implication \[ (\varphi_i) \text{ conservative} \implies (\varphi_i) \text{ faithful} . \]

(ii) Suppose that the fibre products (resp. the amalgamated sums) are representable in \(E\), and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them. Suppose \((\varphi_i)\) faithful or conservative; then for every arrow \(u\) of \(E\), \(u\) is a monomorphism (resp. an epimorphism) if and only if for every \(i \in I\), the same holds for \(\varphi_i(u)\).

(iii) Suppose that in \(E\) the fibre products and the amalgamated sums are representable and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them, and that every arrow in \(E\) that is a bimorphism (i.e. a monomorphism and an epimorphism) is an isomorphism. Then one has the implication \[ (\varphi_i) \text{ faithful} \implies (\varphi_i) \text{ conservative} . \]

(iv) Suppose that in \(E\) the fibre products (resp. the amalgamated sums) are representable, and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them. Then, if \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative for monomorphisms (resp. for epimorphisms) then \((\varphi_i)\) is even conservative.

(v) Let \(D\) be a type of diagram, \(F : d \mapsto F(d)\) a diagram of type \(D\) in \(E\), \(X\) an object of \(E\) and \(u = (u_d)_{d\in D}\) a family of arrows \[ X \to F(d) \qquad (\text{resp. } F(d) \to X) . \] Suppose that \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative, that the projective (resp. inductive) limits of type \(D\) are representable in \(E\), and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them. Then, for \(u\) to make \(X\) a projective (resp. inductive) limit of \(F\) in \(E\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in I\), \(\varphi_i(u)\) make \(\varphi_i(X)\) a projective (resp. inductive) limit of \(\varphi_i(F)\) in \(F_i\).

Proof. (i) For the non-resp. statement, it suffices, for a given double arrow \(u, v : X \rightrightarrows Y\), to express the equality \(u = v\) by the condition that the inclusion \(\mathrm{Ker}(u,v) \to X\) is an isomorphism. Here and in what follows, we dispense with repeating the dual argument for the dual statement.

(ii) If \((\varphi_i)\) is faithful, one expresses the condition that \(u : X \to Y\) be a monomorphism by the equality \(\mathrm{pr}_1 = \mathrm{pr}_2\) for the fibre product \(X \times_Y X\). If \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative, one expresses it by the condition that the diagonal morphism \(\delta : X \to X \times_Y X\) be an isomorphism.

(iv) As in this last argument, one sees that it in fact sufficed to suppose \((\varphi_i)\) conservative for monomorphisms. But this then implies that \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative outright. Indeed, if \(u \in \mathrm{fl}\, E\) is such that \(\varphi_i(u)\) are isomorphisms, one concludes that they are monomorphisms by what precedes, hence isomorphisms by the hypothesis on \((\varphi_i)\).
(iii) Is a trivial consequence of (ii).
(v) Is a trivial consequence of the definitions.
Let us note the following consequence of (i) (ii) (iv):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 6.3

Suppose that in \(E\) the fibre products and the amalgamated sums are representable and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them, and that the kernels of double arrows or the cokernels of double arrows are representable and that the \(\varphi_i\) commute with them. (It suffices, for example, that the finite projective limits and the finite inductive limits be representable in \(E\), and that the \(\varphi_i\) be exact functors.) Then the following conditions are equivalent:

a) \((\varphi_i)\) is faithful.

b) \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative.

c) \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative for monomorphisms.

c') \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative for epimorphisms.
Let us also mention, for the record:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.4

Let \(\varphi : E \to F\) be a functor admitting a right adjoint \(\psi\) (hence \(\mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X),Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(X,\psi(Y))\)). For \(\varphi\) (resp. \(\psi\)) to be faithful, it is necessary and sufficient that for every element \(X\) of \(E\) (resp. every element \(Y\) of \(F\)), the adjunction morphism \(X \to \psi\varphi(X)\) be a monomorphism. For \(\varphi\) (resp. \(\psi\)) to be fully faithful, it is necessary and sufficient that the preceding adjunction morphism be an isomorphism.

Indeed, if \(X', X\) are two objects of \(E\), the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X',X) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X'),\varphi(X)) \tag{\(*\)} \] is identified with the map deduced from \[ X \to \psi\varphi(X) \tag{\(**\)} \] by application of the functor \(\mathrm{Hom}(X',-)\). Hence for \((*)\) to be a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism) for every \(X'\), \(X\) being fixed, it is necessary and sufficient that the adjunction morphism \((**)\) be a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6.5

Let \(p : E' \to E\) be a functor. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(p\) is faithful, conservative and fibrant (SGA 1 VI 6.1).

(ii) \(p\) is a fibrant functor whose fibres are discrete categories.

(iii) For every \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, E'\), the functor \(E'_{/X'} \to E_{/p(X')}\) induced by \(p\) is an equivalence of categories, surjective on objects.

(iv) (When \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category). There exists an element \(F \in \mathrm{ob}\, \widehat{E}\) and an equivalence of categories over \(E\) (SGA 1 VI 4.3) \[ E' \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } E_{/F} \] (where \(E_{/F}\) is the full subcategory of \(\widehat{E}_{/F}\) formed of the arrows \(X \to F\) whose source is in \(E\)).

Recall that a category \(C\) is said to be discrete if it is a groupoid (i.e. every arrow in it is invertible) and if it is rigid (i.e. the group of automorphisms of every object is reduced to the trivial group); it amounts to the same to say that the category is equivalent to the category \(C'\) defined by a set \(I\) (with \(\mathrm{ob}\, C' = I\), and as sole arrows the identity arrows). When one already supposes that \(C\) is a groupoid, then to say that \(C\) is discrete amounts to saying that for two objects \(X, Y\) of \(C\), there exists at most one arrow from \(X\) to \(Y\), i.e. that \(C\) is isomorphic to the category defined by a preordered set.
The equivalence of conditions (i) and (ii) of 6.5 is an immediate consequence of the preceding reminders and of the following.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 6.5.2

Let \(p : E' \to E\) be a fibrant functor. Then:

(i) For \(p\) to be conservative, it is necessary and sufficient that its fibre categories be groupoids.

(ii) For \(p\) to be faithful, it is necessary and sufficient that its fibre categories be ordered categories.

Proof of 6.5.2. (i) Suppose \(p\) conservative. For every arrow \(u\) of a fibre \(E'_X\), \(p(u) = \mathrm{id}_X\) is an isomorphism, hence \(u\) is an isomorphism in \(E'\), hence also in \(E'_X\) (since an inverse of \(u\) in \(E'\) will obviously be an inverse in \(E'_X\)). Hence \(E'_X\) is a groupoid. Conversely, suppose the \(E'_X\) are groupoids, and let \(u'\) be an arrow of \(E'\) such that \(p(u')\) is an isomorphism; let us prove that \(u\) is an isomorphism. For this one notes that, \(p\) being fibrant, one can factor \(u' : X' \to Y'\) into a composite \(X' \to u^*(Y') \to Y'\), where the first arrow is an \(X\)-morphism (NB \(X = p(X')\), \(u = p(u')\)) and the second is a cartesian morphism over \(u\). The first arrow is an isomorphism since \(E'_X\) is a groupoid, and the second is one, since a cartesian morphism of a fibred category is obviously an isomorphism as soon as its projection is.

(ii) Suppose \(p\) faithful, and let \(X', Y'\) be two objects of a fibre category \(E'_X\). Then two arrows from \(X'\) to \(Y'\) are over the same arrow \(\mathrm{id}_X\) of \(E\), hence are identical, hence \(E'_X\) is ordered.

Conversely, suppose the fibre categories ordered, and let us prove that \(p\) is faithful. Let then \(u', v' : X' \rightrightarrows Y'\) be arrows of \(E'\) over one and the same arrow \(u : X \to Y\) of \(E\). They then factor into \(X' \rightrightarrows u^*(Y') \to Y'\), where the two arrows \(X' \rightrightarrows u^*(Y')\) are arrows of \(E'_X\) with the same source and the same target; these are therefore equal, hence \(u' = v'\), q.e.d.

Let us return to the proof of 6.5. We have proved (i) ⟺ (ii). On the other hand (ii) ⟺ (iv) is quite clear: indeed, on the one hand the category \(E_{/F}\) is fibred over \(E\) with fibre categories the discrete categories defined by the sets \(F(X)\), as follows at once from the definitions; on the other hand, if \(p\) is as in (ii), then by virtue of the sorites SGA 1 VI 8 the category \(E'\) fibred over \(E\) is \(E\)-equivalent to the split category over \(E\) defined by the functor \(E \to (\mathrm{Cat})\) defined by the functor \(F : E \to (\mathrm{Ens})\), associating to every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) the set of isomorphism classes of objects of \(E'_X\). But this split category is \(E\)-isomorphic to the category \(E_{/F}\). Since (iv) ⟹ (iii) is clear, it remains to prove (iii) ⟹ (i). Now it is clear that for \(p\) to be faithful (resp. conservative) it is necessary and sufficient that the induced functors \(E'_{/X'} \to E_{/p(X')}\) be so, a fortiori it suffices that these be fully faithful; hence it remains only to prove that (iii) implies that \(p\) is fibrant. But one sees again that a functor \(p\) is fibrant if and only if the induced functors \(E'_{/X'} \to E_{/p(X')}\) are so. This is in particular the case if these are equivalences of categories surjective on objects.
7. Generating and cogenerating subcategories

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 7.1

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\). One says that \(C\) is a subcategory of \(E\) generating by strict epimorphisms (resp. by epimorphisms) if for every object \(X\) of \(E\), the family of arrows of \(E\) with target \(X\), with source \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), is epimorphic (resp. strictly epimorphic) (1.3). One says that \(C\) is a generating subcategory of \(E\) (resp. generating for monomorphisms, resp. generating for strict monomorphisms) if for every arrow \(u : Y \to X\) (resp. every monomorphism of \(E\), resp. every strict monomorphism of \(E\) (10.5)), such that for every \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the corresponding map \(\mathrm{Hom}(X',Y) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X',X)\) is bijective, \(u\) is an isomorphism. Finally, one says that a family \((X_i)\) of objects of \(E\) is generating by strict epimorphisms (resp. .....) if the full subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) generated by this family is generating by strict epimorphisms (resp. .....).

Note that in terms of the family \((h_{X'})_{X'\in\mathrm{ob}\, C}\) of functors \[ h_{X'} : E \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \qquad (X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C) \] represented by the \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), one can express the condition that \(C\) be generating (resp. generating for monomorphisms, resp. generating for strict monomorphisms) by the condition that the family \((h_{X'})\) be conservative (resp. conservative for monomorphisms, resp. conservative for strict monomorphisms) (6.1). It also follows immediately from the definitions that \(C\) is generating by epimorphisms if and only if the family \((h_{X'})_{X'\in\mathrm{ob}\, C}\) is faithful (6.1). We shall also give below (7.2 (i)) an analogous interpretation for the condition on \(C\) of being generating by strict epimorphisms.

As with the notions introduced in 6.1, the notions of 7.1 are especially useful when \(E\) possesses suitable exactness properties, in which case the various notions introduced have a marked tendency to be all equivalent (7.3). This is why the question of which of these notions 7.1 should be regarded as the most important scarcely arises; in the most important cases, these notions coincide, and the term "generating subcategory" may therefore be interpreted indifferently as referring to any one of the properties considered in 7.1 (for example the first, which is the strongest of all, as we shall see (7.2 (ii))).

Suppose that \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and consider the canonical functor \[ \varphi : E \to \widehat{C} = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C^\circ, \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}) \tag{7.1.3.1} \] composed of the functors \(E \to \widehat{E} \to \widehat{C}\), where the first functor is the canonical functor (1.3.3), and the second the restriction functor to \(C\). Note that it is obvious that it amounts to the same to say that the preceding functor \(\varphi\) is conservative (resp. faithful), or to say that the family of functors \(h_{X'} : X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(X',X) = \varphi(X)(X')\), for variable \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), is a conservative (resp. faithful) family, that is to say also (7.1.2) that \(C\) is generating (resp. generating by epimorphisms). Likewise \(\varphi\) is conservative for monomorphisms (resp. for strict monomorphisms) if and only if the family of \(h_{X'}\) (\(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\)) is conservative for monomorphisms (resp. for strict monomorphisms), i.e. if and only if the subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) is generating for monomorphisms (resp. for strict monomorphisms).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.2

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(C\) a full subcategory.

(i) The following conditions are equivalent:

a) \(C\) is a subcategory generating by strict epimorphisms.

b) For every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), denoting by \(C_{/X}\) the full subcategory of \(E_{/X}\) formed by the arrows \(X' \to X\) with source \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the natural arrow from the inclusion functor \(j : C_{/X} \to E\) to the constant functor on \(C_{/X}\) with value \(X\) makes \(X\) an inductive limit of \(j\): \[ X \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} X' . \]

c) The canonical functor \(\varphi\) of (7.1.3.1) is fully faithful.

(ii) One has the following implications between the notions of 7.1:

1) \(C\) generating by strict epim. (\(\varphi\) fully faithful)

2) \(C\) generating by epimorphisms (\(\varphi\) faithful)

3) \(C\) generating (\(\varphi\) conservative)

4) \(C\) generating for monomorphisms (\(\varphi\) conservative for mon.)

5) \(C\) generating for strict mon. (\(\varphi\) conservative for strict mon.)

\[ \xymatrix@R=1.2em@C=3em{ 1) \ar@{=>}[dr] & \\ 2) & 3) \ar@{=>}[d] \\ & 4) \ar@{=>}[d] \\ & 5) } \]

(iii) One has the following conditional implications:

a) If in \(E\) the epimorphic families of arrows are strict epimorphic, one has 2) ⟹ 1). If in \(E\) the monomorphisms are strict, one has 5) ⟹ 4).

b) If in \(E\) the kernels of pairs of arrows (resp. the fibre products) are representable, then one has 3) ⟹ 2) (resp. 4) ⟹ 3)).

c) If in \(E\) every family of morphisms \(X_i \to X\) with the same target \(X\) factors as a strict epimorphic (resp. epimorphic) family \(X_i \to Y\) followed by a monomorphism (resp. a strict monomorphism) \(Y \to X\), then one has 4) ⟹ 1) (resp. 5) ⟹ 2)).
Let us point out at once the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.3

All the notions considered in 6.1 (and taken up again in the implication diagram of (ii) above) are equivalent in each of the two following cases:

(i) In \(E\), the kernels of double arrows and the fibre products are representable, the monomorphisms are strict and the epimorphic families of arrows are strict epimorphic.

(ii) In \(E\), every family \((X_i \to X)_{i\in I}\) of arrows with the same target \(X\) factors as an epimorphic family \((X_i \to Y)\) followed by a monomorphism \(Y \to X\), every monomorphism of \(E\) is strict, and every epimorphic family of arrows of \(E\) is strict.

Indeed, in case (i) one has 4) ⟹ 3) and 3) ⟹ 2) thanks to b), and 5) ⟹ 4) and 2) ⟹ 1) thanks to a). In case (ii) one has, thanks to c), the implications 4) ⟹ 1) and 5) ⟹ 2). One therefore concludes thanks to the implication diagram 7.2 (ii).

Proof of 7.2. (i) The implication b) ⟹ a) follows at once from the definitions. Let us prove a) ⟹ b). So under hypothesis a), we must prove that for all \(X, Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), every system of arrows \[ u_{X'} : X' \to Y \] indexed by the \(X' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_{/X}\), such that \(u_{X'} f = u_{X''}\) for every arrow \(f : X'' \to X'\) in \(C_{/X}\), factors through an arrow (necessarily unique by hypothesis a)) \(X \to Y\). By hypothesis a), it suffices to check that for every object \(Z\) of \(E_{/X}\) and every pair of morphisms \(v' : Z \to X'\), \(v'' : Z \to X''\) in \(E_{/X}\), with \(X'\) and \(X''\) in \(C_{/X}\), one has \(u_{X'} v' = u_{X''} v''\). Now, thanks to hypothesis a), the family of arrows \(w : X''' \to Z\), with \(X''' \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), is epimorphic, and it therefore suffices to check that for every such \(w\), one has \((u_{X'} v')w = (u_{X''} v'')w\), which may also be written \(u_{X'}(v'w) = u_{X''}(v''w)\) and follows at once from the hypothesis made on the family of the \(u\).

Let us now prove the equivalence of conditions b) and c). For this let us note that for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), the object \(\varphi(X)\) of \(\widehat{C}\) is the inductive limit in \(\widehat{C}\) of the functor canonical \(\widehat{C}_{/\varphi(X)} \to \widehat{C}\) (3.4); now \(\widehat{C}_{/\varphi(X)}\) is canonically isomorphic to \(C_{/X}\), so that one has in \(\widehat{C}\) \[ \varphi(X) = \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} X', \] where one identifies the object \(X'\) of \(C\) with the functor \(\in \widehat{C}\) that it represents. Consequently, for a second object \(Y\) of \(E\), one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X),\varphi(Y)) &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C_{/X}} \mathrm{Hom}(X',\varphi(Y)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C_{/X}} \varphi(Y)(X') \quad (1.4) \\ &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{C_{/X}} \mathrm{Hom}(X',Y) . \end{aligned} \tag{\(*\)} \] This being so, the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X),\varphi(Y)) \] defined by \(\varphi\) is none other, via the isomorphism between the outer terms of \((*)\), than the map \[ \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y) \to \varprojlim_{C_{/X}} \mathrm{Hom}(X',Y) \] deduced from the inductive system of arrows \(X' \to X\) indexed by \(C_{/X}\) considered in 7.2 (i) b). Thus the first map is bijective for every \(Y\) (\(X\) being fixed) if and only if \(X\) is an inductive limit of the inclusion functor \(j : C_{/X} \to E\), which proves the equivalence of b) and c).

(ii) The implications 1) ⟹ 2) and 3) ⟹ 4) ⟹ 5) are trivial by virtue of the definitions. The implication 1) ⟹ 3) is obtained by interpreting property 1) via the full faithfulness of \(\varphi\) thanks to (i), and by observing that a fully faithful functor is conservative. Now we have already observed (7.1.1) that 3) means that \(\varphi\) is conservative.
