(iii) Assertion a) is a tautology. Assertion b) follows from 6.2 (i) (resp. 6.2 (iv)) applied to the functor \(\varphi\), taking into account that the latter is left exact. Let us finally prove c). Consider, for an \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), the family of all the morphisms \(X_i \to X\), with \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\); by the hypothesis on \(E\) it factors as an effective epimorphic (resp. epimorphic) family \(X_i \to Y\) followed by a monomorphism (resp. a strict monomorphism) \(Y \to X\). Then hypothesis 4) (resp. 5)) implies that \(Y \to X\) is an isomorphism, so the family considered is strict epimorphic (resp. epimorphic), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.4

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\), \(X\) an object of \(E\). Suppose \(C\) generating in \(E\) (resp. \(C\) generating for monomorphisms, and that the fibre product of two subobjects of \(X\) over \(X\) is representable in \(E\)). Then a strict subobject (10.11) (resp. a subobject) \(X'\) of \(X\) is known once one knows, for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the part of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)\) that is the image of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\). Consequently, the cardinal of the set of strict subobjects (resp. of the set of subobjects) of \(X\) is bounded above by \(\prod_{T\in\mathrm{ob}\, C} 2^{\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)}\), and if \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), it is bounded above by \(2^{\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Fl}\, C}\).

Let us first prove the resp. assertion. Let \(X', X''\) be two subobjects of \(X\) such that for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the images of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\) and \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X'')\) in \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)\) are equal. They are therefore also equal to the image of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X''')\), where \(X'''\) is the fibre product of \(X'\) and \(X''\) over \(X\). Since \(C\) is generating for monomorphisms, it follows that the monomorphisms \(X''' \to X'\) and \(X''' \to X''\) are isomorphisms, so \(X'\) and \(X''\) are equal, being separately equal to the subobject \(X'''\) of \(X\).

Let us prove the non-resp. assertion. By definition of the notion of strict subobject, it suffices to check that knowledge of the part \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\) of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)\) for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) implies knowledge of those double arrows \(X \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} T\) such that \(ui = vi\), where \(i : X' \to X\) is the canonical injection. Now since \(C\) is generating, the relation \(ui = vi\) is equivalent to the relation \((ui)f = (vi)f\) for every \(f \in \mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\), i.e. to \(ug = vg\) for every \(g \in \mathrm{Hom}(T,X)\) coming from \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\) (i.e. of the form \(if\), with \(f \in \mathrm{Hom}(T,X')\)), which proves our assertion.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.5

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full generating subcategory, \(X\) an object of \(C\). Then a strict quotient (10.8) \(X'\) of \(X\) is known once one knows, for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the part of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)^2\) formed by the pairs \((u,v)\) such that \(qu = qv\), where \(q : X \to X'\) is the canonical morphism. Hence the cardinal of the set of strict quotients of \(X\) is bounded above by \(\prod_{T\in\mathrm{ob}\, C} 2^{\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)^2}\).

Indeed, by definition, a strict quotient \(X'\) of \(X\) is known once one knows, for every object \(Y\) of \(E\), the part of \(\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)\times\mathrm{Hom}(Y,X)\) formed by the pairs \((u,v)\) such that \(qu = qv\), where \(q : X \to X'\) is the canonical morphism. Now the relation \(qu = qv\) is equivalent to the relation \((qu)f = (qv)f\) for every morphism \(f : T \to Y\) with source \(T\) in \(C\), since \(C\) is generating. This relation may again be written \(q(uf) = q(vf)\), which proves the first assertion of 7.5. The second follows from it at once.

One can generalize 7.5 by introducing, for a family of objects \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(E\), the notion of strict quotient in \(E\) of the family, by which one means a family strict epimorphic \((p_i : X_i \to X')_{i\in I}\) of morphisms of \(E\), — it being understood, as for ordinary quotients, that two such families \((p_i : X_i \to X')\) and \((q_i : X_i \to X'')\) are identified if one can find an isomorphism \(v : X' \to X''\) (necessarily unique) such that \(v p_i = q_i\) for every \(i \in I\). With this terminology, the proof of 7.5 applies ne varietur to give the

blocks.title: Variant
blocks.html:
Variant 7.5.2

Let \(E, C\) be as in 7.5, and \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) a family of objects of \(E\). Then a strict quotient \(X'\) of \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(E\) (7.5.1) is known once one knows, for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), and every pair \((i,j) \in I\times I\), the part of \(\mathrm{Hom}(T,X_i)\times\mathrm{Hom}(T,X_j)\) formed by the pairs \((u,v)\) such that \(p_i u = p_j v\), where for every \(i \in I\), \(p_i : X_i \to X'\) denotes the canonical morphism. Consequently, the cardinal of the set of strict quotients of \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(E\) is bounded above by \(\prod_{T\in\mathrm{ob}\, C} \prod_{i,j\in I} 2^{\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X_i)\times\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X_j)}\).

One sees at once that the analogous conclusion holds if one supposes only that \(C\) is generating for strict monomorphisms, provided one supposes that the products \(X_i \times X_j\) are representable and that one restricts to the effective quotients of the family \((X_i)_{i\in I}\), i.e. to the strict quotients \(X'\) such that the fibre products \(X_i \times_X X_j\) are representable in \(E\) (which is not a restriction if \(E\) is stable under fibre products).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.6

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\) generating by epimorphisms (7.1), \(\pi_0\) an infinite cardinal \(\geq \mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Fl}\, C\), \(\pi \geq \pi_0\) a cardinal, \((u_i : X_i \to X)_{i\in I}\) a universal epimorphic family (10.3) in \(E\) formed of squarable morphisms (10.7) with sources \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), and such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\). Then \(\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Fl}\, C_{/X} \leq \pi^{\pi_0}\).

Let \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\); it will suffice to prove that one has \[ \mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X) \leq \pi^{\pi_0}, \tag{7.6.1} \] for from this one will conclude successively \[ \mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{ob}\, C_{/X} \leq (\pi^{\pi_0}) \times \mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{ob}\, C \leq (\pi^{\pi_0})\times\pi_0 = \pi^{\pi_0}, \] finally \[ \mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Fl}\, C_{/X} \leq ((\pi^{\pi_0})^2)\times\pi_0 = \pi^{\pi_0}, \] since for two objects \(S, T\) of \(C_{/X}\), one has \(\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}_{C_{/X}}(S,T) \leq \pi_0\) because \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(S,T) \leq \pi_0\). To prove 7.6.1, let us first note the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 7.6.2

Let \(J\) be a set such that \(\mathrm{card}\, J = \pi_0\). For every object \(T\) of \(C\), and every homomorphism \(f : T \to X\), there exists an epimorphic family \((v_j : S_j \to T)_{j\in J}\), with sources \(S_j \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), and for every \(j \in J\) an \(i(j) \in I\) and a \(g_j : S_j \to X_{i(j)}\) such that \(u_{i(j)} g_j = f v_j\).

Indeed, the family of the \(X_i \times_X T \to T\) is epimorphic by hypothesis; on the other hand, since \(C\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, for every \(i\), the family of arrows \(S \to X_i \times_X T\) with source \(S \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) is epimorphic, so by transitivity the family of arrows \(v : S \to T\) with source in \(\mathrm{ob}\, C\) that factor through one of the \(X_i \times_X T\) is epimorphic. Now these are the arrows \(v : S \to T\) with source in \(C\) for which there exist an \(i \in I\) and a \(g : S \to X_i\) such that \(u_i g = fv\). Since the set of these arrows \(v : S \to T\) is contained in \(\mathrm{Fl}\, C\), hence of cardinal \(\leq \pi_0\), it can be indexed by the index set \(J\), whence the lemma.

Let us now note that a morphism \(f : T \to X\) is known once one knows the \(f v_j\), which are known once one knows the \(g_j\). Thus \(\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{Hom}(T,X)\) is bounded above by the cardinal of the set of families \((i(j), S_j, v_j, g_j)_{j\in J}\); since the cardinal of the set of maps \(j \to I\) is \(\leq \pi^{\pi_0}\), and since for such a fixed map \(j \mapsto i(j)\), the cardinal of the set of corresponding families \(S_j, f_j, v_j\) is bounded above by that of the set of maps from \(J\) to \(\mathrm{Fl}\, C \times \mathrm{Fl}\, C\), which is \(\leq \pi_0^{\pi_0}\) since \(\mathrm{card}(\mathrm{Fl}\, C \times \mathrm{Fl}\, C) = \pi_0^2 = \pi_0\), one finds that the left-hand side of (7.6.1) is bounded above by \(\pi^{\pi_0} \times \pi_0^{\pi_0} = \pi^{\pi_0}\), which completes the proof of 7.6.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.7

Let \(E\) be a category in which the fibre products are representable, \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\) a generating family of objects of \(E\), \((\varphi_i)_{i\in I}\) a family of functors \(\varphi_i : E \to E_i\) commuting with fibre products. For \((\varphi_i)\) to be conservative (6.1), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(\alpha \in A\) and for every subobject \(X'\) of \(X_\alpha\) distinct from \(X_\alpha\), there exist an \(i \in I\) such that \(\varphi_i(X') \to \varphi_i(X_\alpha)\) is not an isomorphism. In this case, if \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category and if \(A\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, there exists a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small part \(J\) of \(I\) such that \((\varphi_j)_{j\in J}\) is already a conservative family of functors.

The necessity of the conservativity condition considered being obvious, let us prove its sufficiency. By virtue of 6.1 (iv), it suffices to prove that \((\varphi_i)\) is conservative for the monomorphisms. Let \(u : Y' \to Y\) be a monomorphism in \(E\) that is not an isomorphism; we must prove that there exists \(i \in I\) such that \(\varphi_i(u)\) is not an isomorphism. By the hypothesis on \((X_\alpha)\), there exist an \(\alpha\) and a morphism \(X_\alpha \to Y\) that does not factor through \(Y'\), in other words, such that the inverse image \(X'\) of \(Y'\) is a subobject of \(X_\alpha\) distinct from \(X_\alpha\). By hypothesis, there exists an \(i \in I\) such that \(\varphi_i(X') \to \varphi_i(X_\alpha)\) is not an isomorphism. Since \(\varphi_i(X') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varphi_i(X_\alpha) \underset{\varphi_i(Y)}{\times} \varphi_i(Y')\), it indeed follows that \(\varphi_i(Y') \to \varphi_i(Y)\) is not an isomorphism.
The second assertion of 7.7 follows at once from the first, taking 7.4 into account.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.7.1

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which the fibre products are representable, and admitting a generating family of objects that is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small. Then for every generating family \((Y_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(E\), there exists a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small generating subfamily \((Y_j)_{j\in J}\) (\(\mathrm{card}\, J \in \mathcal{U}\)).

Indeed, it suffices to apply 7.7 to the \(\mathcal{U}\)-small generating family \((X_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\) of \(E\) and to the family of functors \(\varphi_i\) (\(i \in I\)) represented by the \(Y_i\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.8

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full subcategory generating by strict epimorphisms, \(D\) a category, \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}'(E,D)\) the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,D)\) formed of the functors that commute with the inductive limits of type \(C_{/X}\), where \(X\) is an arbitrary object of \(E\). Then the functor \(F \mapsto F|C\) induces a fully faithful functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}'(E,D) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,D) . \]

Consequently, if \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,D)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category (1.1.), for example (1.1.1. b)) if \(C\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small and \(D\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, then \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,D)\) is likewise a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

Let \(F, G : E \to D\) be two functors in the left-hand side, and \(u : F \to G\) a homomorphism. If \(X = \varinjlim X_i\) in \(E\) and if \(F\) and \(G\) commute with the inductive limit considered, then \(u(X) : F(X) \to G(X)\) is identified with the limit of the morphisms \(u(X_i) : F(X_i) \to G(X_i)\), and is therefore known once one knows the \(u(X_i)\). This shows that the functor considered in 7.8 is faithful, taking into account the implication a) ⟹ b) in 7.2 (i). Conversely, let \(v : F|C \to G|C\) be a homomorphism; let us prove that it comes from a homomorphism \(u : F \to G\). One defines, for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), \[ u(X) : F(X) = \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} F(X_i) \to G(X) = \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} G(X_i) \] as the inductive limit of the \(v(X_i)\). It is immediate that one indeed obtains a homomorphism functorial in \(X\), hence a \(u : F \to G\), and finally that the morphism induced by \(u\) from \(F|C\) to \(G|C\) is \(v\), which completes the proof.
7.9. Cogenerating families and subcategories.

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\). One says that \(C\) is cogenerating by strict monomorphisms (resp. cogenerating by monomorphisms, resp. cogenerating, resp. cogenerating for epimorphisms, resp. cogenerating for strict epimorphisms) if the full subcategory \(C^\circ\) of \(E^\circ\) is generating by strict epimorphisms (resp. .....). Analogous terminology for families. All the results of the present section concerning the notion of generating subcategory and its variants (7.1) thus yield corresponding results for the dual notions, which we leave to the reader to formulate for their personal satisfaction.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7.10

Let \(E\) be a category, \(C\) a full generating subcategory (7.1), \(D\) a full subcategory of \(E\). For \(D\) to be cogenerating (7.9), it is necessary and sufficient that for every double arrow \(T \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} X\) in \(E\) with source \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), with \(u \neq v\), there exist an arrow \(w : X \to I\) with target \(I \in \mathrm{ob}\, D\), such that \(wu \neq wv\).

By definition, to say that \(D\) is cogenerating means that for every double arrow \(Y \underset{v}{\overset{u}{ ightrightarrows}} X\) in \(E\) such that \(u eq v\), there exists an arrow \(w : X o I\), with \(I \in \mathrm{ob}\, D\), such that \(wu eq wv\). Thus 7.10 means simply that it suffices to test this property when \(Y \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). Now since \(C\) is generating, the hypothesis \(u eq v\) implies that there exists \(f : T o Y\) such that \(uf eq vf\), whence by hypothesis the existence of a \(w : X o I\) with target \(I \in \mathrm{ob}\, D\) such that \(w(uf) eq w(vf)\), whence \(wu eq wv\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.11

The notations being those of 7.10, suppose that the objects \(I\) of \(D\) are injective objects of \(E\), i.e. such that for every monomorphism \(X \to Y\) in \(E\), the corresponding map \(\mathrm{Hom}(Y,I) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X,I)\) is surjective. Suppose moreover that every double arrow \(T \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} X\) in \(E\) factors as an epimorphic (resp. effective epimorphic) double arrow \(T \underset{v'}{\overset{u'}{\rightrightarrows}} X'\) followed by a monomorphism \(i : X' \to X\). Then in criterion 7.10 for \(D\) to be cogenerating, one may restrict to the double arrows \((u,v)\) that are epimorphic (resp. effective epimorphic).
One concludes from this:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 7.12

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category admitting a small generating subcategory \(C\), and such that every object of \(E\) is the source of a monomorphism into an object injective of \(E\). Suppose moreover that for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\), the sum \(T \sqcup T\) in \(E\) is representable, and that every morphism with source \(T \sqcup T\) factors as an epimorphism effective followed by a monomorphism. Then \(E\) admits a full cogenerating subcategory \(D\). More precisely, one can take \(D\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{ob}\, D \leq \prod_{T,T'\in\mathrm{ob}\, C} 2^{\mathrm{card}(\mathrm{Hom}(T',T\sqcup T))^2}\).

Indeed, by virtue of 7.11, it suffices, for every \(T \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) and for every effective quotient \(X\) of \(T \sqcup T\), to choose an embedding of \(X\) into an injective object \(I\) of \(E\), and to take for \(D\) the full subcategory of \(E\) generated by these \(I\). The conclusion then follows from 7.5.

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 7.13

To construct small cogenerating subcategories in terms of small generating subcategories, one is thus led to seek conditions for a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(E\) to admit "enough injectives", i.e. for every object to embed into an injective object (by a monomorphism). It is well known [Tohoku] that this condition is satisfied in an abelian \(\mathcal{U}\)-category with exact (small) filtered inductive limits (axiom AB 5 of loc. cit.) admitting a small generating family. The construction of loc. cit. is moreover not essentially tied to abelian categories, and works equally in the category of sheaves of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets on a topological space \(X \in \mathcal{U}\). We shall not state here the exactness properties that make the construction in question work, and shall confine ourselves to pointing out that in the particular case of the category of sheaves of sets on \(X\), one reduces immediately to the case of loc. cit. in the following way. One notes that if \(\mathcal{O}_X\) is a Ring on \(X\), then every injective object \(I\) of the category of \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-Modules is also injective as an object of the category of sheaves of sets. Indeed, if \(F\) is a sheaf of sets, and \(\mathcal{O}_X[F]\) the "free \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-Module generated by \(F\)", one has by definition a homomorphism of sheaves of sets \[ F \to \mathcal{O}_X[F] \tag{\(*\)} \] giving rise to an isomorphism, functorial in \(F\) \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{O}_X}(\mathcal{O}_X[F], I) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}(F,I) . \] Since the functor \(F \mapsto \mathcal{O}_X[F]\) manifestly transforms monomorphisms into monomorphisms, it follows at once that if \(I\) is an injective \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-Module, it is also an injective sheaf of sets. It follows that if the morphism \((*)\) is a monomorphism (which is the case if one takes for \(\mathcal{O}_X\) a constant Ring with value a ring \(A \neq 0\)), then an embedding of \(\mathcal{O}_X[F]\) into an injective \(\mathcal{O}_X\)-Module \(I\) gives an embedding of \(F\) into the injective sheaf of sets underlying \(I\).

The same argument applies, without change, to the case of the category of sheaves of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sets on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site, which will be introduced in the following exposé.

The interest of the existence of a small cogenerating subcategory lies above all in the representability criterion 3.12.7 below.
8. Ind-objects and pro-objects
8.1. Cofinal functors and cofinal subcategories

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.1

Let \[ \varphi : I \to I' \tag{8.1.1.1} \] be a functor. One says that \(\varphi\) is a cofinal functor if for every category \(C\) and for every functor \(u : I' \to C\), regarding \(\varinjlim u\) and \(\varinjlim u\circ\varphi\) as objects of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C, (\mathcal{V}\text{-Ens}))^\circ\) (2.1, 2.3.1) (where \(\mathcal{V}\) is a universe such that \(I, I' \in \mathcal{V}\), and such that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{V}\)-category), the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim u\circ\varphi \to \varinjlim u \tag{8.1.1.2} \] is an isomorphism. When \(\varphi\) is the inclusion functor of a subcategory of \(I'\), one says that \(I\) is a cofinal subcategory if \(\varphi\) is cofinal.
Let us remark that for given \(\varphi, u\), the bijectivity of (8.1.1.2) does not depend on the choice of the universe \(\mathcal{V}\).

Returning to the definition of the terms appearing in (8.1.1.2) (2.1, 2.3.1), one sees that to say that \(\varphi\) is cofinal also means that for every universe \(\mathcal{V}\) such that \(I\) and \(I'\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, and every functor \[ v : I'^\circ \to (\mathcal{V}\text{-Ens}) , \] the canonical homomorphism \[ \varprojlim v \to \varprojlim v\circ\varphi \tag{8.1.2.1} \] is an isomorphism i.e. a bijection. To see that this condition is indeed necessary, one observes, setting \(u = v^\circ\), that it also means that the condition of definition 8.1.1 is satisfied when one takes \(C = (\mathcal{V}\text{-Ens})^\circ\) there (which implies that the inductive limits considered in (8.1.1.2) are representable in \(C\)).
It is immediate from the definition that the composite of two cofinal functors is cofinal.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.3

Let \(\varphi : I \to I'\) be a functor.

a) For \(\varphi\) to be cofinal, it is necessary that \(\varphi\) satisfy the condition

F 1) For every object \(i'\) of \(I'\), there exists an object \(i\) of \(I\) such that \(\varphi(i)\) majorizes \(i'\) (i.e. such that \(\mathrm{Hom}(i',\varphi(i)) \neq \varnothing\)).

b) Suppose \(I\) filtered. For \(\varphi\) to be cofinal, it is necessary and sufficient that \(\varphi\) satisfy condition F 1) as well as the following condition:

F 2) For every object \(i\) of \(I\) and every double arrow \(i' \underset{g'}{\overset{f'}{\rightrightarrows}} \varphi(i)\) in \(I'\) with target \(\varphi(i)\), there exists an arrow \(h : i \to j\) in \(I\) such that \(\varphi(h)f' = \varphi(h)g'\).

Moreover, if \(\varphi\) is cofinal, \(I'\) is filtered.

c) Suppose \(I'\) filtered, and \(\varphi\) fully faithful. For \(\varphi\) to be cofinal, it is necessary and sufficient that it satisfy condition F 1) of a). This implies that \(I\) is filtered.

Proof. For the necessity in a) and b), one uses definition 8.1.1 in the sole case where \(u\) is the canonical inclusion functor (1.3.3) \[ u : I' \hookrightarrow \widehat{I'} \] (a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(I, I'\) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-small having been chosen). One can then interpret (8.1.1.2) as an arrow of \(\widehat{I'}\) (3.1), whose target is the final functor on \(I'\) (3.4). One sees immediately that condition F 1) expresses that this arrow is an epimorphism of \(\widehat{I'}\), i.e. is surjective on each argument (taking into account that the inductive limits in \(\widehat{I'}\) are computed "argument by argument"). This proves a). Now suppose \(I\) filtered and \(\varphi\) cofinal. Then \(I'\) is filtered: indeed, the condition that two objects of \(I'\) be majorized by a third follows at once from the same condition on \(I\), and from F 1), and it only remains to prove condition PS 2) of 2.7, i.e. that for every double arrow \[ f', g' : i' \rightrightarrows j' \] in \(I'\), there exists an arrow \(h' : j' \to k'\) of \(I'\) such that \(h'f' = h'g'\). Now by virtue of F 1) one can suppose \(k'\) of the form \(\varphi(i)\). But since by the hypothesis \(\varphi\) cofinal, for every object \(i'\) of \(I'\) \(\varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(i',\varphi(i))\) is the set reduced to one element, it follows from the standard description of filtered inductive limits in \((\mathrm{Ens})\) (2.8.1) that this implies the existence of an arrow \(h : i \to j\) in \(I\) such that \(\varphi(h)f' = \varphi(h)g'\). This therefore completes the proof that \(I'\) is filtered, and at the same time proves condition F 2).

To prove that the conditions stated in b) are sufficient for \(\varphi\) to be cofinal, one uses form 8.1.2 of the definition. One observes at once that condition F 1) implies that (8.1.2.1) is a monomorphism i.e. is injective on each argument, while condition F 2) (together with F 1)) ensures that it is bijective (taking into account the computation of projective limits in \(\widehat{I'^\circ}\) argument by argument). This therefore proves b).
Finally, if \(I'\) is filtered and \(\varphi\) fully faithful, then it is immediate that condition F 1) implies that \(I\) is filtered, and implies condition F 2). Thus c) follows from a) and b).

When \(I'\) is a filtered category, \(I\) a full subcategory of \(I'\), one thus sees by 8.1.3 c) that the condition that \(I\) be cofinal in \(I'\) depends only on the part \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I\) of the preordered set \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I'\) (for the preorder relation "\(x \leq y\)" ⟺ "\(\mathrm{Hom}(x,y) \neq \varnothing\)"). If \(J'\) is a preordered set, \(J\) a part of \(J'\), one will sometimes say that \(J\) is a cofinal part of \(J'\) when every element of \(J'\) is majorized by an element of \(J\). When \(J'\) is filtered, this therefore means that the inclusion functor \(J \hookrightarrow J'\) for the associated categories is cofinal.

In what follows, we shall use the notion of cofinal functor only in the cases where the categories \(I\) and \(I'\) are filtered. Classically, one even restricted oneself to categories associated with preordered sets (i.e. in which there exists at most one arrow with given source and target). It appears, however, that this restriction is troublesome in the applications, the "natural" filtered categories that arise in numerous applications not being ordered categories. The following result, due to P. DELIGNE, shows however that there is no essential difference between the two points of view:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.1.6

Let \(I\) be a small filtered category. Then there exists a small ordered set \(E\), and a cofinal functor \(\varphi : \underline{E} \to I\), where \(\underline{E}\) denotes the category associated with \(E\).

Suppose first that the preordered set \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I\) has no greatest element. Let us call subdiagram of \(I\) a pair \(D = (\underline{O}, F)\) formed of a part \(F\) of \(\mathrm{Fl}(I)\) and a part \(\underline{O}\) of \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I\), such that for every \(f \in F\), the source and target of \(f\) belong to \(\underline{O}\). An element \(e\) of \(\underline{O}\) is called final object of the subdiagram \(D\) if for every \(x \in \underline{O}\), the set \(\mathrm{Hom}(x,e) \cap F\) of arrows of \(D\) with source \(x\) and target \(e\) has exactly one element \(f_x\), if for every arrow \(g : x \to y\) of \(D\), one has \(f_x = f_y \circ g\), and if \(f_e = \mathrm{id}_e\). Let \(E\) be the set of finite subdiagrams \(D\) of \(I\) having a unique final element \(\varphi(D)\), and let us order \(E\) by inclusion. If \(D, D'\) are two elements of \(E\) and \(D \subset D'\), then there exists a unique arrow \(\varphi(D',D)\) of \(D'\) with source \(\varphi(D)\), with target \(\varphi(D')\), and if one has inclusions \(D \subset D' \subset D''\) in \(E\), one evidently has \(\varphi(D'',D) = \varphi(D'',D')\varphi(D',D)\); one also has \(\varphi(D,D) = \mathrm{id}_{\varphi(D)}\). One thus finds a functor \(\varphi : \underline{E} \to I\), and everything comes down to proving that \(E\) is filtered and that \(\varphi\) is cofinal. Taking 8.1.3 b) into account, one must make three verifications:

1) Condition F 1) of 8.1.3: for every \(i \in I\), one takes for \(D\) the subdiagram of \(I\) reduced to the object \(i\) and its identity arrow, then \(i \leq \varphi(D) = i\). This condition F 1) shows at the same time that \(E \neq \varnothing\).

2) Condition F 2): For every \(i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\), every \(D \in E\) and every double arrow \(i \rightrightarrows \varphi(D)\), find a diagram \(D' \in E\), containing \(D\), such that \(\varphi(D',D) : \varphi(D) \to \varphi(D')\) equalizes the double arrow. Now since \(I\) is filtered, there exists an object \(j\) of \(I\) and an arrow \(f : \varphi(D) \to j\) that equalizes the double arrow. Since \(I\) has no greatest element, one can suppose that \(j\) is a strict upper bound of \(\varphi(D)\), which implies that it is distinct from all the other objects of \(D\). Let then \(D'\) be the subdiagram of \(I\) whose set of objects is \(\underline{O} \cup \{j\}\), and whose set of arrows is formed of the arrows of \(D\), plus the composites \(x \xrightarrow{f_x} \varphi(D) \xrightarrow{f} j\), where \(x\) is an object of \(D\) and \(f_x\) is the unique arrow of \(D\) with source \(x\) and target \(\varphi(D)\), and \(\mathrm{id}_j\). It is then clear that \(D'\) is a finite subdiagram of \(I\), that it admits \(j\) as unique final object, so \(D' \in E\), and \(D'\) satisfies the desired condition.

3° Two subdiagrams \(D, D' \in E\) are contained in a common \(D'' \in E\). Indeed, one can find a strict upper bound \(j\) of \(\varphi(D)\) and of \(\varphi(D')\), \[ \xymatrix{ \varphi(D) \ar[dr]^-{f} & \\ & j \\ \varphi(D') \ar[ur]_-{f'} & } \] and one takes for \(D''\) the subdiagram whose set of objects is the union of the set of objects of \(D\), of \(D'\) and of \(\{j\}\), and whose set of arrows is the union of the set of arrows of \(D\), of \(D'\), of the set of composites \(f \circ f_x\) (\(x\) object of \(D\)) and \(f' \circ f'_{x'}\) (\(x'\) object of \(D'\)), and \(\{\mathrm{id}_j\}\). One thus indeed obtains a finite subdiagram of \(I\); let us show that, up to replacing \(j, f, f'\) by \(j', gf, gf'\) with a suitable \(g : j \to j'\), one can arrange for \(j\) to be a final object of \(D''\). It amounts to the same to say that for every \(x\) that is both an object of \(D\) and of \(D'\), one has \(f f_x = f' f'_{x'}\). Now this is a finite set of double arrows that one has to equalize by a \(g : j \to j'\), which is possible since \(I\) is filtered.

This completes the proof in the case considered. One reduces the general case to this one by introducing the filtered category \(\underline{\mathbb{N}}\) associated with the ordered set \(\mathbb{N}\) of natural integers, and by noting that the category \(\underline{\mathbb{N}} \times I\) is filtered, that it has no greatest element, and that the projection \(\underline{\mathbb{N}} \times I \to I\) is a cofinal functor.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.1.7

Let \(I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. For there to exist a small filtered ordered set \(E\), and a cofinal functor \(\underline{E} \to I\), it is necessary and sufficient that \(I\) be filtered and that \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I\) admit a small cofinal part \(I'\) (8.1.4).
It is necessary by virtue of 8.1.3 a), and sufficient by virtue of 8.1.6 applied to the full subcategory of \(I\) defined by \(I'\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 8.1.8

Let \(I\) be a filtered category. One says that \(I\) is essentially small if \(I\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and if it satisfies the equivalent conditions of 8.1.7.
8.2. Ind-objects and ind-representable functors.

In what follows we fix a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\), which we always regard as embedded in the category \(\widehat{C}\) of \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaves by means of the canonical functor (1.3.1) \[ h : C \hookrightarrow \widehat{C} . \tag{8.2.1.1} \] We shall call ind-object of \(C\) (or inductive system of \(C\)), any functor \[ \varphi : I \to C , \tag{8.2.1.2} \] where \(I\) is a filtered category (2.7), called the index category of the ind-object. (\(I\) is moreover arbitrary, and we do not require, in particular, that \(I\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.) It will often be convenient to designate an ind-object \(\varphi\) by the index notation \((X_i)_{i\in\mathrm{ob}\, I}\), or even (by a further abuse of notation) \((X_i)_{i\in I}\), or \((X_i)_i\) or \((X_i)\), where \(X_i = \varphi(i)\) for \(i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I\). This notation is neither more nor less abusive than the notation classically used for inductive systems indexed by filtered ordered sets (where the mention of the transition morphisms is likewise absent). The \(X_i\) are called the component objects of the ind-object \(\underline{X}\). One should note that in the general case considered here, the "transition morphisms" \(\varphi(f)\) of the inductive system are indexed by the set \(\mathrm{Fl}\, I\) of arrows of \(I\), which does not in general identify with a part of \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I \times \mathrm{Ob}\, I\); in other words, for given \(i\) and \(j\), \(j\) majorizing \(i\), there may exist more than one transition morphism from \(X_i\) to \(X_j\).

The most useful ind-objects \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(C\) are those for which the index category \(I\) is essentially small (8.1.8); such an ind-object is called essentially small. If \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) is thus, using the fact that in \(\widehat{C}\) the small inductive limits are representable (3.1), one can consider \[ L(\underline{X}) \overset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} \varinjlim h\cdot\underline{X} = \varinjlim_I X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, \widehat{C} , \tag{8.2.2.1} \] where the last limit is taken in \(\widehat{C}\). Thus \(L(\underline{X})\) is the presheaf \[ L(\underline{X}) : Y \mapsto \varinjlim_I \mathrm{Hom}(Y,X_i) \tag{8.2.2.2} \] on \(C\). One says that this presheaf is the presheaf ind-represented by the ind-object \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(C\). A presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) is called an ind-representable presheaf if it is isomorphic to a presheaf \(L(\underline{X})\) ind-represented by an essentially small ind-object. It moreover follows from 8.1.6 that in this definition, one can suppose that \(I\) is a small category, and even that \(I\) is associated with an ordered set \(\in \mathcal{U}\).

Consider an ind-object \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\), given by a functor \(\varphi : I \to C\), and let \[ u : I' \to I \] be a functor, where \(I'\) is a second filtered category. Then the functor \(\varphi \circ u\) is an ind-object \(\underline{X}'\) of \(C\) with index category \(I'\), which in index notation is written \((X_{u(i')})_{i'\in I'}\), which one calls the ind-object of \(C\) deduced from \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) by change of index categories by means of the functor \(u\). If \(I\) and \(I'\) (i.e. \(\underline{X}\) and \(\underline{X}'\)) are essentially small, one finds a canonical morphism \[ L(\underline{X}') = \varinjlim_{i'} X_{u(i')} \to L(\underline{X}) = \varinjlim_i X_i \tag{8.2.3.1} \] between the presheaves ind-represented by \(\underline{X}'\) and \(\underline{X}\) respectively. When \(u\) is a cofinal functor (8.1.1), then \(\underline{X}\) is essentially small if and only if \(\underline{X}'\) is (8.1.7), and the preceding homomorphism (8.2.3.1) is an isomorphism \[ L(\underline{X}') \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } L(\underline{X}) . \tag{8.2.3.2} \]

Let \[ \underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I} , \quad \underline{Y} = (Y_j)_{j\in J} \tag{8.2.4.1} \] be two essentially small ind-objects of \(C\), indexed by (filtered and essentially small) categories \(I\) and \(J\). One calls morphism from the ind-object \(\underline{X}\) to the ind-object \(\underline{Y}\) any morphism \[ L(\underline{X}) \to L(\underline{Y}) \tag{8.2.4.2} \] between the presheaves that they ind-represent. One sets \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{ind\text{-}ob}}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) = \mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{C}}(L(\underline{X}),L(\underline{Y})) . \tag{8.2.4.3} \] (One drops the subscript ind-ob on Hom if there is no fear of confusion.) One defines the composition of ind-objects of \(C\) as the composition of the morphisms of the presheaves that they ind-represent. If \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\) is a universe containing \(\mathcal{U}\), and if one restricts to the essentially small ind-objects that are \(\in \mathcal{V}\), these therefore form the set of objects of a category, whose set of arrows is formed of the triples \((\underline{X}, \underline{Y}, u)\), where \(\underline{X}\) and \(\underline{Y}\) are essentially small ind-objects \(\in \mathcal{V}\) and where \(u : \underline{X} \to \underline{Y}\) is a morphism of ind-objects, i.e. a morphism \(L(\underline{X}) \to L(\underline{Y})\). The category thus obtained is denoted \[ \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) . \tag{8.2.4.4} \] When \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{U}\), one denotes it simply \[ \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{U}}(C) \quad \text{or} \quad \mathrm{Ind}(C) , \tag{8.2.4.5} \] and one calls it category of ind-objects of \(C\) relative to \(\mathcal{U}\), dropping the mention of \(\mathcal{U}\) when no confusion is to be feared.

Evidently, if \(\mathcal{V} \subset \mathcal{V}'\) are two universes containing \(\mathcal{U}\), \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U})\) is a full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}'}(C,\mathcal{U})\); it then follows from 8.2.3 that the functor of inclusion is an equivalence of categories: \[ \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}'}(C,\mathcal{U}) . \tag{8.2.4.6} \] This shows in particular that every essentially small ind-object of \(C\) defines an element of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), up to unique isomorphism. This observation justifies the abuse of language, rather common in practice, consisting of identifying every essentially small ind-object of \(C\) with an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

It follows at once from the definitions that for every universe \(\mathcal{V}\), we have a functor canonical \[ L : \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \to \widehat{C} \tag{8.2.4.7} \] which is fully faithful. These functors are evidently known up to unique isomorphism, thanks to (8.2.4.6), once one knows one of them, and in particular once one knows the canonical functor \[ L : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \widehat{C} . \tag{8.2.4.8} \] Since this functor is fully faithful, one frequently uses it to identify an object of the left-hand side with the functor that it ind-represents, or even to identify \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) with its essential image in \(\widehat{C}\), formed of the ind-representable presheaves. One should note however that this identification presents distinctly more drawbacks than the analogous identification of \(C\) with a full subcategory of \(\widehat{C}\) by the functor \(h\) (8.2.1.1), for unlike the latter, the functor (8.2.4.8) is not in general injective on objects.

Let us make definition (8.2.4.3) explicit in terms of the index expressions (8.2.4.1) of the ind-objects considered. One finds, taking definition (8.2.2.1) into account: \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,\underline{Y}) \overset{\mathrm{dfn}}{=} \varprojlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i, L(\underline{Y})) = \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \mathrm{Hom}_C(X_i,Y_j), \] the last equality coming from (8.2.2.2) applied to \(\underline{Y}\). One thus finds a bijection canonical \[ \mathrm{Hom}((X_i)_{i\in I},(Y_j)_{j\in J}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_{i\in I} \varinjlim_{j\in J} \mathrm{Hom}_C(X_i,Y_j) . \tag{8.2.5.1} \] We leave to the reader the task of making explicit the composition of morphisms of ind-objects on this formula. Let us note that it follows at once from this formula that the set \(\mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y})\) of homomorphisms of ind-objects is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, i.e. that the categories (8.2.4.4) are \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. It amounts to the same to say (by virtue of (8.2.4.6)) that the category \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, i.e. that the right-hand side of (8.2.5.1) is small when \(I, J \in \mathcal{U}\), which follows at once from the fact that \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, hence the \(\mathrm{Hom}_C(X_i,Y_j)\) are small.

Let \(I\) be an essentially small filtered category. Then one sees from (8.2.5.1), or from the functoriality of the inductive limit of a functor \(I \to \widehat{C}\) with respect to said functor, that one has a canonical functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I,C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) . \tag{8.2.6.1} \] One should note that this functor is not in general fully faithful, nor even faithful.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.2.7

The definitions of 8.2.4 make clear the notion of isomorphy of two (essentially small) ind-objects, which also means the isomorphy of the presheaves that they ind-represent. One should note that this is a very weak notion of isomorphy, if one compares it with the notion of isomorphy in categories of the form \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I,C)\). Thus, a great many rather natural relations that one may impose on an ind-object (such as that of having its components in a given strictly full subcategory, or that of being strict (8.12 below)) are not stable under isomorphism. It will therefore be necessary, if one insists on working with notions stable under isomorphism of ind-objects, to "saturate" the notions considered by passing to the strictly full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) generated by the subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) formed of the objects satisfying the condition considered. See for example the notion of essentially constant ind-object, introduced below (8.4).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.2.8

Let \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\) be two universes and \(C\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category belonging to \(\mathcal{V}\). One denotes by \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) the following category:

a) The objects of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) are the functors \(\varphi : I \to C\) where \(I\) is a category filtered, essentially \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, belonging to \(\mathcal{V}\).

b) Let \((I,\varphi)\) and \((J,\psi)\) be two objects of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\). A morphism of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) from \((I,\varphi)\) to \((J,\psi)\) is a pair \((m,u)\), where \(m : I \to J\) is a functor and \(u : \varphi \to \psi\circ m\) is a morphism of functors. The composition of morphisms in \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) is defined in the obvious way.

Let us denote by \(S\) the set of morphisms \((m,u) : (I,\varphi) \to (J,\psi)\) of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) such that \(m\) is cofinal and \(u\) an isomorphism. Let \((I,\varphi)\) be an object of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\). The category \(\mathrm{Fl}(I)\) of arrows of \(I\) maps by two natural functors into \(I\): the source and the target. Moreover these two functors are linked by the canonical morphism of functors \(v : \mathrm{source} \to \mathrm{but}\). Whence two morphisms in \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\) from \((\mathrm{Fl}(I),\varphi\circ\mathrm{source})\) into \((I,\varphi)\): \(p_1(I,\varphi) = (\mathrm{source}, \mathrm{id})\), \(p_2(I,\varphi) = (\mathrm{but}, \varphi\ast v : \varphi\circ\mathrm{source} \to \varphi\circ\mathrm{but})\). Let us denote \(p : \mathrm{SysInd}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) the obvious functor. Let \(B\) be a category. Show that the functor \(F \mapsto F\circ p\): \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Ind}(C),B) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{SysInd}(C),B) \] is fully faithful, and that a functor \(G : \mathrm{SysInd}(C) \to B\) belongs to the essential image if and only if it possesses the two following properties:

1) For every \(s \in S\), \(G(s)\) is an isomorphism of \(B\).

2) For every object \((I,\varphi)\) of \(\mathrm{SysInd}(C)\), \(G(p_1(I,\varphi)) = G(p_2(I,\varphi))\).
8.3. Characterization of ind-representable functors

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.3.1

Let \(F\) be an ind-representable presheaf on \(C\). Then \(F\) is left exact, i.e. (2.3.2) for every finite category \(J\) and every functor \(\varphi : J \to C\) such that \(\varinjlim \varphi\) is representable (i.e. \(\varprojlim \varphi^\circ\) is representable), the canonical map \[ F(\varinjlim \varphi) \to \varprojlim F\circ\varphi \] is bijective.
Indeed, the representable presheaves being evidently left exact, it follows at once from 2.8 that the same holds for every filtered inductive limit of such functors, q.e.d.

\(F\) being a presheaf on \(C\), we shall often have to work with the category \[ C_{/F} \hookrightarrow \widehat{C}_{/F} , \tag{8.3.2.1} \] which denotes the full subcategory of the right-hand side formed of the arrows \(X \to F\) with source in \(C\). It follows from 1.4 that the objects of this category are identified with the pairs \((X,u)\), where \(X\) is an object of \(C\) and \(u \in F(X)\). A morphism from \((X,u)\) to \((X',u')\) is then interpreted as an arrow \(f : X \to X'\) in \(C\) such that \(F(f)(u') = u\). The "forgetting the target" functor from \(\widehat{C}_{/F}\) to \(\widehat{C}\) induces a functor (called canonical). \[ C_{/F} \to C , \tag{8.3.2.2} \] already considered in 3.4, where one proves that the inductive limit of this functor exists in \(\widehat{C}\) (without smallness condition on \(C_{/F}\)) and is canonically isomorphic to \(F\).

Let us note that if in \(C\) the finite inductive limits are representable, and if \(F\) is left exact (i.e. transforms them into finite projective limits of \((\mathrm{Ens})\)), then the same holds in \(C_{/F}\), and a fortiori (2.7.1) \(C_{/F}\) is filtered. If, more generally, in \(C\) the sums of two objects and the cokernels of double arrows are representable, and if \(F\) transforms them into products resp. into kernels, then \(C_{/F}\) is stable under the same types of finite inductive limits, so it is filtered if and only if it is non-empty, i.e. if and only if the functor \(F\) is not the constant functor with value \(\varnothing\).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 8.3.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and \(F \in \mathrm{ob}\, \widehat{C}\), \(F : C^\circ \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-presheaf on \(C\). The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(F\) is ind-representable (8.2.2).

(ii) The category \(C_{/F}\) (8.3.2) is filtered and essentially small.

(iii) (If in \(C\) the finite inductive limits are representable.) The functor \(F\) is left exact, and ob \(C_{/F}\) admits a small cofinal part (8.1.4).

(iii bis) (If in \(C\) the sums of two objects and the cokernels of double arrows are representable.) The functor \(F\) transforms the sum of two objects of \(C\) into products, cokernels of double arrows of \(C\) into kernels, the category \(C_{/F}\) is non-empty i.e. the functor \(F\) is not the constant functor with value \(\varnothing\), and finally there exists a small family of objects of \(C_{/F}\) such that every object \(X\) of \(C_{/F}\) is majorized by an object \(X_i\), i.e. admits an \(F\)-morphism \(X_i \to X\).

(iv) (If the category \(C\) is equivalent to a small category.) The category \(C_{/F}\) is filtered.

(v) (If the category \(C\) is equivalent to a small category, and if the filtered inductive limits are representable in it.) The functor \(F\) is left exact.

Proof. (i) ⟹ (ii). Suppose \(F\) ind-represented by \((X_i)_{i\in I}\), with \(I\) small. Let us prove that \(C_{/F}\) is filtered. Let \(X, X'\) be two objects of \(C_{/F}\), i.e. objects of \(C\) equipped with morphisms \(X \to F\), \(X' \to F\); let us prove that they are majorized by a third object of \(C_{/F}\). Now the morphisms \(X \to F\), \(X' \to F\) come from morphisms \(X \to X_i\), \(X' \to X'_i\), and up to replacing \(i, i'\) by a common upper bound in \(\mathrm{Ob}\, I\), one can suppose \(i = i'\), and one takes as common upper bound of \(X, X'\) the object \(X_i\) equipped with the morphism canonical \(X_i \to F\). Now let \(X \underset{g}{\overset{f}{\rightrightarrows}} X' \xrightarrow{\ h\ } F\) be a double arrow in \(C_{/F}\); let us prove that it is equalized by an arrow \(X' \to X''\) of \(C_{/F}\). Now \(h : X' \to F\) is given by a morphism \(h_i : X' \to X_i\), and the condition \(hf = hg\) means that there exists \(\alpha : i \to j\) in \(I\) such that \(\varphi(\alpha)(h_i f) = \varphi(\alpha)(h_i g)\), i.e. up to replacing \(h_i\) by \(\varphi(\alpha)h_i\), one equalizes \(f\) and \(g\). This proves that \(C_{/F}\) is filtered. It is then immediate that it is essentially small since the objects \((X_i \to F)_{i\in\mathrm{Ob}\, I}\) form a small family in \(\mathrm{Ob}\, C_{/F}\) that is cofinal.

(ii) ⟹ (i). Set \(I = C_{/F}\), and consider the canonical functor (8.3.2.2) \[ \varphi : I = C_{/F} \to C . \] One knows that the presheaf represented by this ind-object of \(C\) is \(F\) (3.4), so \(F\) is ind-representable by definition (8.2.2).

(ii) ⟺ (iii). Indeed, (ii) ⟹ (iii) because an ind-representable functor is left exact (8.3.1), and (iii) ⟹ (ii) because one has pointed out (8.3.1) that \(F\) left exact implies that \(C_{/F}\) is filtered, and one applies definition 8.1.8 to conclude that this category is essentially small.
(ii) ⟺ (iii bis) is proved in the same way as (ii) ⟺ (iii).

The equivalences (ii) ⟺ (iv) and (iii) ⟺ (v) are trivial, since for \(C\) equivalent to a small category, \(C_{/F}\) is evidently likewise equivalent to a small category and a fortiori it is automatically essentially small as soon as it is filtered. This completes the proof of 8.3.3.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.3.4

Let \(F : C' \to C''\) be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. It appears that the notion of left exactness (2.3.2) is of hardly any interest in practice unless in \(C'\) the finite projective limits are representable. In the case where \(C'' = (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\), and where \(C'\) is \(\mathcal{U}\)-small, writing \(C'\) in the form \(C^\circ\) (so \(C = C'^\circ\)), it is appropriate to consider that the "good notion" which replaces, in the general case, that of left exactness is that of ind-representability of \(F\) (regarded as a presheaf on \(C^\circ\); i.e. that of pro-representability of \(F\), regarded as a functor on \(C'\), cf. 8.10). This notion does coincide well with that of left exactness when in \(C'\) the finite projective limits are representable i.e. in \(C\) the finite inductive limits are representable (8.3.3). When one no longer supposes \(C'\) \(\mathcal{U}\)-small or at least equivalent to a \(\mathcal{U}\)-small category, then the two notions for a functor \(F\), of left exactness and of pro-representability, no longer necessarily coincide, even if in \(C'\) the finite projective limits are representable (cf. 8.12.9). In fact, it seems that in this case, the left exact functors non-ind-representable should be considered as being of pathological nature, the "good" objects remaining the ind-representable functors; compare 8.13.3 . For the case of functors \(F : C' \to C''\), with \(C'\) and \(C''\) again arbitrary \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, we shall develop below (8.11.5), more generally, a notion that "improves" on that of left exactness, (namely that of a functor admitting a pro-adjoint functor).
8.4. Constant, essentially constant ind-objects

Let us choose a final category \(\underline{e}\), i.e. such that \(\mathrm{Ob}\, \underline{e}\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}\, \underline{e}\) are reduced to one element (for example, one may take for \(\underline{e}\) the full subcategory of \((\mathrm{Ens})\) formed by the empty set, if one wants a canonical choice). It is evidently a filtered and small category. If \(X\) is an object of \(C\), one associates with it the constant ind-object indexed by \(\underline{e}\), with value \(X\), namely \(c(X)\). It is clear that for variable \(X\), one thus finds a fully faithful functor \[ c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) , \tag{8.4.1} \] moreover injective on objects, and by which we shall identify \(C\) with a full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). One will note that the composite functor \[ C \xrightarrow{\ c\ } \mathrm{Ind}(C) \xrightarrow{\ L\ } \widehat{C} \tag{8.4.2} \] is the canonical functor \(h\) (8.2.1.1).

More generally, let \(I\) be a filtered category. The constant functor on \(I\) with value at an object \(X\) of \(C\) is also called the constant ind-object with value \(X\) indexed by \(I\). It is clear, if \(I\) is essentially small, that this ind-object ind-represents the functor \(h(X)\) represented by \(X\), so this ind-object is isomorphic to \(c(X)\).

An ind-object \(\underline{X}\) of \(C\) is said to be essentially constant if it is isomorphic (in a category \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{V}')\), for suitable \(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{V}'\)) to an ind-object of the form \(c(X)\), \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). The object \(X\), which is then determined up to canonical isomorphism, is called the value of the essentially constant ind-object considered. Thus by definition, the functor \(c\) of (8.4.1) induces an equivalence of \(C\) with the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) formed of the ind-objects that are essentially constant, this subcategory being the essential image of the functor \(c\).
Evidently a constant ind-object is essentially constant, the converse being true only in the sole, trivial, case where \(C\) is empty or a punctual category.
8.5. Filtered inductive limits in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.5.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. In \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), the small inductive filtered limits are representable, and the canonical functor (8.2.4.8) \[ L : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \widehat{C} \] commutes with them.
Taking into account the fact that \(L\) is fully faithful, the assertions of the proposition are equivalent to the following:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.5.2

Every small filtered inductive limit (in \(\widehat{C}\)) of presheaves ind-representable is ind-representable.
This follows easily from criterion 8.3.3 (ii). The detail of the verification is left to the reader.

The "tautological" case of filtered inductive limits in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is the one where one starts from an essentially small ind-object \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(C\). One then has, in \(\widehat{C}\) hence also in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) (or in \(\widehat{\widehat{C}}\)): \[ \underline{X} = \varinjlim_I X_i . \tag{8.5.3.1} \] One should note, in writing this formula, that it is not an inductive limit in \(C\), and that even when the latter exists, it is not isomorphic in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) to \(\underline{X}\): indeed, the canonical functor (8.4.1) \(c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) does not in general commute with filtered inductive limits. (Cf. 8.5.5 below.)

To obviate this possibility of confusion in writing (8.5.3.1), "certain authors" (= P. Deligne) prefer to write it \[ \underline{X} = \text{«}\varinjlim_I\text{»}\, X_i , \tag{8.5.3.2} \] the role of the guillemets being to indicate that the inductive limit is taken in a category of Ind-objects \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). By extension, it would then be appropriate to denote by "\(\varinjlim\)" every inductive-limit operation in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) (without the components of the inductive system considered in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) necessarily being in the image, or the essential image, of \(c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\)).

To compute the inductive or projective limit of a functor \[ \varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) , \tag{8.5.4.1} \] where \(J\) is now an arbitrary category, it is often convenient to make \(\varphi\) explicit by means of a functor \[ \widehat{\varphi} : J\times I \to C , \tag{8.5.4.2} \] where \(I\) is an essentially small filtered category, or preferably small. Such a \(\widehat{\varphi}\) indeed defines a functor \[ j \mapsto (i \mapsto \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)) : J \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I,C) , \] whence, on composing with the canonical arrow (8.2.6.1) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I,C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\), a functor \[ j \mapsto (i \mapsto \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)) : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) . \tag{8.5.4.3} \] One may say that \(\widehat{\varphi}\) is an index expression of \(\varphi\), indexed by the (filtered) category \(I\), if the corresponding functor (8.5.4.3) is isomorphic to \(\varphi\). We shall study below (8.8) general conditions for the existence of an index expression for a functor \(\varphi\) given, and shall confine ourselves here to starting from a functor \(\varphi\) given in index form (8.5.4.3), in the case where \(J\) is a small filtered category, in order to indicate in this case the computation of "\(\varinjlim\)" \(\varphi = \text{«}\varinjlim_j\text{»} \varphi(j)\). Formula (8.5.3.2), and the associativity formula for inductive limits (2.5.0) then immediately give the "tautological computation" of "\(\varinjlim\)" \(\varphi\): \[ \text{«}\varinjlim_J\text{»} \varphi = \text{«}\varinjlim_{J\times I}\text{»} \widehat{\varphi} , \tag{8.5.4.4} \] i.e. \[ \text{«}\varinjlim_J\text{»} (i \mapsto \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)) = \text{«}\varinjlim_{J\times I}\text{»} \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) . \tag{8.5.4.5} \] Thus, the inductive system sought is none other than \(\widehat{\varphi}\) itself (the index category being \(J\times I\), which is indeed filtered since \(J\) and \(I\) are).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.5.5

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category

a) Prove that the following conditions are equivalent:

(i) In \(C\) the small inductive limits are representable, and the functor \(c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) commutes with them.

(iii) The functor \(c\) is an equivalence of categories.

(ii) In \(C\) the small inductive limits are representable, and for every \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), the functor \(Y \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y)\) commutes with the said limits.

(iv) The small filtered inductive limits are representable in \(C\), and the functor \(\varinjlim c : \mathrm{Ind}\, C \to C\) (cf. 8.7.1.5) is fully faithful (or again, an equivalence).

b) If \(C\) is a finite category, prove that the preceding conditions are equivalent to the following: for every projector in \(C\) (10.6), the image is representable in \(C\).
8.6. Extension of a functor to ind-objects

Let \[ f : C \to C' \tag{8.6.1.1} \] be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. For every ind-object \[ \varphi : I \to C \] of \(C\) (\(I\) a filtered category), the composite functor \(f\circ\varphi\) is an ind-object of \(C'\), also denoted \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)(\varphi)\). In index notation, if \(\varphi\) is written in the form \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\), one obtains \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f)(X_i)_{i\in I} = (f(X_i))_{i\in I} . \tag{8.6.1.2} \] Let \(\underline{Y} = (Y_j)_{j\in J}\) be a second inductive system of \(C\). One then finds an obvious map, also denoted \(u \mapsto \mathrm{Ind}(f)(u)\): \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) = \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,Y_j) &\to \\ \mathrm{Hom}(\mathrm{Ind}(f)(\underline{X}), \mathrm{Ind}(f)(\underline{Y})) &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_i \varinjlim_j \mathrm{Hom}(f(X_i),f(Y_j)) . \end{aligned} \tag{8.6.1.3} \] One immediately observes that these maps are compatible with the composition of morphisms of ind-objects, by referring to the unwritten formula for composition of morphisms of ind-objects (8.2.5). One has thus obtained, for every universe \(\mathcal{V}\), a functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \to \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C',\mathcal{U}) \tag{8.6.1.4} \] (notations of (8.2.4.5)), and in particular a functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C') . \tag{8.6.1.5} \]

If one has a second functor \[ g : C' \to C'' , \] one evidently has an identity of functors between Ind categories (or \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}\), as one wishes): \[ \mathrm{Ind}(gf) = \mathrm{Ind}(g)\circ\mathrm{Ind}(f) , \tag{8.6.1.6} \] and for \(C' = C\), one has the everlasting formula \[ \mathrm{Ind}(\mathrm{id}_C) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)} . \tag{8.6.1.7} \] Figuratively, one may therefore say that the category \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) depends functorially on \(C\) (covariantly)∗. We leave to the reader the task of making explicit even a dependence 2-functorial, by defining, for every pair of \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories \(C, C'\), a canonical functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,C') \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Ind}(C), \mathrm{Ind}(C')) , \tag{8.6.1.8} \] and by specifying the functorial nature of the identity isomorphisms (8.6.1.6) and (8.6.1.7).

Let us take up again the functor (8.6.1.1), and consider the corresponding functor (5.1) \[ f_! : \widehat{C} \to \widehat{C'} , \tag{8.6.2.1} \] and the diagram of functors \[ \xymatrix{ \mathrm{Ind}(C) \ar[rr]^-{\mathrm{Ind}(f)} \ar[d]_-{L_C} & & \mathrm{Ind}(C') \ar[d]^-{L_{C'}} \\ \widehat{C} \ar[rr]_-{f_!} & & \widehat{C'} } \tag{8.6.2.2} \] where the vertical arrows denote the canonical functors \(L\) of (8.2.4.8). Since the functor \(f_!\) "extends \(f\)" and commutes with inductive limits (5.4.3), and the functors \(L_C\) and \(L_{C'}\) commute with small filtered inductive limits (8.5.1), it follows from (8.5.3.2) that for every ind-object \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(C\), one has in \(\widehat{C'}\) an isomorphism canonical \[ f_!(L_C((X_i)_{i\in I})) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_i f_! L_C(X_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_i L_{C'} f(X_i) = L_{C'}(f(X_i)_{i\in I}) \] i.e. a canonical isomorphism \[ f_! L_C(\underline{X}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } L_{C'}(\mathrm{Ind}(f)(\underline{X})) . \] We leave to the reader the task of verifying that the latter is functorial, i.e. that it corresponds to a canonical isomorphism \[ f_! L_C \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } L_{C'}\circ\mathrm{Ind}(f) . \tag{8.6.2.3} \] In other words, the square (8.6.2.2) is commutative up to canonical isomorphism. Taking into account the fact that \(f_!\) commutes with small inductive limits, and 8.5.1, one concludes from this:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.6.3

Let \(f : C \to C'\) be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. Then the functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C') \] commutes with filtered inductive limits. Moreover, it makes the following diagram commutative \[ \xymatrix{ C \ar[rr]^-{f} \ar[d]_-{c_C} & & C' \ar[d]^-{c_{C'}} \\ \mathrm{Ind}(C) \ar[rr]_-{\mathrm{Ind}(f)} & & \mathrm{Ind}(C') } \] where the vertical arrows \(c_C, c_{C'}\) are the canonical functors (8.4.1).

The last assertion is trivial from the definitions, and has been included for the convenience of references. Note moreover that the properties stated in 8.6.3 characterize the functor \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) up to unique isomorphism, as being induced by the functor \(f_!\) (8.6.2.1), as follows from the proof just given of (8.6.2.3).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.6.4

The notations are those of 8.6.3.

a) For \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) to be faithful (resp. fully faithful), it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) be so.

b) For \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) to be an equivalence of categories, it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) be fully faithful, and that every object of \(C'\) be isomorphic to a direct summand (10.6) of an object in the image of \(f\).

Proof. a) The necessity evidently follows from the fact that \(f\) is induced by \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\). For the sufficiency, it suffices to use form (8.6.1.3) of \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) on the sets \(\mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y})\), recalling that filtered inductive limits of sets, and the limits projective of any kind, transform monomorphisms into monomorphisms, isomorphisms into isomorphisms.

b) One may already suppose \(f\), hence \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\), fully faithful. Since every object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C')\) is a small filtered inductive limit of objects of \(C'\), the full faithfulness of \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) implies that for this functor to be essentially surjective, it amounts to the same that every object \(X'\) of \(C'\) be in the essential image. Now if one has an isomorphism \[ X' \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim\text{»} f(X_i) , \] this isomorphism factors through one of the \(f(X_i)\), which shows that \(X'\) is a direct summand of \(f(X_i)\), which proves the necessity in b). For the sufficiency, using the full faithfulness of \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\), it follows at once from the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.6.5

In \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) the images of projectors (10.6) are representable, and the functor \(\mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C')\) commutes with the formation of the said images.

This indeed follows from the fact that in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) the small filtered inductive limits are representable (8.5.1) and that \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) commutes with them (8.6.3), taking into account that the image of a projector \(p : X \to X\) is interpreted as the inductive limit of a filtered inductive system indexed by \(\mathbb{N}\) \[ X \xrightarrow{\ p\ } X \xrightarrow{\ p\ } X \to \ldots \] or, if one prefers, as the inductive limit of the functor that one guesses on the filtered category \(P\) having a single object, and a non-identity arrow \(\pi\) such that \(\pi^2 = \pi\).
8.7. The functor \(\varinjlim_C : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to C\). Universal characterizations of the category \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

Let us take up again a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\), and the canonical functor \[ c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) . \tag{8.7.1.1} \] Let \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) be an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). It follows immediately from the definition of the representable inductive limits (2.1, 2.1.1) that \(\varinjlim_i X_i\) is representable in \(C\) if and only if the left adjoint of \(c\) is defined at \(\underline{X}\), and that in that case \(\varinjlim_i X_i\) (computed in \(C\)) is none other than the value at \(\underline{X}\) of the said left adjoint: \[ \mathrm{Hom}_C(\varinjlim_i X_i, Y) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)}((X_i)_{i\in I}, c(Y)) . \tag{8.7.1.2} \]

If one denotes by \[ \mathrm{Ind}(C)' \subset \mathrm{Ind}(C) \tag{8.7.1.3} \] the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) formed of the ind-objects of \(C\) that admit a limit inductive in \(C\), it follows from the preceding observation that this subcategory is strictly full, and that one has a canonical functor \[ \varinjlim_C : \mathrm{Ind}(C)' \to C , \tag{8.7.1.4} \] whose value at each object \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)'\) is its inductive limit in \(C\). In the particular case where in \(C\) the small filtered inductive limits are representable, one thus obtains a natural functor \[ \varinjlim_C : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to C . \tag{8.7.1.5} \]

Of course, one can define the preceding functors likewise on categories of the type \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U})'\), \(\mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U})\), but, taking (8.2.4.6) into account, they are already determined (up to unique isomorphism) by knowledge of the preceding functors, corresponding to the case \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{U}\).

From the preceding construction of \(\varinjlim_C\) as a left adjoint functor, it follows immediately that this functor commutes with arbitrary inductive limits, and in particular with small filtered inductive limits (the latter being representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) (8.5.1)). Let us note also that \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)'\) always contains the essential image of \(c\) (formed of the essentially constant ind-objects), and that one has a canonical isomorphism functorial in \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Ind}(C)'\): \[ \varinjlim_C c(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X , \tag{8.7.1.8} \] i.e., in the favorable case where \(C\) is stable under small inductive limits, one has a canonical isomorphism \[ \varinjlim_C \circ\, c \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{id}_C . \tag{8.7.1.9} \]

Let us now consider a functor \[ f : C \to E , \tag{8.7.2.1} \] where \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which the small inductive limits are representable, so that one has a functor \[ \varinjlim_E : \mathrm{Ind}(E) \to E . \] Since one has also defined (8.6) \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(E) , \] one can consider the composite \[ \overline{f} = \varinjlim_E \circ\, \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E , \tag{8.7.2.2} \] which one sometimes calls the canonical extension of \(f\) to ind-objects (but which one will take care not to confuse with \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\)!). As the composite of two functors commuting with small filtered inductive limits (8.6.3, 8.7.1.7), this functor itself commutes with small filtered inductive limits. Moreover, it follows from isomorphism (8.7.1.9) applied to \(E\), and from (8.6.2.3), that \(\overline{f}\) extends \(f\) up to isomorphism, i.e. that one has an isomorphism canonical \[ \overline{f} \circ c_C \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f . \tag{8.7.2.3} \]

It is moreover fairly clear, taking into account the fact that every object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is a small filtered inductive limit of objects of \(C\), that the two preceding properties still characterize \(\overline{f}\), up to unique isomorphism. One can make this point precise so as to obtain at the same time a universal characterization, up to equivalence, of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) among the \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories \(E\) in which the small filtered inductive limits are representable. If \(E\) and \(F\) are two such \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, let us denote by \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)' \subset \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F) \tag{8.7.2.4} \] the full subcategory of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\) formed of the functors that commute with small filtered inductive limits. One then has:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.7.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and let us use the notation above (8.7.2.4). Then the canonical functor \[ c_C : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) \] is 2-universal among the functors with source \(C\) and target a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category with small limits inductive filtered representable. In other words, \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is such a category (8.2.5, 8.5.1), and if \(E\) is such a category, the functor \[ g \mapsto g\circ c_C : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Ind}(C),E)' \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,E) \tag{8.7.3.1} \] is an equivalence of categories.

To prove this last point, it suffices to check that the map \(f \mapsto \overline{f}\) defined by (8.7.2.2) can be made precise by a functor \[ f \mapsto \overline{f} = \varinjlim_E \circ\, \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,E) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Ind}(C),E)' , \tag{8.7.3.2} \] and that the latter is a quasi-inverse of (8.7.3.1). The detail of the verification, essentially trivial, is left to the reader. One can also invoke 7.8 to conclude first that (8.7.3.1) is fully faithful, and (8.7.2.3) to conclude that it is essentially surjective.

Let us take up again a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories \[ f : C \to E , \tag{8.7.4.1} \] where \(E\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which the small filtered inductive limits are representable, whence a functor \[ \overline{f} : (X_i)_{i\in I} \mapsto \varinjlim_i f(X_i) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E . \tag{8.7.4.2} \] We propose to study conditions on \(f\) that ensure that \(\overline{f}\) is fully faithful, resp. an equivalence of categories. Since \(f\) is isomorphic to the composite \(\overline{f}\circ c_C\), and \(c_C : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is fully faithful, one sees that for \(\overline{f}\) to be fully faithful, it is necessary that \(f\) be so. Up to replacing \(C\) by its essential image in \(E\), one thus sees that one does not in general lose anything, essentially, by supposing that \(f\) is the inclusion functor of a subcategory \(C\) of \(E\), which we shall suppose in what follows, to simplify the notations.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.7.5

The notations are those of 8.7.4.

a) For the functor \(\overline{f}\) to be fully faithful, it is necessary and sufficient that one have:

(i) Every object \(X\) of \(C\) satisfies the following condition:

(PF) For every small filtered inductive system \((Y_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(C\), with inductive limit \(\varinjlim_i Y_i\) in \(E\), the canonical map \[ \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y_i) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X, \varinjlim_i Y_i) \tag{8.7.5.1} \] is bijective.

b) For the functor \(\overline{f}\) to be an equivalence of categories, it is necessary and sufficient that \(C\) satisfy condition (i), and the two following conditions:

(ii) \(C\) is a subcategory of \(E\) generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1).

(iii) For every object \(X\) of \(E\), the full subcategory \(C_{/X}\) of \(E_{/X}\) formed of the objects \(X'\) over \(X\) with source in \(\mathrm{Ob}\, C\), is filtered and essentially small.

Condition (iii) is verified in particular if \(C\) is equivalent to a small category, and if the finite inductive limits in \(C\) are representable and the inclusion functor \(f : C \to E\) commutes with them (i.e. for every finite category \(J\) and every functor \(\varphi : J \to C\) the inductive limit of \(f\varphi\) is representable and is isomorphic in \(E\) to an object of \(C\)).

Proof. a) With the notations of condition (i), if \(\underline{Y}\) denotes the ind-object \((Y_i)\), \(\underline{X}\) the constant ind-object defined by \(X\), then (8.7.5.1) is none other than the map canonical \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\overline{f}(\underline{X}),\overline{f}(\underline{Y})) , \] so if \(\overline{f}\) is fully faithful this map is indeed bijective. Conversely, if \(\underline{X} = (X_j)_{j\in J}\) and \(\underline{Y} = (Y_i)_{i\in I}\) are two arbitrary ind-objects of \(E\), then the map \(u : \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\overline{f}(\underline{X}),\overline{f}(\underline{Y}))\) is the projective limit over \(j\) of the maps \[ u_j : \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X}_j,\underline{Y}) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\overline{f}(\underline{X}_j),\overline{f}(\underline{Y})) , \] where \(\underline{X}_j\) is the constant ind-object with value \(X_j\); so \(u\) is bijective if the \(u_j\) are, and (i) therefore implies that \(\overline{f}\) is fully faithful.

b) Suppose (i), (ii), (iii) verified, and let us prove that \(\overline{f}\) is an equivalence. It remains to prove that it is essentially surjective, hence that every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) is in the image essential. Now hypothesis (ii) means that \(\varinjlim_{C_{/X}} Z \to X\) is an isomorphism, and (iii) that the category \(C_{/X}\) is filtered and essentially small, so \(X\) is the image of the ind-object of \(E\) defined by the natural functor \(C_{/X} \to E\). Conversely, suppose that \(\overline{f}\) is an equivalence, so by virtue of a), it remains to verify (ii) and (iii). One can suppose that \(E = \mathrm{Ind}(C)\), \(C\) being identified with the subcategory \(c(C)\) of \(E\). But one knows (8.3.3 (ii)) that for every \(X \in \mathrm{Ind}(C)\), identified if one wishes with the functor \(F\) on \(C^\circ\) that it ind-represents, \(C_{/X} = C_{/F}\) is a filtered essentially small category (which proves (iii)) and that the inductive limit in \(\widehat{C}\) of the functor \(C_{/F} \to \widehat{C}\) is \(F\). A fortiori, this holds in the full subcategory \(E\) of \(\widehat{C}\), since \(F = X\) is in \(E\), which proves (ii). It remains to prove the last assertion of b). Now the hypothesis made on \(C\) evidently implies that in the category \(C_{/X}\), the finite inductive limits are representable, a fortiori the category \(C_{/X}\) is filtered.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.7.5.2

The reasoning just carried out shows more generally that when condition (i) is verified, then the essential image of the fully faithful functor \(\overline{f}\) (8.7.4.2) is formed of the \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) such that the category \(C_{/X}\) is filtered and essentially small (a condition automatically satisfied if \(C\) satisfies the conditions stated at the end of b)), and such that the inductive limit of the canonical functor \(C_{/X} \to E\) is \(X\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.6

Let \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) be the full subcategory of \(E\) formed of the objects satisfying condition (PF) of 8.7.5 a). Then for every functor \(J \to E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), \(J\) a finite category, which admits an inductive limit \(X\) in \(E\), one has \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E_{\mathrm{PF}}\). The functor canonical \((X_i)_{i\in I} \mapsto \varinjlim_{i,\,E} X_i\) deduced from the inclusion \(g : E_{\mathrm{PF}} \hookrightarrow E\) \[ \overline{g} : \mathrm{Ind}(E_{\mathrm{PF}}) \to E \tag{8.7.6.1} \] is fully faithful, and if in \(E\) the finite inductive limits are representable and if \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is equivalent to a small category, then the essential image of the functor \(\overline{g}\) is formed of the objects \(X\) of \(E\) such that the canonical morphism \(\varinjlim_{(E_{\mathrm{PF}})_{/X}} Y \to X\) is an isomorphism. If one supposes moreover that the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) of \(E\) is generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1), then the functor (8.7.6.1) is an equivalence of categories.
All the facts are evident, in the order in which they are given, taking 8.7.5 into account, using 2.8 for the first assertion.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.7.7

Suppose that in \(E\) the finite inductive limits are representable. Let \(C\) be a full subcategory of \(E\), equivalent to a small category, and consider the functor \((X_i)_{i\in I} \mapsto \varinjlim_{i,\,E} X_i\): \[ \overline{f} : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E . \tag{8.7.7.1} \] Let \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) be as in 8.7.6. The following conditions are equivalent:

(i) The functor \(\overline{f} : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to E\) is an equivalence.

(ii) The category \(C\) in \(E\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, contained in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and every object of \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is isomorphic in \(E\) (or in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), it amounts to the same (8.7.6)) to a direct summand of an object of \(C\).

When the subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) is stable under direct summands (10.6), the preceding conditions are again equivalent to the following:

(ii bis) \(C = E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and \(C\) is generating in \(E\) by strict epimorphisms.

(iii) The subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, contained in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and the finite inductive limits are representable in it.

When moreover in \(E\) the finite inductive limits are representable, these conditions are also equivalent to

(iii bis) The subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, contained in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and stable in \(E\) under finite inductive limits (or what amounts to the same, under finite sums, and under cokernels of double arrows).

One already knows (8.7.5) that condition (i) implies that \(C \subset E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), and that \(C\) is generating by strict epimorphisms; let us also prove that then every object \(X\) of \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is isomorphic to a direct factor of an object of \(C\). Indeed one knows that \(X\) is a limit inductive filtered \(\varinjlim_i X_i\) in \(E\) of objects of \(C\), and by definition of \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\), one sees that for suitable \(i\) the canonical homomorphism \(X_i \to X\) admits a left inverse, so that \(X\) is indeed a direct factor of the object \(X_i\) of \(C\). This proves that (i) ⟹ (ii) (without hypothesis on \(C\) or \(E\), moreover). Let us prove (ii) ⟹ (i). Since \(C\) is equivalent to a small category and every object of \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is a direct factor of an object of \(C\), one sees that \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is likewise equivalent to a small category, so by virtue of 8.7.6 the functor (8.7.6.1) is an equivalence of categories, and one concludes thanks to 8.6.4 b) applied to the inclusion \(C \hookrightarrow E_{\mathrm{PF}}\).

When every direct summand in \(E\) of an object of \(C\) is in \(C\), it is clear that (ii) ⟺ (ii bis). On the other hand (ii bis) implies (iii) resp. (iii bis) by virtue of 8.7.6. Finally, (iii) (and a fortiori (iii bis)) implies (i) by virtue of 8.7.5. This completes the proof.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.7.8

(Karoubi envelopes). Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, \(E = \mathrm{Ind}(C)\), and \(E_{\mathrm{PF}} \supset C\) the full subcategory of \(E\) defined in 8.7.6.

a) Prove that in \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) the images of projectors are representable, and that every object of \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) is a direct summand of an object of \(C\).

b) Let us call karoubian a category \(F\) in which the images of projectors are representable.
