Let then \[ \varphi : C \to K \] be a fully faithful functor, such that \(K\) is karoubian and every object of \(K\) is a direct summand of an object of the image of \(C\). Prove that \(\varphi\) is 2-universal among the functors from \(C\) with values in karoubian categories, precisely: for every karoubian category \(F\), the functor \[ g \mapsto g\circ\varphi : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(K,F) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F) \] is an equivalence of categories. (One will use the fact that every functor commutes with images of projectors.) The category \(K\) equipped with \(\varphi\), determined up to equivalence (itself determined up to unique isomorphism) by the preceding properties, is called the Karoubi envelope \(\widetilde{C}\) of \(C\). (Compare also IV 7.5.)

c) Deduce from a) and b) that \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)_{\mathrm{PF}}\), equipped with the functor \(C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)_{\mathrm{PF}}\) induced by \(c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\), makes \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)_{\mathrm{PF}}\) a Karoubi envelope of \(C\).

d) Show that every functor \(f : C \to C'\) extends in an essentially unique way to a functor \(\widetilde{f} : \widetilde{C} \to \widetilde{C'}\) of the Karoubi envelopes, and that if one takes these envelopes of Karoubi as in c), \(\widetilde{f}\) is the functor induced by \(\mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C')\). Show that the conditions of 8.6.4 b) are again equivalent to the following: \(\widetilde{f}\) is an equivalence of categories.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.7.9

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

a) Show that the conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(E\) is equivalent to a category of the form \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), with \(C\) a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

(i bis) As (i), with moreover \(C\) karoubian (8.7.8 b)).

(ii) The subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) of \(E\) (8.7.6) is generating by strict epimorphisms, and for every object \(X\) of \(E\), \((E_{\mathrm{PF}})_{/X}\) is a filtered essentially small category.

Show that if \(C\) is a karoubian \(\mathcal{U}\)-category such that \(E\) is equivalent to \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), then \(C\) is equivalent to \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) (by an equivalence determined up to isomorphism unique). Establish a 2-equivalence between the 2-category formed of the categories \(E\) satisfying the preceding conditions and the functors between them commuting with small filtered inductive limits, and the 2-category formed of the karoubian \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories and the arbitrary functors between them.

b) Show that the following conditions are equivalent:

(i) \(E\) is equivalent to a category of the form \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), where \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which the finite inductive limits are representable.

(i bis) As (i), but with moreover \(C\) karoubian.

(ii) The finite inductive limits in \(E\) are representable, the subcategory \(E_{\mathrm{PF}}\) of \(E\) generating by strict epimorphisms, and for every object \(X\) of \(E\), there exists a small part \(I\) of \(\mathrm{Ob}\,(E_{\mathrm{PF}})_{/X}\) such that every object of \((E_{\mathrm{PF}})_{/X}\) is majorized by an object of \(I\). (Use 8.9.5 b.)
8.8. Index representation of a functor \(J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\)

Let \[ \varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \varphi \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C)) \] be a functor, \(C\) being a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Let us recall (8.5.4) that an index representation of \(\varphi\) is by definition an ind-object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\) \[ \widehat{\varphi} : I \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C) , \] \(I\) an essentially small filtered category, whose inductive limit in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\) is isomorphic to \(\varphi\) by a given isomorphism. Thus \(\varphi\) admits an index representation if and only if it is isomorphic to an essentially small filtered inductive limit in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\) of objects of the full subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\). We shall say that the category \(J\) is admissible for \(C\) if every functor \(\varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) admits an index representation.

Since in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) the small filtered inductive limits are representable (8.5.1), the same holds in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\), and they are computed "argument by argument". Consequently, the inclusion functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C) \hookrightarrow \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C)) \tag{8.8.1.1} \] extends canonically to a functor \[ \mathrm{Ind}(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C)) \tag{8.8.1.2} \] (8.7.2). The elements of the essential image of this functor are then precisely the \(\varphi\) admitting an index representation; so to say that \(J\) is admissible for \(C\) also means that the functor (8.8.1.2) is essentially surjective. Let us point out in this connection:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.8.2

If the category \(J\) is equivalent to a finite category, the functor canonical (8.8.1.2) is fully faithful; so \(J\) is admissible for \(C\) if and only if it is an equivalence of categories.

By virtue of 8.7.5 a) everything reduces to proving that for every small filtered inductive system \((\varphi_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\) and every object \(\varphi\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\), the canonical map \[ \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi,\varphi_i) \to \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi, \varinjlim_i \varphi_i) \tag{8.8.2.1} \] is bijective, where \(\varinjlim_i \varphi_i\) denotes the inductive limit taken in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\). Now, if \(\varphi, \psi\) are two functors \(J \to C\), we have an exact diagram of sets, functorial in \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\): \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi,\psi) \to \prod_{X\in\mathrm{Ob}\, J} \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X),\psi(X)) \mathrel{\substack{f\in\mathrm{Fl}\, J \\ \textstyle\rightrightarrows \\ f:X\to Y}} \prod \mathrm{Hom}(\varphi(X),\psi(Y)) . \] Since filtered inductive limits commute with kernels of double arrows and with finite products, the bijectivity of (8.8.2.1) follows when \(J\) is finite. The case where \(J\) is equivalent to a finite category reduces at once to the preceding case.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.8.3

Let \(\varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) be a functor, with \(J\) equivalent to a small category. For \(\varphi\) to admit an indexed representation, it suffices that it satisfy the following two conditions, and this is also necessary when \(J\) is equivalent to a finite category:

a) The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi}\) (formed of the arrows of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\) with target \(\varphi\) and source in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\)) is filtered.

b) For every object \(j\) of \(J\), the functor \[ \psi \mapsto \psi(j) : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi} \to C_{/\varphi(j)} \tag{8.8.3.1} \] is cofinal, i.e. satisfies conditions F 1), F 2) of 8.1.3.

Proof. Suppose a) and b) hold; let us prove that \(\varphi\) admits an indexed representation. We may evidently assume \(J\) small. Let \[ I = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi} , \tag{8.8.3.2} \] which is a filtered category by hypothesis, and let us first assume \(I\) essentially small, so that "the inclusion" of \(I\) into \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\) defines an ind-object of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\), \(i \mapsto \psi_i\). Moreover, we have a canonical homomorphism \[ \varinjlim_i \psi_i \to \varphi , \tag{8.8.3.3} \] given argument by argument by the homomorphism \[ \varinjlim_I \psi_i(j) \to \varphi(j) = \varinjlim_{C_{/\varphi(j)}} X \] deduced from the functor (8.8.3.1). Since the latter is cofinal, we conclude that (8.8.3.3) is an isomorphism, whence the conclusion. In the case where we do not assume \(I\) essentially small, it suffices to construct an essentially small full subcategory \(I'\), such that (8.8.3.3) remains an isomorphism when \(\varinjlim_{I'}\) is taken instead of \(\varinjlim_I\). For this, it suffices that the composite functors \[ I' \to I \to C_{/\varphi(j)} \] induced by the functors (8.8.3.1) all be cofinal. We conclude by means of the following lemma, whose proof is immediate from the criterion (8.1.3 b)), and is left to the reader:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.8.3.4

Let \(I\) be a filtered \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and let \[ f_j : I \to I_j \quad (j \in J) \] be a small family of cofinal functors from \(I\) to essentially small filtered categories. Then there exists a full subcategory \(I'\) of \(I\) that is filtered and essentially small, and such that the functors induced by the \(f_j\) are cofinal.

Let us finally prove necessity in 8.8.3 when we assume \(J\) equivalent to a finite category. An indexed representation of \(\varphi\) by means of an essentially small filtered index category \(I\) defines a functor \(\psi\) \[ \xymatrix{ I \ar[rr]^-{\psi} \ar@{-->}[dr]_-{\psi_j} & & \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi} \ar@{-->}[d] \\ & & C_{/\varphi(j)} } \tag{8.8.3.5} \] and it suffices to prove that \(\psi\) and each of the functors \(\psi_j\) deduced from it are cofinal: by virtue of 8.1.3 b) it will then follow that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi}\) is filtered, and by definition 8.1.1 that the vertical arrow of (8.8.3.5) is likewise cofinal. By virtue of 8.8.2 we may identify \(\varphi\) with an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(E)\), where \(E = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\), and the fact that the functor \[ \psi : I \to E_{/\varphi} , \] deduced from the ind-object \(\varphi\) of \(E\) indexed by \(I\), is cofinal is a general fact, which is verified immediately by means of criteria F 1) and F 2) of 8.1.3. The same reasoning (with \(E, \varphi\) replaced by \(C, \varphi(j)\)) shows that \(\psi_j\) is cofinal, which completes the proof.

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 8.8.4

a) In the case where \(J\) is equivalent to a finite category, if \(\varphi\) admits an indexed representation, we have seen that (8.8.3.5) is a cofinal functor, which implies that the category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi}\) is itself essentially small.

b) Suppose that in \(C\) finite inductive limits are representable. Then the same holds in \(E = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)\), and these are computed argument by argument, and they are likewise inductive limits in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\widehat{C})\) and a fortiori in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,\mathrm{Ind}(C))\). It follows at once that condition a) of 8.8.3 is then automatically satisfied, and everything comes down to examining condition b). I do not know whether it is automatically satisfied when \(J\) is moreover assumed small.
We now come to the main result of the present section:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.8.5

Let \(J\) be a category equivalent to a finite category, and suppose moreover that \(J\) is rigid, i.e. that for every \(j \in \mathrm{Ob}\, J\), every endomorphism of \(j\) is the identity. Then \(J\) is admissible for \(C\) (whatever the \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\) may be), i.e. every functor \(J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) admits an indexed representation.

After replacing \(J\) by an equivalent category if necessary, we may assume that \(J\) is reduced, i.e. that two isomorphic objects of \(J\) are identical. Then \(J\) is even finite. We proceed by induction on \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Ob}\, J\), the case where this number is \(\leq 0\) being trivial; we shall therefore assume it \(\geq 1\). Let \(j_0\) be a maximal object of \(J\), i.e. one such that for every arrow \(j_0 \to j\), there exists an arrow \(j \to j_0\); given that \(J\) is rigid, this implies that \(j_0 \to j\) is an isomorphism, and since \(J\) is reduced, this implies \(j_0 = j\). Let \(J'\) then be the full subcategory obtained from \(J\) by removing the object \(j_0\), and \(J''\) the full subcategory reduced to the object \(j_0\). The proposition then follows from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.8.5.1

Let \(J\) be a finite category, \(J'\) and \(J''\) two full subcategories such that \(\mathrm{Ob}\, J = \mathrm{Ob}\, J' \cup \mathrm{Ob}\, J''\), and such that for every \(j' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, J'\) and \(j'' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, J''\), we have \(\mathrm{Hom}(j'',j') = \varnothing\). If \(J'\) and \(J''\) are admissible for \(C\), so is \(J\).

Everything comes down to proving criteria a) and b) of 8.8.3, which amounts to making six elementary verifications, namely the last two conditions for filtered categories for \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi}\), and conditions F 1) and F 2) for the functors (8.8.3.1), in the case \(j \in \mathrm{Ob}\, J'\) and \(j \in \mathrm{Ob}\, J''\) successively; these latter conditions moreover imply that \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J,C)_{/\varphi}\) is nonempty. The rather tedious verification presents no difficulty, and is left to the reader. (The writer has searched in vain for an elegant proof that would bypass these unpleasant verifications.)

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.8.6

a) Let \(J, J'\) be two categories admissible for \(C\), one of them being finite. Prove that \(J\times J'\) is admissible for \(C\). (Use 8.8.2.)

b) Prove that a small discrete category is admissible for every category \(C\).

c) Let \(J\) be a category satisfying the following conditions: (i) \(J\) is rigid, (ii) \(\mathrm{Ob}\, J\) is countable, (iii) for any two objects \(j, j'\) of \(J\), \(\mathrm{Hom}(j,j')\) is finite, (iv) for every object \(j\) of \(J\), the set of objects of \(J\) that are bounded above by \(j\), i.e. that are the source of an arrow with target \(j\), is finite. Show that \(J\) is admissible for every \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\). (First show that \(J\) can be written as a filtered union of finite full subcategories \(J_n\), such that every object of \(J\) bounded above by an object of \(J_n\) lies in \(J_n\). Then verify criteria a), b) of 8.8.3.)

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.8.7

In our notation we identify an ordered set with the category it defines.

a) Let \(C\) be an ordered set. Let \(\widetilde{C}\) be the set of subsets \(A\) of \(C\) that are filtered and such that \(x \in A\) and \(y \leq x\) imply \(y \in A\). Let \(L_0 : C \to \widetilde{C}\) be the map that associates to every \(x \in C\) the set \(L_0(x)\) of \(y \in C\) such that \(y \leq x\). Show that \(L\) is an injective map and that the order on \(C\) is induced by that of \(\widetilde{C}\). For every \(A \in \widetilde{C}\), consider the inclusion \(f(A) : A \to C\); it is an ind-object of \(C\); for every ind-object \(\varphi : I \to C\) of \(C\), let \(g(\varphi) \in \widetilde{C}\) be the subset of \(C\) formed of the elements of \(C\) bounded above by an element of the form \(\varphi(i)\). Show that we thus obtain two quasi-inverse equivalences of one another \[ \mathrm{Ind}(C) \underset{f}{\overset{g}{\rightleftarrows}} \widetilde{C} , \] taking the functor \(L_0\) to the canonical functor \(L : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

b) Suppose that for every \(x \in C\), the set of elements bounding \(x\) above (resp. below) is finite. Show that every ind-object (resp. pro-object) of \(C\) is essentially constant, and even that for every such \(\varphi : I \to C\) (resp. \(\varphi : I^\circ \to C\)) there exists an \(i_0 \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\) such that the functor induced on \(I_{/i_0}\) is constant (i.e. takes every arrow to an isomorphism).

c) Take \(C \subset \mathbb{N}^\circ \times \mathbb{N}\) formed of the pairs of natural numbers \((j,i)\) such that \(i \geq j\). Show that \(\widetilde{\mathbb{N}}\) is isomorphic to the ordered set obtained from \(\mathbb{N}\) (identified with an ordered subset of \(\widetilde{\mathbb{N}}\) as in a)) by adjoining to it a greatest element \(\infty\). Show that \(\widetilde{C}\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{N}^\circ \times \widetilde{\mathbb{N}}\). Consider the functor \[ \varphi : \mathbb{N}^\circ \to \widetilde{C} , \quad \varphi(j) = (j,\infty) . \] Show that: 1) the projective limit of \(\varphi\) is not representable in \(\widetilde{C}\), although filtered projective limits in \(C\) are representable (and are essentially constant, by virtue of b)). 2) For every functor \(\psi : \mathbb{N}^\circ \to C\), we have \(\mathrm{Hom}(\psi,\varphi) = \varnothing\), and a fortiori the functor \(\varphi\) does not admit a representation in indexed form.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.8.8

Let \(X = \mathbb{N} \sqcup \mathbb{N}\) be the sum set of two copies of \(\mathbb{N}\), \(s\) the symmetry of \(X\), and for every \(i \in \mathbb{N}\), let \(X_i\) be the subset \(\Delta_{i+1} \sqcup \Delta_i\) of \(X\) (where \(\Delta_i\) denotes the subset of \(\mathbb{N}\) formed of the \(j\) such that \(j \leq i\)). Let \(C\) be the subcategory of the category of subsets of \(X\), whose objects are the \(X_i\), and whose arrows are the maps between the \(X_i\) that are induced by the identity of \(X\) or by its symmetry \(s\), and let \(\widetilde{C}\) be the category defined analogously, but where we also allow the object \(X\).

a) Show that \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is equivalent to \(\widetilde{C}\), the canonical functor \(C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) corresponding to the inclusion \(C \to \widetilde{C}\). Show that there is no pair \((Y,f)\) of an object \(Y\) of \(C\) and an endomorphism \(f\) of \(Y\), together with a morphism of objects-with-endomorphism of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) from \((Y,f)\) to \((X,s)\).

b) Deduce that if \(J\) is the category having a single object, and, besides the identity arrow, a single arrow of order 2, then the functor \(J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) defined by \((X,s)\) does not admit an indexed representation.
8.9. Exactness properties of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\)

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.9.1

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

a) The canonical functors \(L\) (8.2.4.8) and \(c\) (8.4.1) \[ C \xrightarrow{\ c\ } \mathrm{Ind}(C) \xrightarrow{\ L\ } \widehat{C} \] commute with projective limits.

b) Suppose that in \(C\) finite inductive limits are representable, and that \(C\) is equivalent to a small category. Then in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) small projective limits are representable.

c) If in \(C\) small projective limits (resp. finite projective limits) are representable, then the same holds in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). Let \(J\) be a category that is finite and rigid, or discrete; if projective limits of type \(J\) are representable in \(C\), this same type of projective limits is representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

d) Small filtered inductive limits in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) (they are representable by virtue of 8.5.1) are left exact, i.e. commute with finite projective limits.

Proof. a) The fact that \(L\) commutes with projective limits follows from the fact that it is fully faithful and from the computation of projective limits in \(\widehat{C}\) "argument by argument", which implies that in order to verify that a projective system of morphisms \(F \to F_i\) (\(i \in I\)) in \(\widehat{C}\) makes \(F\) a projective limit of the \(F_i\), it suffices to verify that the analogous assertion holds for the projective systems of set-theoretic maps \(\mathrm{Hom}(X,F) \to \mathrm{Hom}(X,F_i)\), for every \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\). Now \(C \subset \mathrm{Ind}(C)\).
The fact that \(c\) commutes with projective limits follows formally from the fact that \(L\) commutes with them, as does the composite \(L\circ c : C \to \widehat{C}\).

b) Taking a) into account, the assertion amounts to saying that every projective limit of ind-representable presheaves is ind-representable, which follows at once from criterion 8.3.3 (v), given that a projective limit of left exact functors is left exact (which follows from the fact that "projective limits commute with projective limits" (2.5.0)).

c) Follows formally from the analogous property of \(\widehat{C}\) (3.3), and from the fact that \(L\) is conservative (being fully faithful) and commutes with the limits of the type in question (a) and 8.5.1).

d) It is well known (cf. 2.3) that the representability of finite projective limits is equivalent to that of projective limits of the types \[ \text{empty}\ , \quad \cdot\quad\cdot\ , \quad \cdot \to \cdot \leftarrow \cdot \] (corresponding to particular finite ordered sets), and that of small projective limits amounts to that of products and finite projective limits. Hence the second assertion made in c) implies the first.

Suppose first that \(I\) is finite. Using the result 8.8.5 on the representability of the functor \(\varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) in indexed form (8.5.4) \[ \widehat{\varphi} : J\times I \to C , \tag{8.9.1.1} \] the existence of \(\varprojlim \varphi\) is thus a special case of the following more precise and more general result:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.9.2

Consider a functor \(\varphi : J \to \mathrm{Ind}(C)\) given in indexed form \(\widehat{\varphi}\) (8.9.1.1), \(J\) being a finite category. If for every \(i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\), the partial functor \(j \mapsto \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)\) has a projective (resp. inductive) limit representable in \(C\), then \(\varphi\) has a projective (resp. inductive) limit representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), and we have a canonical isomorphism \[ \varprojlim_j \varphi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} \varprojlim_j \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) \tag{8.9.2.1} \] (resp. \[ \varinjlim_i \varphi \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} \varinjlim_j \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) ) , \tag{8.9.2.2} \] where \(\varprojlim_j\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_j\)) is computed in \(C\).

For the first formula, we simply use that in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) filtered inductive limits commute with \(\varprojlim_j\), and that \(c\) commutes with \(\varprojlim_j\) (8.9.1 d) and a)): \[ \varprojlim_j \varphi = \varprojlim_j \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»}\,\varprojlim_j^{\mathrm{Ind}(C)} \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»}\,\varprojlim_j^{C} \widehat{\varphi}(j,i) . \] The second is proved similarly, using the commutation of inductive limits of type \(I\) with inductive limits of type \(J\) (2.5.0) and the fact that \(c\) commutes with inductive limits of type \(J\), proved in 8.9.4 a) below.
The case \(J\) discrete. This case is contained in the following more precise assertion:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.9.3

Let \(I_\alpha\) be essentially small filtered categories indexed by a small set \(A\), and for every \(\alpha \in A\), let \(X(\alpha) = (X(\alpha)_{i_\alpha})_{i_\alpha\in I_\alpha}\) be an ind-object of \(C\) indexed by \(I_\alpha\). Let \(I\) be the product category of the \(I_\alpha\), and suppose that for every \(i = (i_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A} \in I\), the product \(\prod_{\alpha\in A} X(\alpha)_{i_\alpha}\) is representable in \(C\). Then the product \(\prod_{\alpha\in A} X(\alpha)\) is representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), and it is canonically isomorphic to the ind-object indexed by \(I\) given by the formula \[ \prod_{\alpha\in A} \text{«}\varinjlim_{i_\alpha\in I_\alpha}\text{»} X(\alpha)_{i_\alpha} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varinjlim_{i=(i_\alpha)_{\alpha\in A}\in I}\text{»} \Bigl(\prod_{\alpha\in A} X(\alpha)_{i_\alpha}\Bigr) , \tag{8.9.3.1} \] where the product on the right-hand side is the product computed in \(C\). (Note that \(I\) is filtered and essentially small, since the \(I_\alpha\) are.)

Indeed, it is well known (and immediate by reduction to the case where one works in the category of sets) that the formula in question holds when the limits are computed in \(\widehat{C}\). The conclusion then follows from the fact that \(L\) commutes with the limits in question (8.9.1 a) and 8.5.1).

blocks.title: Remarks
blocks.html:
Remarks 8.9.4

The proof given of 8.9.2, 8.9.3 shows, more generally, that if for every \(i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\), \(\varprojlim_j \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_j \widehat{\varphi}(j,i)\)) computed in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is representable, then so is \(\varprojlim_j \varphi\) (resp. \(\varinjlim_j \varphi\)). This, together with the argument of c), shows that for a given category \(J\) arising from a finite or discrete ordered set (or more generally, that is \(C\)-admissible (8.8.1)), the projective (resp. inductive) limits of type \(J\) are representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) if (and only if) for every functor \(\varphi : J \to C\), the projective (resp. inductive) limit of \(\varphi\) computed in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is representable. In the non-resp. case, this also means, by virtue of a), that every projective limit of type \(J\) of presheaves representable on \(C\) is ind-representable.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.9.5

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

a) The canonical functor \[ c : C \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) \] is right exact (hence exact, given 8.9.1 a)).

b) If finite inductive limits (resp. finite sums) are representable in \(C\), then small inductive limits (resp. small sums) are representable in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). Let \(J\) be a finite or discrete preordered set; if inductive limits of type \(J\) are representable in \(C\), the same holds in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

Proof. a) Suppose that in \(C\) we have \(X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_j X_j\), where \(J\) is a finite category, \(X\) and the \(X_j\) in \(C\). Then, for every ind-object \(\underline{Y} = (Y_i)_{i\in I}\) of \(C\): \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Hom}(X,\underline{Y}) &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X,Y_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_i \varprojlim_j \mathrm{Hom}(X_j,Y_i) \\ &\overset{2.8}{\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }} \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_j,Y_i) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_j \mathrm{Hom}(X_j,\underline{Y}) , \end{aligned} \] and the desired conclusion follows from comparing the extreme terms.

b) We have already noted in 8.9.4 that the assertions made follow from a) and from 8.9.2, at least for finite inductive limits. To prove the conclusions made in the infinite cases, we are reduced to the case of sums, which can be interpreted as a filtered inductive limit of finite sums, and we conclude accordingly by 8.5.1.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.9.6

We have already observed that the functor \(c\) does not commute in general with filtered inductive limits, and hence not with infinite sums either, unlike what happens for \(L : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \widehat{C}\). On the other hand, apart from commutation with filtered inductive limits (8.5.1), \(L\) practically never has commutation properties with any other type of inductive limit (initial object, sum of two objects, cokernels of double arrows). Thus, if \(C\) has an initial object \(\varnothing_C\), which is therefore an initial object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) by virtue of a), \(\varnothing_C\) is never an initial object of \(\widehat{C}\) (i.e. identical to the constant presheaf with value \(\varnothing\)), since \(\mathrm{Hom}(\varnothing_C,\varnothing_C) \neq \varnothing\)!

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.9.7

Let \[ f : C \to C' \] be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, and let \(J\) be a finite and rigid category (8.8.5). If inductive (resp. projective) limits of type \(J\) are representable in \(C\) and \(f\) commutes with them, then \(\mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C')\) also commutes with this type of limits.
This follows at once from 8.8.5 and from the computation 8.9.2 of finite limits in a category of ind-objects, for a functor represented in indexed form.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.9.8

If in \(C\) finite inductive (resp. projective) limits are representable, and if \(f\) is right exact (resp. left exact), then so is \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\); in the non-resp. case, \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) even commutes with arbitrary small inductive limits.
The first assertion follows from 8.9.7. The second follows from the first, given that \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) commutes with filtered inductive limits (8.6.3).

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.9.9

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

a) Suppose that finite sums are representable in \(C\). Show that if in \(C\) the finite sums are disjoint (resp. universal) (cf. II 4.5), then in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) the small sums are disjoint (resp. universal).

b) Suppose that in \(C\) every morphism factors as an epimorphism followed by a monomorphism (resp. as an effective epimorphism followed by a monomorphism, resp. as an epimorphism followed by an effective monomorphism, resp. an effective epimorphism followed by an effective monomorphism). Show that \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) satisfies the same property. In the last resp. case, we conclude that every epimorphism of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is effective, every monomorphism of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is effective, every bimorphism of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is an isomorphism; show that in this case every epimorphism (resp. monomorphism) of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) can be represented by an inductive system of epimorphisms (resp. of monomorphisms) of \(C\). If we further assume that in \(C\) every epimorphism (resp. every monomorphism) is universal, the same property holds in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\).

c) Suppose \(C\) additive (resp. abelian); then \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is likewise.

d) Let \(X = \text{«}\varinjlim_I\text{»} X_i\) be an ind-object of \(C\), \(R \rightrightarrows X\) an equivalence relation on \(X\). For every \(i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\), let \(R_i \rightrightarrows X_i\) be the equivalence relation on \(X_i\) (regarded as an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\)) induced by \(R\) via \(X_i \to X\). (We assume that the fibre product \(R_i = R \times_{X\times X} (X_i\times X_i)\) in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) is representable by an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), which is the case if finite projective limits are representable in \(C\).) Show that for \(R\) to be effective, it suffices that the \(R_i\) be so.

e) Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\), \(R\) an equivalence relation on \(c(X)\), i.e. on \(X\) regarded as an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). Suppose that fibre products are representable in \(C\). For \(R\) to be effective, it is necessary that \(R\) be of the form \(\text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} R_i\), where the \(R_i\) are equivalence relations on \(X\) (regarded as an object of \(C\)), and this condition is sufficient if we assume that equivalence relations are effective in \(C\).

f) Suppose that in \(C\) every morphism factors as an effective epimorphism followed by an effective monomorphism, and that finite projective limits are representable. Let \(X\) be an object of \(C\), and \(R\) a subobject of \(X\times X\), regarded as an element of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\). Let us write \(R\) in the form \(\text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} Z_i\), where \((Z_i)_{i\in I}\) is an increasing filtered family of subobjects of \(X\times X\) in \(C\) (this is possible by b)). Show that for \(R\) to be an equivalence relation on \(X\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every \(i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\), there exist a \(j \in \mathrm{Ob}\, I\) containing \(s(Z_i)\) and \(Z_i \circ Z_i\), where \(s\) is the symmetry of \(X\times X\).

g) Suppose that in \(C\) finite projective limits as well as finite sums are representable, that every equivalence relation there is effective, and that every morphism factors there into an effective epimorphism followed by an effective monomorphism. Show that in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) equivalence relations are universal if and only if \(C\) satisfies the following condition:

(ST) For every object \(X\) of \(C\) and every subobject \(Z\) of \(X\times X\) in \(C\), if we define by induction the sequence of subobjects \(Z_n\) (\(n \geq 0\)) of \(X\times X\) in \(C\) by \(Z_0 = Z\), \(Z_{n+1} = \mathrm{Sup}(Z_n, s(Z_n), Z_n \circ Z_n)\) (the Sup taken in the set of subobjects of \(X\times X\), which exists thanks to the hypotheses made on \(C\)), then the sequence \((Z_n)_{n\geq 0}\) is stationary.

k) Show that in \(\mathrm{Ind}((\mathrm{Ens}))\), equivalence relations are not necessarily effective.

NB. For criteria for \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) to be a topos, cf. VI 8.9.9 .

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.9.10

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Set \(\mathrm{Pro}(C) = (\mathrm{Ind}(C^\circ))^\circ\) (cf. 8.11).

a) Suppose that finite sums (resp. small sums) are representable in \(C\). Show that if they are disjoint (cf. II 4.5), then \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) satisfies the same condition.

b) Let \(J\) be a small set, such that sums indexed by \(J\) are representable in \(C\), hence also in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\). Let \((X(\alpha))_{\alpha\in J}\) be a family of elements of \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\), with \(X(\alpha) = \text{«}\varprojlim_{I_\alpha}\text{»} X_{i_\alpha}\). Show that for the sum of the \(X(\alpha)\) in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) to be universal, it suffices that the same hold for each of the families \(\varprojlim_J X_{i_\alpha}\), where \((i_\alpha)_{\alpha\in J} \in \prod_{\alpha\in J} I_\alpha\). Deduce that if in \(C\) sums of type \(J\) are universal, then for the same to hold in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\), it is necessary and sufficient that for every family \((X(\alpha))_{\alpha\in J}\) as above, with \(I_\alpha = I\) for every \(\alpha\in J\), the canonical homomorphism in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) \[ \text{«}\varprojlim_I\text{»} \coprod_\alpha X(\alpha)_i \leftarrow \text{«}\varprojlim_{I^J}\text{»} \coprod_{\alpha\in J} X(\alpha)_{i_\alpha} \] be an isomorphism. Deduce that in \(\mathrm{Pro}((\mathrm{Ens}))\) sums of type \(J\) are universal if and only if \(J\) is finite.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.9.11

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

a) Let \((X_i \to X)_{i\in I}\) be a family of morphisms in \(C\). Show that for it to be epimorphic in \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\), it suffices that there exist a finite subfamily that is epimorphic in \(C\). Prove that this condition is also necessary when we assume that in \(C\) every finite family of morphisms with target \(X_i\) factors as an epimorphic family, followed by an effective monomorphism (10.5). (For this last assertion, let \(P\) be the set of finite subsets of \(I\), ordered by inclusion, and let \(X' = (X_J')_{J\in P}\) be the ind-object formed of the images of the finite subfamilies of the given family, and finally let \(X'' = X \sqcup_{X'} X = \text{«}\varinjlim\text{»} X \sqcup_{X_J'} X\). Show that the two canonical morphisms \(X \rightrightarrows X''\) are distinct, but coincide on the \(X_J'\).)

b) Suppose that in \(C\) every finite family of morphisms with the same target factors as an epimorphic family, followed by an effective monomorphism. Prove that \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) admits a small generating subcategory by epimorphisms (7.1) if and only if \(C\) admits a small subcategory \(C'\) such that every object of \(C\) is the target of a finite epimorphic family with source in \(C'\). When we assume that \(C\) admits a small generating subcategory (7.1), then \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) admits a small generating subcategory by epimorphisms if and only if \(C\) is equivalent to a small category. (For this last statement, use 7.5.2).

c) \(\mathrm{Ind}((\mathrm{Ens}))\) does not admit a small generating subcategory.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 8.9.12

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and consider \(\mathrm{Pro}(C) = \mathrm{Ind}(C^\circ)^\circ\).

a) Show that if \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) admits a small subcategory \(P'\) generating by epimorphisms (7.1), then there exists a small subcategory \(C'\) of \(C\) that is generating by epimorphisms in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\). (Take the category of components of the objects of \(P'\).)

b) Show that the category \(\mathrm{Pro}((\mathrm{Ens}))\) has no small generating subcategory by epimorphisms. (If \(C'\) is as in a), choose a set \(X\) whose cardinal strictly exceeds the cardinals of the elements of \(C'\), and consider the pro-set \(\underline{X}\) formed by the complements in \(X\) of the subsets of cardinal \(< \mathrm{card}(X)\). Show that for every set \(Y\) nonempty of cardinal \(< \mathrm{card}(X)\), we have \(\mathrm{Hom}(Y,\underline{X}) = \varnothing\), but that \(\underline{X}\) is not isomorphic to the constant pro-set \(\varnothing\).)
8.10. Dual notions: pro-objects, pro-representable functors

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. We call a pro-object of \(C\) any functor \[ \varphi : I^\circ \to C , \tag{8.10.1} \] where \(I\) is an essentially small filtered category (called the index category), and as usual \(I^\circ\) denotes the opposite category. Let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a universe such that \(\mathcal{V} \supset \mathcal{U}\). Note that the pro-objects of \(C\) indexed by \(I \in \mathcal{V}\) are in one-to-one correspondence with the ind-objects of \(C^\circ\) indexed by \(I \in \mathcal{V}\), by associating to every such ind-object \(\psi : I \to C^\circ\) the pro-object \(\varphi = \psi^\circ : I^\circ \to C\). Following this correspondence, we define "by transport of structure and reversal of arrows" the notion of morphism between pro-objects of \(C\) from the analogous notion (8.2.4.2), (8.2.5.1) for ind-objects, and we define accordingly the category of pro-objects of \(C\) indexed by \(I \in \mathcal{V}\), and a canonical isomorphism: \[ \mathrm{Pro}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Ind}_{\mathcal{V}}(C^\circ,\mathcal{U})^\circ ; \tag{8.10.2} \] for \(\mathcal{V} = \mathcal{U}\) we simply speak of the category of pro-objects of \(C\), denoted \(\mathrm{Pro}_{\mathcal{U}}(C)\) or simply \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\), which is thus defined by \[ \mathrm{Pro}(C) = \mathrm{Pro}_{\mathcal{U}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Ind}(C^\circ)^\circ . \tag{8.10.3} \] If two pro-objects are given in indexed form \[ \underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I} , \quad \underline{Y} = (Y_j)_{j\in J} , \tag{8.10.4} \] formula (8.2.5.1) here takes the form \[ \mathrm{Hom}(\underline{X},\underline{Y}) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,Y_j) . \tag{8.10.5} \] The functor (8.4.1) applied to \(C^\circ\) gives, by passing to opposite categories, a canonical functor (denoted by the same letter \(c\) when there is no risk of confusion), allowing us to identify \(C\) with a full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\): \[ c : C \to \mathrm{Pro}(C) ; \tag{8.10.6} \] it is in order to have such a functor, rather than \(C \to \mathrm{Pro}(C)^\circ\), that we "reversed the arrows" in the definition of morphisms of pro-objects from the analogous definition for ind-objects. The pro-objects in the essential image of (8.10.6) are also called essentially constant pro-objects.

Let us set \[ \check{C} = (C^\circ)^\wedge = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,(\mathrm{Ens})) , \tag{8.10.7} \] then the functor (8.2.4.7) can be regarded as a canonical fully faithful functor \[ L : \mathrm{Pro}_{\mathcal{V}}(C,\mathcal{U}) \to \check{C}^\circ , \tag{8.10.8} \] and in particular we find \[ L : \mathrm{Pro}(C) \hookrightarrow \check{C}^\circ . \tag{8.10.9} \]

We shall leave it to the reader to translate, as the need arises, the results of the preceding sections and of those that follow from the language of ind-objects into that of pro-objects. Depending on the mathematical context, it is one language or the other that is the more useful, not to mention the cases where the two notions arise simultaneously, for example when it is appropriate to consider complex categories such as \(\mathrm{Pro}(\mathrm{Ind}(C))\) or \(\mathrm{Ind}(\mathrm{Pro}(C))\). We content ourselves with giving a few additional indications, in order to fix the terminology and notation, and to make precise the "yoga".

A covariant functor \(F : C \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) is said to be a pro-representable functor if it lies in the essential image of (8.10.9) (or of 8.10.8, which amounts to the same thing); the full subcategory of \(\check{C}\) formed of these functors is thus equivalent to \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)^\circ\). One will generally prefer to work in the opposite category, the essential image as a subcategory of (8.10.9), which is thus equivalent to \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) itself. In keeping with this usage, it is often preferable to regard covariant functors \[ F : C \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] as objects of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,(\mathrm{Ens}))^\circ = \check{C}^\circ\), and accordingly to write the category of homomorphisms \[ X \to F \quad \text{in} \quad \check{C}^\circ , \] i.e. of pairs \((X,u)\) of an object \(X\) of \(C\) and a \(u \in F(X)\), as \[ {}_F\backslash C . \tag{8.10.11} \] With this convention, we thus find a covariant functor (source functor) \[ {}_F\backslash C \to C , \tag{8.10.12} \] and 3.4 is rewritten in the form \[ F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \text{«}\varprojlim\text{»}_{({}_F\backslash C)^\circ} X . \tag{8.10.13} \]

Criterion 8.3.3 applied to \(C^\circ\) becomes a criterion for pro-representability of \(F\): it is necessary and sufficient that \(({}_F\backslash C)^\circ\) be filtered and essentially small, this latter condition being superfluous if \(C\) is equivalent to a small category; if moreover finite projective limits are representable in \(C\), it amounts to the same to say that \(F\) commutes with them, i.e. is left exact.

In \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) small filtered projective limits are representable and the functor (8.10.9) commutes with them; in other words, this functor transforms projective limits in \(\mathrm{Pro}(C)\) into inductive limits of \(\check{C} = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,(\mathrm{Ens}))\), just like its composite \(C \to \check{C}^\circ\) with (8.10.6), which shares with it the unfortunate property of being contravariant when regarded as taking values in \(\check{C}\). Note that the pro-representable functors from \(C\) to \((\mathrm{Ens})\) are the functors that are small filtered inductive limits of representable functors (and not projective limits, as the terminology might possibly suggest).
8.11. Ind-adjoints and pro-adjoints

Let \[ f : C \to C' \tag{8.11.1.1} \] be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories, whence a functor \(F \mapsto F\circ f\) \[ f^* : \widehat{C'} \to \widehat{C} . \tag{8.11.1.2} \] We say that \(f\) admits an ind-adjoint if the preceding functor carries ind-representable functors to ind-representable functors. Since \(f^*\) commutes with inductive limits, and the full subcategory of \(\widehat{C'}\) formed of the ind-representable functors is stable under small filtered inductive limits, it amounts to the same to say that \(f\) admits an ind-adjoint, or that \(f^*\) carries objects of \(C\) (identified with a full subcategory of \(\widehat{C}\)) to ind-representable functors on \(C\), i.e. \[ X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(f(X),Y') \text{ is ind-representable for every } Y' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C'. \tag{8.11.1.3} \] Another way of expressing the condition that \(f\) admits an ind-adjoint is to say that there exists a functor \[ g : \mathrm{Ind}(C') \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) \tag{8.11.1.4} \] that is essentially induced by \(f^*\), i.e. such that we have an isomorphism of bifunctors \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)}(X,g(\underline{Y'})) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C')}(f(X),\underline{Y'}) , \tag{8.11.1.5} \] where \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\) and \(\underline{Y'} \in \mathrm{Ob}\, \mathrm{Ind}(C')\). In fact, it even suffices to have a functor \[ g_0 : C' \to \mathrm{Ind}(C) \tag{8.11.1.6} \] and an isomorphism of bifunctors \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)}(X,g_0(Y')) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{C'}(f(X),Y') \tag{8.11.1.7} \] in \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), \(Y' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C'\). The functor \(g\) (resp. \(g_0\)) is evidently determined up to unique isomorphism by \(f\), and conversely \(f\) is recovered up to canonical isomorphism from the knowledge of this \(g\) (resp. \(g_0\)). It is clear from (8.11.1.5) that the functor \(g\) commutes with inductive limits, and that it "extends" the functor \(g_0\); this therefore determines it up to unique isomorphism in terms of \(g_0\) (8.7.2). The functor \(g\), and sometimes also the functor \(g_0\) that it extends, is called the ind-adjoint functor of \(f\) (there is no need here to specify: on the right, since the other one, if it exists, will be called the pro-adjoint, cf. 8.11.5 below).

Of course, when \(f\) admits a right adjoint \[ f^{\mathrm{ad}} : C' \to C , \] it admits an ind-adjoint \(g\), and the latter is canonically isomorphic to the canonical extension of \(f\) to ind-objects: \[ g \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Ind}(f^{\mathrm{ad}}) . \tag{8.11.1.8} \] The notion of ind-adjoint is thus a natural generalization of the notion of right adjoint.
Let us now consider the canonical extension \[ \mathrm{Ind}(f) : \mathrm{Ind}(C) \to \mathrm{Ind}(C') . \tag{8.11.1.9} \] We then have:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.11.2

For the functor \(f : C \to C'\) to admit an ind-adjoint, it is necessary and sufficient that the functor \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) (8.11.1.9) admit a right adjoint. The latter is canonically isomorphic to the ind-adjoint (8.11.1.4).

Sufficiency and the last assertion are trivial from the formula of ind-adjunction (8.11.1.5). For necessity, we note that by passing to the projective limit in this formula over the \(X_i\), we deduce an adjunction isomorphism in the ind-objects \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) and \(\underline{Y'}\): \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C)}(\underline{X}, g(\underline{Y'})) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Ind}(C')}(\mathrm{Ind}(f)(\underline{X}),\underline{Y'}) , \tag{8.11.2.1} \] Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.11.3

If \(f\) admits an ind-adjoint, then \(\mathrm{Ind}(f)\) commutes with inductive limits, and the ind-adjoint \(g\) commutes with projective limits.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.11.4

For the functor \(f : C \to C'\) to admit an ind-adjoint, it is necessary that \(f\) be left exact, and this condition is sufficient when \(C\) is equivalent to a small category.
This follows from the criterion (8.11.1.3), and from 8.3.1 and 8.3.3 (iv).
For another criterion in terms of the notion of accessible functor, cf. 8.13.3.

Let us now consider the functor \(F \mapsto F\circ f\) \[ f^{\circ *} : \check{C'} \to \check{C} \tag{8.11.5.1} \] induced by \(F\). We say that \(f\) admits a pro-adjoint if the preceding functor carries pro-representable functors to pro-representable functors, i.e. if there exists a functor (called the pro-adjoint functor of \(f\)) \[ g : \mathrm{Pro}(C') \to \mathrm{Pro}(C) , \tag{8.11.5.2} \] and an isomorphism of bifunctors \[ \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Pro}(C)}(g(\underline{Y'}),X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{Pro}(C')}(\underline{Y'},f(X)) . \tag{8.11.5.3} \] Of course, to say that \(f\) admits a pro-adjoint means that \(f^\circ\) admits an ind-adjoint, so that the notions and results for ind-adjoints translate trivially in terms of pro-adjoints. Let us merely note that \(f\) admits a pro-adjoint if and only if \(\mathrm{Pro}(f) : \mathrm{Pro}(C) \to \mathrm{Pro}(C')\) admits a right adjoint, and that in this case the preceding functor \(g\) is such a right adjoint of \(\mathrm{Pro}(f)\); and that for this it is necessary that \(f\) be left exact, this condition being likewise sufficient when \(C\) is equivalent to a small category. In this case, \(f\) is thus exact if and only if it admits both an ind-adjoint and a pro-adjoint.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 8.11.6

Consider the case of a functor \[ f : C \to (\mathrm{Ens}) . \] If this functor admits a pro-adjoint, it is pro-representable, and the converse holds if and only if the full subcategory of \(\check{C}\) formed of the pro-representable functors is stable under small products; this is the case in particular if \(C\) is equivalent to a small category (8.10.14) or if small products are representable in \(C\) (8.9.5 b) applied to \(C^\circ\)). More or less, we may thus say that for a functor \(f : C \to C'\), the notion of the existence of a pro-adjoint is the natural generalization of the notion of pro-representability of \(f\), which is defined when \(C' = (\mathrm{Ens})\).
8.12. Strict ind-objects and pro-objects. Application to a representability criterion

Let \[ \underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I} \] be an ind-object of the \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C\), and let \(F\) be the presheaf that it ind-represents. We then see at once that it amounts to the same to say that the canonical morphisms \[ X_i \to F = \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} X_i \] are monomorphisms of \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) (or, equivalently, of \(\widehat{C}\), i.e. monomorphisms of functors "argument by argument"), or to say that for every arrow \(i \to j\) of \(I\), the corresponding transition arrow \[ X_i \to X_j \] is a monomorphism. When these conditions are satisfied, and if moreover \(I\) is an ordered category, we say that \(\underline{X}\) is a strict ind-object. Note that this condition is not invariant under isomorphism of ind-objects; an ind-object will be called essentially strict if it is isomorphic to a strict ind-object. A presheaf will be called strictly ind-representable if it is ind-representable by a strict ind-object; hence \(F = \text{«}\varinjlim_i\text{»} X_i\) is strictly ind-representable if and only if \(\underline{X} = (X_i)_{i\in I}\) is essentially strict.

Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\), and consider the full subcategory of \(C_{/F}\) formed of the arrows \(X \to F\) with source in \(C\) that are monomorphisms. We shall call it the category of representable subfunctors of \(F\); it is the category associated to the ordered set of representable subfunctors of \(F\), ordered by the order induced from that of the set of subobjects of \(F\). It then follows at once from the definitions:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.12.2

For the presheaf \(F\) on \(C\) to be strictly ind-representable, it is necessary and sufficient that the (ordered) category \(I\) of representable subfunctors of \(F\) be filtered and essentially small and that we have \[ \varinjlim_I X_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } F , \tag{8.12.2.1} \]

When, for every object \(X\) of \(C\), the set of subobjects of \(X\) in \(C\) is small (for example if \(C\) admits a small generating subcategory (7.4)), this implies that the category of representable subfunctors is even small.

If \(F\) is strictly ind-representable, there is thus a privileged way of ind-representing it by an ind-object, and the latter is even a strict ind-object: we take the representation (8.12.2.1). A strict ind-object \(\underline{Y}\) is said to be saturated if it is isomorphic to an ind-object of the form \((X_i)\) occurring in (8.12.2.1), for suitable \(F\); hence there exists, up to unique isomorphism, a single saturated strict ind-object isomorphic to the given strict ind-object, namely the one considered in 8.12.2, taking \(F = \varinjlim \underline{Y}\) (limit in \(\widehat{C}\)).

Suppose that we already know that one can find a small cofinal subset in the set \(\mathrm{Ob}\, C_{/F}\), which is the case in particular if \(F\) is ind-representable; then it follows that the same condition holds in the full subcategory \(I\) considered in 8.12.2, so that in criterion 8.12.2 we may omit the condition that \(I\) be essentially small.

Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\), and consider an object \[ u : X \to F \] of \(C_{/F}\). We say that \(u\) (or the pair \((X,u)\)) is minimal if for every factorization of \(u\) as \[ X \xrightarrow{\ p\ } X' \xrightarrow{\ u'\ } F , \tag{8.12.3.1} \] with \(p\) a strict epimorphism (10.2), \(p\) is an isomorphism. Regarding \(u\) as an object of \(F(X)\) (1.4) , to say that \(u\) is minimal thus means that every strict epimorphism \(p : X \to X'\) such that \(u \in \mathrm{Im}(F(p) : F(X') \to F(X))\) is an isomorphism. This notion is clarified by part a) of the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.12.4

Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\).

a) Suppose that \(F\) transforms cokernels into kernels and consider a morphism \[ u : X \to F , \] with \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\). For \(u\) to be a monomorphism it suffices, when the cokernels of double arrows are representable in \(C\), that \(u\) be minimal; this condition is also necessary if the fibre products are representable in \(C\).

b) Suppose that in \(C\) the finite \(\varprojlim\) are representable. For the subcategory of representable subfunctors of \(F\) (8.12.1.1) to be filtered (not necessarily small) and to have \(F\) as its inductive limit, it suffices that \(F\) be left exact and that every morphism \(u : X \to F\), with \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), factor as \[ X \to X' \xrightarrow{\ u'\ } F , \] with \(u'\) minimal; this condition is also necessary if the fibre products are representable in \(C\).

c) Suppose that \(C\) admits a small generating subcategory (7.1), and that \(I\), the category of representable subfunctors of \(F\), is filtered; then \(I\) is small.

Proof. a) Suppose \(u\) minimal; let us prove that \(u\) is a monomorphism, i.e. that for every double arrow \(v, v' : Y \rightrightarrows X\) such that \(uv = uv'\), we have \(v = v'\). Indeed, if \(X' = \mathrm{Coker}(v,v')\), then \(u\) factors as \(X \xrightarrow{\ p\ } X' \xrightarrow{\ u'\ } F\) (\(F\) transforming cokernels into kernels), and since \(p\) is a strict epimorphism by construction, it follows that \(p\) is an isomorphism, i.e. \(v = v'\). Suppose that \(u\) is a monomorphism; let us prove that it is minimal. Consider a factorization (8.12.3.1); since \(p\) is a strict epimorphism, it is the cokernel of the canonical double arrow \(v, v' : X\times_{X'} X \rightrightarrows X\), and since \((u'p)v = (u'p)v'\) and \(u'p = u\) is a monomorphism, we have \(v = v'\), hence \(p\) is an isomorphism.

b) Sufficiency: Since \(F\) is left exact, \(C_{/F}\) is filtered. Since we know that \(F = \varinjlim_{C_{/F}} X\), we are reduced by 8.1.3 c) to proving that the full subcategory \(I\) of \(C_{/F}\) consisting of the subobjects of \(F\) is cofinal in \(C_{/F}\); but by virtue of the "it suffices" in a), this is what is guaranteed by the assumption that every object of \(C_{/F}\) is dominated by a "minimal" object. Necessity: Since every filtered inductive limit of right-exact functors is likewise so, the first condition is trivially necessary. The second then follows from the "it is necessary" in a).

c) A representable subfunctor \(X \hookrightarrow F\) of \(F\) is known once one knows the full subcategory \(C'_{/X}\) of \(C'_{/F}\), where \(C'\) is a fixed small generating subcategory of \(C\). (Use the assumption that \(I\) is filtered.) Since \(C'_{/F}\) is small, the set of its full subcategories is small, whence the conclusion.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.12.5

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which finite inductive limits are representable, and admitting a small generating subcategory (7.1). Let \(F\) be a presheaf on \(C\). For \(F\) to be strictly ind-representable it suffices that it satisfy the following two conditions, and these are also necessary if the fibre products are representable in \(C\):

a) \(F\) is left exact.

b) Every pair \((X,u)\), with \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\) and \(u \in F(X)\), is dominated in \(C_{/F}\) by a minimal pair (8.12.3), i.e. there exist a minimal pair \((X',u')\) (\(X' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\), \(u' \in F(X')\)) and a morphism \(f : X \to X'\) such that \(u = F(f)(u')\).
The sufficiency follows from 8.12.2 and from 8.12.4 b), c), the necessity from 8.3.1 and from 8.12.4 a).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 8.12.6

When \(F\) transforms amalgamated sums in \(C\) into fibre products, one sees at once that for a pair \((X,u)\) given as in b), the set of strict quotients \(X'\) of \(X\) such that \(u \in \mathrm{Im}(F(X') \to F(X))\) is decreasingly filtered, which implies that if the set of strict quotients of \(X\) is artinian, then condition b) of 8.12.5 is automatically satisfied. Hence if the preceding condition on \(X\) is satisfied for every object \(X\) of \(C\) (one then also says, sometimes, that the objects of \(C^\circ\) are artinian), then it follows from 8.12.5 that \(F\) is strictly ind-representable if and only if \(F\) is left exact; in this case, \(F\) is therefore strictly ind-representable as soon as it is ind-representable (8.3.1).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.12.7

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which small projective limits are representable, and admitting a small cogenerating subcategory (7.9, 7.13). Then a functor \(F : C \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) is representable if and only if \(F\) commutes with small projective limits.

The necessity is clear. For the sufficiency, we apply 8.12.5 to the opposite category \(C^\circ\). To prove first that \(F\) is (strictly) pro-representable, we are reduced to proving that every pair \((X,u)\), \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\) and \(u \in F(X)\), is dominated by a "minimal" pair. Now the family \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) of strict subobjects of \(X\) such that \(u \in \mathrm{Im}(F(X_i) \to F(X))\) is small (7.5 in dual form). Thanks to the fact that \(F\) is left exact, it is \(\infty\)-filtered (8.12.6), and thanks to the fact that \(F\) commutes with small projective limits we see that \(X' = \varprojlim_I X_i\) is a smallest object of this family. (Use the fact that \(F\), being left exact, transforms monomorphisms into monomorphisms.) If \(u' \in F(X')\) is the unique element whose image in \(F(X)\) is \(u\), we then see that \((X',u')\) is a minimal pair dominating \((X,u)\). This proves that \(F\) is pro-representable, and the conclusion then follows from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 8.12.8.1

Let \(F : C \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) be a functor, where \(C\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category in which the small projective limits are representable. For \(F\) to be representable it is necessary and sufficient that it be pro-representable and that it commute with small projective limits.

The necessity is clear; let us prove the sufficiency. To say that \(F\) is representable evidently means that \({}_F\backslash C\) admits an initial object (in fact, the initial objects of \({}_F\backslash C\) are precisely the isomorphisms \(F \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X\), i.e. the representation data for \(F\)). Now since \(F\) is pro-representable, \(({}_F\backslash C)^\circ\) is filtered and equivalent to a small category, so \(X = \varprojlim_{({}_F\backslash C)^\circ} X\) is representable in \(C\), and since \(F\) commutes with the limit under consideration, it follows that \(X\) is an initial object of \({}_F\backslash C\), q.e.d.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.12.8

The hypotheses on \(C\) being those of 8.12.7, let \(f : C \to C'\) be a functor from \(C\) to a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(C'\). For \(f\) to admit a left adjoint it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) commute with small projective limits.
This indeed reduces trivially to 8.12.7, by applying that statement to the composite functors of the form \(X \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(Y',f(X))\).

blocks.title: Examples
blocks.html:
Examples 8.12.9

As we pointed out in 7.13, the hypotheses on \(C\) of 8.12.7 and 8.12.8 are satisfied if \(C\) is the category of \(\mathcal{U}\)-sheaves of sets on a topological space \(X \in \mathcal{U}\) (or more generally, on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (II 3.0.2)). Let us give an instructive example∗ which shows that the hypothesis of existence of a small cogenerating subcategory \(D\) of \(C\) is not superfluous in 8.12.7. Take for \(C\) the category of groups that are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\). Let \(J\) be the set of isomorphism classes of simple groups \(\in C\), choose for each \(j \in J\) a simple group \(G_j\) in the class of \(j\), and let \(I\) be the filtered ordered set of \(\mathcal{U}\)-small subsets of \(J\), and for \(i \in I\), let \(X_i = \coprod_{j\in i} G_j\). The \(X_i\) then form a projective system \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(C\), with transition morphisms that are epimorphisms, and the corresponding functor \[ F(X) = \varinjlim_i \mathrm{Hom}(X_i,X) \tag{\(*\)} \] takes its values in \((\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\) (although the index set \(I\) evidently does not have a cardinal \(\in \mathcal{U}\)); more precisely, let us show that for every small full subcategory \(C_0\) of \(C\), there exists an \(i_0 \in I\) such that the restriction of \(F\) to \(C_0\) is representable by \(X_{i_0}\), which will prove both that \(F\) takes its values in \(\mathcal{U}\)-Ens, and that it commutes with the small projective limits. To prove our assertion, it suffices to note that for every \(X \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C_0\), the cardinal of the set \(J(X)\) of \(j \in J\) such that there exists a homomorphism that is nontrivial from \(G_j\) into \(X\) is necessarily small, since such a morphism is necessarily a monomorphism (\(G_j\) being simple); consequently, if \(i_0\) is the subset of \(J\) that is the union of the \(J(X)\) for \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_0\), then \(i_0\) is small, i.e. \(i_0 \in I\), and it does the job. On the other hand it is clear that \(F\) is not representable, since we have card \(I \notin \mathcal{U}\). From this and from 8.12.7 we thus conclude that the category \(C\) of groups \(\in \mathcal{U}\) does not admit a small full cogenerating subcategory. Since the object \(\mathbb{Z}\) of \(C\) is moreover a generator, it then follows from the proof of 7.12 that there exists a group \(G\) with two generators that does not embed into an injective object of the category \(C\) of groups \(\in \mathcal{U}\). It moreover seems plausible that \(C\) admits no injective object other than the trivial groups.
8.13. Pro-representable functors and accessible functors

In the present number, we use some notions and results from the following section, and notably 9.11 and 9.13, to obtain a criterion for pro-representability that we shall use (incidentally) in IV 9.16 . In what follows, \(C\) denotes a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category satisfying condition L of 9.1 b), this condition being fulfilled for example if the small filtered inductive limits are representable in \(C\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8.13.2

Let \(C\) be as above, and \[ f : C \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] a functor.

a) Suppose that each object of \(C\) is accessible (9.3). If \(f\) is pro-representable, then \(f\) is accessible (9.2) and left exact.

b) Suppose that finite projective limits are representable in \(C\), and that \(C\) admits a cardinal filtration (9.12). If \(f\) is accessible and left exact, then \(f\) is pro-representable.

Proof. a) The hypothesis on \(C\) means that the representable covariant functors from \(C\) to \((\mathrm{Ens})\) are accessible. The same therefore holds for every small inductive limit of such functors (9.6 (i)), hence also for every pro-representable functor.

b) By virtue of 8.3.3 (iii), it remains to prove that in \(\mathrm{Ob}({}_F\backslash C)^\circ\) there is a small cofinal subcategory. Now by hypothesis there exists a cardinal \(\pi\) such that \(f\) is \(\pi\)-accessible. Let then \((X,u)\), \(u \in F(X)\), be an object of \({}_F\backslash C\). With the notation of 9.12 c) we then have \(X = \varinjlim_i X_i\), with \(I\) filtered and large relative to \(\pi\) and the \(X_i\) in \(C' = \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(C)\), whence \(F(X) \xleftarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_i F(X_i)\). This shows that the small subcategory \(({}_F\backslash C')^\circ\) is cofinal in \(({}_F\backslash C)^\circ\), and completes the proof.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.13.3

Let \(C\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category satisfying the following conditions:

a) In \(C\) finite projective limits are representable.

b) In \(C\) small filtered inductive limits are representable.

c) The functor \(\mathrm{Ker}\) on the category of double arrows of \(C\) is accessible (for example, it commutes with small filtered \(\varinjlim\)).

d) Every strict epimorphism of \(C\) is a universal strict epimorphism (10.2).

e) There exists a small subcategory of \(C\) generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1).

Under these conditions, a functor \(f : C \to (\mathrm{Ens})\) is pro-representable if and only if it is left exact and accessible (9.2).
Indeed, conditions a) and b) of 8.13.2 on \(C\) are satisfied, by virtue of 9.11 and 9.13 respectively.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 8.13.4

Let \(f : C \to C'\) be a functor between \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories satisfying conditions a) to e) of 8.13.3. For \(f\) to admit a pro-adjoint it is necessary and sufficient that \(f\) be left exact and accessible.

Since the representable functors \[ h_{Y'} : X' \mapsto \mathrm{Hom}(Y',X') : C' \to (\mathrm{Ens}) \] are left exact and accessible (9.11), if \(f\) has these same properties, then so do its composites with the preceding functors, which are therefore pro-representable by 8.13.3, i.e. \(f\) admits a pro-adjoint. Conversely, suppose that \(f\) admits a pro-adjoint, and let \(C'_1\) be a small generating subcategory of \(C\), and \(\pi\) a cardinal such that the \(Y' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C'\) are \(\pi\)-accessible; to prove that \(f\) is \(\pi\)-accessible it suffices then to prove that the same holds for its composites with the \(h_{Y'}\), \(Y' \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C'\); but by hypothesis these composites are pro-representable, hence they are accessible (8.13.3), hence \(\pi\)-accessible provided one takes \(\pi\) large enough, q.e.d.

footnotes.html: (∗) For a contravariant dependence, under certain conditions, cf. 8.11.

pages.title: 9. Accessible functors, cardinal filtrations, and the construction of small generating subcategories.

blocks.html: 9. Accessible functors, cardinal filtrations, and the construction of small generating subcategories.

The present section, of a more technical nature than the other sections of this exposé, will be used in this seminar only in IV 9 and in VI 4, which are not used elsewhere in the Seminar. It is therefore advisable to skip the reading of the present section, at least on a first reading!

All the categories considered in the present number are assumed to be \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories. Except for the small index categories \(I, J \ldots\) that we shall have to use, the developments that follow will mainly apply to "large" categories \(E, F \ldots\) that are stable under small filtered inductive limits. It will however most often suffice that a slightly weaker condition be satisfied (condition L in 9.1 below). All the cardinals considered in the present number are assumed to be \(\in \mathcal{U}\).

Following a suggestion of P. DELIGNE, we shall study, for a functor \(f : E \to F\) between large categories, a condition of commutation of \(f\) with certain types of inductive limits that are filtered, a condition that is remarkably stable, and which will be satisfied for the functors that are most important among those one encounters in nature. The applications we have in view, for our seminar, are 9.13.3, 9.13.4 (used in VI 4) and above all 9.25, which gives, in a nontrivial case, the existence of a small generating family in a category of sections of a fibred category; this result will be used in IV 9.16.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 9.1

a) Let \(I\) be a preordered set and \(\pi\) a cardinal. We say that \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi\) if \(I\) is filtered, and if every subset of \(I\) of cardinal \(\leq \pi\) admits an upper bound in \(I\).

b) Let \(E\) be a category. If \(\pi\) is a cardinal, we say that \(E\) satisfies condition \(L_\pi\) if for every small ordered set \(I\) large relative to \(\pi\), \(E\) is stable under the inductive limits of type \(I\). We say that \(E\) satisfies condition \(L\) if there exists a cardinal \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(E\) satisfies condition \(L_\pi\).

When in 9.1 a) one has \(\pi \geq 2\), the second stated condition already implies that \(I\) is filtered, and if \(\pi\) is finite, "\(I\) large relative to \(\pi\)" simply means that \(I\) is filtered. In what follows we shall hardly be interested in anything other than the case where \(\pi\) is infinite. Note that if \(\pi, \pi'\) are two cardinals such that \(\pi' \geq \pi\), then \(I\) large relative to \(\pi'\) evidently implies \(I\) large relative to \(\pi\).

As announced in 9.0, the conditions \(L_\pi\), \(L\) should be regarded as technical variants of the stronger condition of stability under small filtered inductive limits. It is clear that if \(\pi, \pi'\) are cardinals such that \(\pi' \geq \pi\), then condition \(L_\pi\) implies condition \(L_{\pi'}\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 9.2

Let \(f : E \to F\) be a functor. If \(\pi\) is a cardinal, we say that \(f\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible) if \(E\) satisfies \(L_\pi\) (9.1) and if for every ordered set \(I \in \mathcal{U}\) large relative to \(\pi\), and every inductive system \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(E\) of type \(I\), the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_i f(X_i) \to f(\varinjlim_i X_i) \] is a monomorphism (resp. an isomorphism). We say that \(f\) is preaccessible (resp. accessible) (relative to the universe \(\mathcal{U}\)) if there exists a cardinal \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(f\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible).
The category of \(\pi\)-accessible (resp. accessible) functors from \(E\) to \(F\) will be denoted \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi\) resp. \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_{\mathrm{acc}}\).
Evidently, a functor commuting with small filtered \(\varinjlim\) (e.g. a functor admitting a right adjoint) is \(\pi\)-accessible for every cardinal \(\pi \geq 2\).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 9.3

Let \(E\) be a category, \(X\) an object of \(E\), \[ h_X^\circ : E \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}) \] the covariant functor it represents, \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) a cardinal. We say that \(X\) is a \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible) object of \(E\) if the functor \(h_X^\circ\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible); we say that \(X\) is preaccessible (resp. accessible) if there exists a cardinal \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(X\) is a \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible) object of \(E\).
We denote by \(E_\pi\) the full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the \(\pi\)-accessible objects of \(E\).

When one applies definition 9.3 to a category of the form \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F)\), the terminology introduced presents a priori an ambiguity with the analogous terminology introduced in 9.2, when one interprets the objects of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F)\) as functors; it does not seem, however, that there is any serious risk of confusion.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 9.4

Let \(E\) be a category, \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) a cardinal. We say that \(E\) is a \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible) category if there exists in \(E\) a small full subcategory \(C\) which is generating (7.1) and whose objects are \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible) (9.3). We say that \(E\) is a preaccessible (resp. accessible) category if there exists a cardinal \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(E\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible (resp. \(\pi\)-accessible).
For important examples, cf. 9.11.3 below.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.5

Let \(f : E \to F\) be a functor between categories such that \(F\) is accessible and every object of \(E\) is accessible. Then, if \(f\) admits a left adjoint, \(f\) is accessible.

Indeed, by hypothesis, \(F\) admits a small conservative family of representable functors \(F \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\) that are accessible, so we are reduced at once to showing that the composite of \(f\) with each of the preceding functors is accessible. Now since \(f\) admits a left adjoint, these composites are representable functors \(E \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\), hence accessible by the hypothesis on \(E\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.6

Let \(E\) and \(F\) be two categories, \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) a cardinal, and consider the full subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\) consisting of the \(\pi\)-accessible functors (9.2) from \(E\) to \(F\).

(i) This subcategory is stable under every type of \(\varinjlim\) that is representable in \(F\).

(ii) Suppose \(F\) is \(\pi\)-accessible (9.4), and let \(J\) be a category such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, J \leq \pi\) and such that the \(\varprojlim\) of type \(J\) are representable in \(F\), so that the \(\varprojlim\) of type \(J\) are representable in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\). Then the subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi\) is stable under the \(\varprojlim\) of type \(J\).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.7

Let \(E\) and \(F\) be two categories, with \(F\) accessible (9.4). Then the full subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_{\mathrm{acc}}\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\) consisting of the accessible functors is stable under every type of inductive or projective limit, relative to a small index category \(J\), that is representable in \(F\) (hence in \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\)).

Proof of 9.6. Assertion (i) follows trivially from the commutation of the functor \(\varinjlim\) with arbitrary inductive limits. For (ii), let \((f_j)_{j\in J}\) be a projective system of \(\pi\)-accessible functors \(E \to F\), \(f = \varprojlim f_j\) its projective limit, which is computed "argument by argument"; let us prove that \(f\) is \(\pi\)-accessible, i.e. that for every ordered set \(I \in \mathcal{U}\) large relative to \(\pi\), and every inductive system \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) in \(E\), the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_i ((\varprojlim_j f_j)(X_i)) \to (\varprojlim_j f_j)(\varinjlim_i X_i) \] is an isomorphism. Now the "argument by argument" computation of the functor \(\varprojlim_j f_j\) allows us to identify the preceding canonical morphism with the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_i \varprojlim_j f_j(X_i) \to \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i f_j(X_i) \] associated to the bifunctor \[ (i,j) \mapsto f_j(X_i) : I\times J \to F . \] Thus 9.6 is a consequence of the more general assertion:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.8

Let \(F\) be a \(\pi\)-accessible category, \(I\) an ordered set large relative to \(\pi\), \(J\) a small category such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, J \leq \pi\), and such that the \(\varprojlim\) of type \(J\) are representable in \(F\), \(h : I\times J \to F\) a functor; then the canonical morphism \[ \varinjlim_i \varprojlim_j h(i,j) \to \varprojlim_j \varinjlim_i h(i,j) \tag{9.8.1} \] is an isomorphism. In other words, the functor \[ \varinjlim_i : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(I,F) \to F \tag{9.8.2} \] commutes with projective limits of type \(J\) (for every small category \(J\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}(J) \leq \pi\) and such that the projective limits of type \(J\) are representable in \(F\)). Or again, for every \(J\) as above, the functor \[ \varprojlim_j : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(J, F) \to F \tag{9.8.3} \] is \(\pi\)-accessible.

Since by hypothesis \(F\) admits a conservative family of representable \(\pi\)-accessible covariant functors \(g : F \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\), one sees at once that we are reduced to proving 9.8 in the case where \(F = \mathcal{U}\text{-Ens}\). We shall then prove the assertion in the form of the commutation of (9.8.2) with the \(\varprojlim\) of type \(J\), with \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, J \leq \pi\). Since \(I\) is filtered, we know that (9.8.2) commutes with finite projective limits (2.8). We are thus reduced, by a standard argument (cf. 2.3), to proving that it commutes with products indexed by a set \(J\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, J \leq \pi\). This reduces us to proving the bijectivity of (9.8.1) when \(J\) is discrete. Let us prove injectivity: consider two elements \(a, b\) of the left-hand side; they thus come from \(\prod_j h(i_0,j)\) for a suitable \(i_0 \in I\), say \(\prod_j a(i_0,j)\) and \(\prod_j b(i_0,j)\); suppose that the elements \(\prod_j h(\infty,j)\) of the right-hand side that they define are equal, i.e. that for every \(j\), there exists \(i(j) \geq i_0\) such that \(a(i_0,j)\) and \(b(i_0,j)\) have the same image in \(h(i,j)\). Since \(I\) is large relative to \(\mathrm{card}\, J\), it follows that there exists a common upper bound \(i_1 \in I\) of all the \(i(j)\), which implies that the two elements of \(\prod_j h(i_0,j)\) under consideration have the same image in \(\prod_j h(i_1,j)\), hence define the same element of the left-hand side of (9.8.1), which establishes injectivity. For the surjectivity, let \(\prod_j a(\infty,j)\) be an element of the right-hand side; thus for every \(j \in J\), \(a(\infty,j)\) comes from an element of \(h(i(j),j)\), for a suitable \(i(j) \in I\). As before, one can find a common upper bound \(i \in I\) of the \(i(j)\), so \(\prod_j a(\infty,j)\) comes from an element \(\prod_j a(i,j)\) of \(\prod_j h(i,j)\), hence is in the image of (9.8.1). This completes the proof.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.9

Let \(F\) be a \(\pi\)-accessible (resp. accessible) category; then for every category \(J\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, J \leq \pi\) (resp. every small category \(J\)) and for every functor \((X_j)_{j\in J} : J \to F\) whose inductive limit in \(F\) is representable, if the \(X_j\) are \(\pi\)-accessible (resp. accessible) then so is \(\varinjlim X_j\).

Indeed, the functor \(F \to (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\) represented by \(\varinjlim X_j\) is the projective limit of the functors represented by the \(X_j\), and one applies 9.6 (ii) to the projective system formed by these functors.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 9.10

In the statements 9.6, 9.7, 9.8 and 9.9 one can everywhere replace the words "\(\pi\)-accessible", "accessible" by "\(\pi\)-preaccessible", "preaccessible". The proof given indeed also proves this variant of the preceding statements.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.11

Let \(E\) be a category satisfying condition L (9.1), \(C\) a small generating full subcategory (7.1). We assume the following condition satisfied:

a) \(E\) is stable under kernels of double arrows, and the functor \(\mathrm{Ker}\) on the category of double arrows of \(E\) is accessible (for example, it commutes with small filtered inductive limits).

Then every object of \(E\) is preaccessible (9.3), a fortiori \(E\) is preaccessible. Suppose that \(C\) is even generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1), and suppose that \(E\) satisfies the conditions:

b) \(E\) is stable under fibre products.

c) Every small strict epimorphic family in \(E\) is universally strict epimorphic (10.3), or the small direct sums are representable in \(E\), and every strict epimorphism of \(E\) is a universal strict epimorphism.

Then every object of \(E\) is accessible, a fortiori \(E\) is accessible.
The fact that, given a), every object of \(E\) is accessible, follows from the fact that for every object \(X\) of \(E\), the set of strict subobjects of \(X\) is small (7.4), and from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.11.1

Under the conditions of 9.11 a), let \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) and \(\pi\) a cardinal such that \(E\) satisfies \(L_\pi\) (9.1), that the functor \(\mathrm{Ker}\) in 9.11 a) is \(\pi\)-accessible, and that the set of strict subobjects of \(X\) has cardinal bounded above by \(\pi\). Then \(X\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible.
