Indeed, if \(I\) is a set large relative to \(\pi\), \((Y_i)_{i\in I}\) an inductive system in \(E\) with inductive limit \(Y\), and \((u_i, v_i : X \rightrightarrows Y_i)\) a double arrow such that the composite double arrow \(X \underset{v}{\overset{u}{\rightrightarrows}} Y\) satisfies \(u = v\), let us prove that there exists \(j \geq i\) in \(I\) such that \(u_j = v_j\). For this, consider the inductive system of double arrows \((u_j, v_j : X \rightrightarrows Y_j)_{j\geq i}\), whose inductive limit is \((u,v)\). By hypothesis we have \(X = \mathrm{Ker}(u,v) = \varinjlim_j \mathrm{Ker}(u_j,v_j) = \varinjlim_j X_j\), where \(X_j = \mathrm{Ker}(u_j,v_j)\). Now the \(X_j\) are strict subobjects of \(X\), so there exists a subset \(I'\) of \(I\) consisting of indices \(j \geq i\), such that \(\mathrm{card}\, J \leq \pi\) and such that every \(X_j\) is equal to one of the \(X_{i'}\), (\(i' \in I'\)). Since \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi\), there exists an upper bound \(j\) of \(I'\) in \(I\). Then \(X_j\) contains all the \(X_{j'}\), for \(j' \geq i\), so \(X_j \to X\) is an epimorphism (since the family of \(X_{j'} \to X\) is epimorphic), hence an isomorphism since it is a strict monomorphism. So we have \(u_j = v_j\), which proves 9.11.1.
The second assertion of 9.11 follows from the first, and from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.11.2

Under the conditions of 9.11 a), b), c), let \(X\) be an object of \(E\), and \(\pi\) an infinite cardinal such that \(E\) satisfies \(L_\pi\) (9.1), that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{ob}\, C_{/X} \leq \pi\), that for two objects \(X' \to X\) and \(X'' \to X\) of \(C_{/X}\), \(X'\times_X X''\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible, and finally that \(X\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible. Then \(X\) is \(\pi\)-accessible.

With the notation of the proof of 9.11.1, it suffices to prove that every morphism \(u : X \to Y\) comes from a morphism \(u_i : X \to Y_i\). Now consider the family of morphisms \(Y_i \to Y\), which is strict epimorphic; thanks to b) and c), the family of \(Y_i\times_Y X \to X\) is also strict epimorphic; on the other hand, for every \(i\), since \(C\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, the family of arrows \[ T \to Y_i\times_Y X \] with source in \(C\) is strict epimorphic. In the second alternative considered in c), one can find such a strict epimorphic arrow, with source a (small) sum of objects of \(C\). By virtue of the transitivity of the notion of universal strict epimorphic family (II 2.5) it then follows that the family of arrows \(T_\alpha \xrightarrow{\ f_\alpha\ } X\) with source in \(C\) that factor through one of the \(Y_i\times_Y X\) is strict epimorphic. Let \(J\) be the index set of this family, which has cardinal bounded above by \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{ob}\, C_{/X} \leq \pi\). Choose for every \(\alpha \in J\) an \(i = i(\alpha) \in I\) and an \(X\)-morphism \(T_\alpha \to Y_i\times_Y X\), or what amounts to the same, a \(v_\alpha : T_\alpha \to Y_i\) such that \(p_i v_\alpha = u f_\alpha\), where \(p_i : Y_i \to Y\) is the morphism that is canonical. Since \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi\), one can choose \(i(\alpha)\) independent of \(\alpha\), say \(i\). For every pair of indices \(\alpha, \beta \in J\), consider the composites \[ \mathrm{pr}_1 v_\alpha, \mathrm{pr}_2 v_\beta : T_\alpha\times_X T_\beta \rightrightarrows Y_i . \] Their composites with \(Y_i \to Y\) are equal, so, since \(T_\alpha\times_X T_\beta\) is \(\pi\)-preaccessible by hypothesis, there exists an index \(i' = i(\alpha,\beta) \geq i\) such that the composites of the arrows under consideration with \(Y_i \to Y_{i'}\) are equal. Since the set of pairs \(\alpha, \beta\) has cardinal \(\leq \pi^2 = \pi\) (\(\pi\) being infinite), it again follows that one can choose \(i'\) independent of \(\alpha, \beta\). One may evidently assume \(i' = i\). But then, since the family \((f_\alpha : T_\alpha \to X)\) is strict epimorphic, one can find a morphism \(u_i : X \to Y_i\) such that \(u_i f_\alpha = v_\alpha\). We then have \(p_i u_i = p\), since for every \(\alpha\) we have \((p_i u_i)f_\alpha = p_i(u_i f_\alpha) = p_i v_\alpha = u f_\alpha\), and the family of the \(f_\alpha\) is epimorphic. This completes the proof of 9.11.2.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 9.11.3

One sees, as a special case of 9.11, that in the category \(E\) every object is accessible, in each of the following two cases: 1) \(E\) is an abelian \(\mathcal{U}\)-category with exact filtered inductive limits and admitting a small generating subcategory (here, it is the second alternative of c) that applies). 2) \(E\) is the category of sheaves of sets on a topological space \(X \in \mathcal{U}\). More generally, it suffices that \(E\) be the category of sheaves of sets on a \(\mathcal{U}\)-site (II 2.1), or again, that \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos (IV 1.1).

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 9.12

Let \(E\) be a category. By a cardinal filtration of \(E\) we mean an increasing filtration \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\) of \(E\) by strictly full subcategories \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), indexed by the cardinals \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(\pi \geq \pi_0\) (where \(\pi_0\) is a fixed infinite cardinal, depending on the cardinal filtration under consideration), and satisfying the following conditions:

a) For every \(\pi \geq \pi_0\), \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) is equivalent to a small category.

b) \(E\) satisfies \(L_{\pi_0}\) (9.3), and for every \(\pi \geq \pi_0\), \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) is stable in \(E\) under the filtered inductive limits indexed by ordered sets \(I\) large relative to \(\pi_0\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\).

c) For every \(\pi \geq \pi_0\), and every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), one can find an isomorphism \[ X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X_i , \] where \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) is an inductive system in \(E\) indexed by an ordered set \(I\) large relative to \(\pi\) (9.1), and where the \(X_i\) are in \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\). Moreover, if \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), \(\pi' \geq \pi\), one can take \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi'^\pi\).
Note that it follows from b) and c) that every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) belongs to some \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), for \(\pi\) large enough.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.html:
Example 9.12.2

Take \(E = (\mathcal{U}\text{-Ens})\), \(\pi_0 = \aleph_0\), \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E) = \) the full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the sets such that \(\mathrm{card}\, X \leq \pi\). More generally:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.13

Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. Suppose that \(E\) is stable under small filtered \(\varinjlim\), under the sum of two objects, and under cokernels of double arrows, that \(E\) is stable under fibre products, and that the epimorphic morphisms in \(E\) are universal strict epimorphisms. Let \(C\) be a small full subcategory of \(E\) which is generating by strict epimorphisms. Let \(\pi_0\) be an infinite cardinal \(\geq \mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, C\). For every cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_0\), let \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) be the strictly full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the objects \(X\) of \(E\) such that there exists a strict epimorphic family \((X_i \to X)_{i\in I}\) with target \(X\), such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\) and \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\) for every \(i \in I\). Then \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\) is a cardinal filtration of \(E\). Moreover, for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), the cardinal of the set of arrows of \(C_{/X}\) (and a fortiori, of the set of objects of \(C_{/X}\)) is bounded above by \(\pi^{\pi_0}\).
This last assertion is none other than 7.6.

To show that we have a cardinal filtration, we must prove conditions a), b) and c) of 9.12. Condition a) follows at once from 7.5.2. For b), suppose that we have \(X = \varinjlim_I X_i\), with \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\) and the \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\). Then the family of canonical morphisms \(X_i \to X\) is strict epimorphic, and by the hypothesis on the \(X_i\), there exists for every \(i \in I\) a strict epimorphic family \((X_{ij} \to X_i)_{j\in J_i}\), with \(\mathrm{card}\, J_i \leq \pi\). Passing to the sums \(\coprod_i X_i\) and \(\coprod_{i,j} X_{ij}\), one sees by the transitivity of universal strict epimorphisms (II 2.5 ) that the family of composites \(X_{ij} \to X_i \to X\) (indexed by the sum set of the \(J_i\), for \(i\in I\)) is strict epimorphic. Now we have card \(J \leq \pi^2 = \pi\), whence the conclusion. (NB. we have only used the fact that \(\varinjlim_I X_i\) exists, and not the fact that \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi_0\) nor even filtered.) Let us finally prove c). Note that for every \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\), the family of arrows \(X_i \to X\) with source in \(\mathrm{ob}\, C\) is strictly epimorphic, since \(C\) is generating by strict epimorphisms, and evidently small, so there exists a cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_0\) such that \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\). It remains to prove that if we have cardinals \(\pi' \geq \pi \geq \pi_0\), and if \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^{\pi'}(E)\), then we have an isomorphism \[ X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X_i , \] with \(I\) large relative to \(\pi\), \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi'^\pi\), the \(X_i\) in \(\mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\). Now we have, \(C\) being generating by strict epimorphisms, \[ X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} T . \tag{\(*\)} \] Note also that by successively adjoining to \(C\) the sums and cokernels of double arrows of \(C\), and likewise for the category thus obtained, etc., one reduces to the case where \(C\) is stable under the sum of two objects in \(E\) and under cokernels of double arrows in \(E\), and this without destroying the hypothesis \(\pi_0 \geq \mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, C\). One may moreover assume that, if \(E\) contains a fixed initial object \(\varnothing_E\), then \(\varnothing_E \in \mathrm{ob}\, C\). This implies that the category \(C_{/X}\) is stable under the sum of two objects and cokernels of double arrows. It is then filtered, for it is nonempty, since if it were empty, relation (*) would show that \(X\) is an initial object, so \(C_{/X}\) contains the arrow \(\varnothing_E \to X\), a contradiction. Let then \(I\) be the set, ordered by inclusion, of the full subcategories \(i\) of \(C_{/X}\) that are filtered and such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{ob}\, i \leq \pi\). For every \(i \in I\), let \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\) be the inductive limit of the composite functor \(i \to C_{/X} \to E\), which exists by hypothesis. Then we evidently have \[ \varinjlim_I X_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{C_{/X}} T \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X . \] On the other hand, we have already noted that card ob \(C_{/X} \leq \pi'^{\pi_0}\). It follows that \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi\), and that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq (\pi'^{\pi_0})^\pi = \pi'^{\pi_0\pi} = \pi'^\pi\) by virtue of the following lemma, whose proof is left to the reader (where one takes \(I = C_{/X}\), \(c = \pi'^{\pi_0}\)):

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.13.1

Let \(J\) be a filtered category, \(c\) and \(\pi\) two cardinals such that \(c \geq \mathrm{Sup}(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, J, \pi)\), and such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Hom}(j,j') \leq \pi_0\) for every pair of objects \(j, j'\) of \(J\). Let \(I\) be the set of filtered full subcategories \(i\) of \(J\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{ob}\, i \leq \pi\). Then, ordered by inclusion, \(I\) is large relative to \(\pi\), and we have \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq c^\pi\).
This completes the proof of 9.13.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark 9.13.2

A slight additional effort should allow one to replace in 9.13 the hypothesis that \(E\) is stable under small filtered inductive limits by the hypothesis that \(E\) satisfies L (9.1), if one assumes \(E\) stable under small sums, or that in \(E\) every family that is epimorphic is universally epimorphic. One must then, in the proof of c), choose \(\pi_0\) such that \(E\) satisfies \(L_{\pi_0}\), and restrict to the full subcategories \(i\) of \(C_{/X}\) that are not only filtered, but such that the preordered set ob \(i\) is large relative to \(\pi_0\). Using 8. and the hypothesis that \(E\) satisfies \(L_{\pi_0}\), one then finds that the \(X_i\) exist, and one should conclude by a suitable variant of 9.13.1, which the editor has not checked.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.14

Let \(f : E \to F\) be an accessible functor (9.2) between two categories equipped with cardinal filtrations \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\) and \((\mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(F))_{\pi\geq\pi'_0}\). Then there exists a cardinal \(\pi_1 \geq \mathrm{Sup}(\pi_0,\pi'_0)\) such that for every cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_1\), one has \[ f(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)) \subset \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi^{\pi_1}}(F) . \tag{9.14.1} \] In particular, if one has \(\pi = 2^c\) with \(c \geq \pi_1\), whence \(\pi^{\pi_1} = 2^{c\pi_1} = 2^c = \pi\), one has \[ f(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)) \subset \mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(F) . \tag{9.14.2} \]
Let us point out at once the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.15

Let \(E\) be a category, equipped with two cardinal filtrations \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\) and \((\mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi'_0}\). Then there exists a cardinal \(\pi_1 \geq \mathrm{Sup}(\pi_0,\pi'_0)\) such that, for every cardinal \(c \geq \pi_1\), setting \(\pi = 2^c\), one has \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E) = \mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(E)\).

Proof of 9.14. Let \(c\) be a cardinal such that \(c \geq \mathrm{Sup}(\pi_0,\pi'_0)\), and such that \(f\) is \(c\)-admissible. Let on the other hand \(\pi_1 \geq c\) be such that one has \[ f(\mathrm{Filt}^c(E)) \subset \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi_1}(F) . \tag{\(*\)} \] Such a \(\pi_1\) exists, thanks to the fact that \(\mathrm{Filt}^c(E)\) is equivalent to a small category (9.12 a)), hence so is \(f(\mathrm{Filt}^c(E))\), so that one can apply 9.12.1 to the objects of the latter to find a \(\mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(F)\) that contains them all (taking into account that the \(\mathrm{Filt}'^\pi(F)\) are full subcategories). Let then \(\pi \geq \pi_1\), and \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\); let us prove that \(f(X) \in \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi^{\pi_1}}(F)\). Let us indeed write \[ X = \varinjlim_I X_i , \] with the \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^c(E)\), \(I\) large relative to \(c\), \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi^c \leq \pi^{\pi_1}\) (9.12 c)). Since \(f\) is \(c\)-admissible, \(I\) large relative to \(c\), one has \[ f(X) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I f(X_i) , \] and since \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi^{\pi_1}\) and \(f(X_i) \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi_1}(F) \subset \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi^{\pi_1}}(F)\) by (*), one has \(f(X) \in \mathrm{Filt}'^{\pi^{\pi_1}}(F)\) by 9.12 b), q.e.d.

The notion of cardinal filtration 9.12 is of hardly any interest except when the objects of \(E\) are accessible. Let us point out that it follows from 9.11 that this condition is satisfied when, in addition to the hypotheses of 9.13, one assumes that the functor \(\mathrm{Ker}\) on the category of double arrows of \(E\) is accessible. Let us point out on the other hand:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9.16

Let \(E\) be a category equipped with a cardinal filtration \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\). Suppose that the elements of \(\mathrm{Filt}^{\pi_0}(E)\) are accessible objects of \(E\); then there exists a cardinal \(\pi_1 \geq \pi_0\) in \(\mathcal{U}\) such that the objects of \(\mathrm{Filt}^{\pi_0}(E)\) are \(\pi_1\)-accessible; if \(\pi_1\) is chosen thus, then for every cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_1\), one has (with the notation of 9.3.1): \[ E_\pi \subset \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E) \subset E_{(\pi^{\pi_0})} . \tag{9.16.1} \]

The existence of \(\pi_1\) follows immediately from the fact that \(\mathrm{Filt}^{\pi_0}(E)\) is equivalent to a small category (9.12 a)). Let then \(\pi \geq \pi_1\). If \(X\) is in \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), writing \(X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X_i\) with \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi^{\pi_0}\), \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^{\pi_0}(E)\) for every \(i\) (9.12 c)), then it follows from 9.9 that \(X\) is \(\pi^{\pi_0}\)-accessible, whence the second inclusion (9.16.1). Suppose that \(X\) is \(\pi\)-accessible, and write \(X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X_i\), with \(I\) large relative to \(\pi\) and the \(X_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) (9.12 c)). By the hypothesis on \(X\), the isomorphism that is given \(X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X_i\) factors through one of the \(X_i\), so \(X\) is isomorphic to a direct summand of this \(X_i\). We conclude that \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), hence the first inclusion (9.16.1), thanks to the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.16.2

Every object of \(E\) that is a direct summand of an object of \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) is in \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\).

Indeed, if \(X\) is the image of a projector \(p\) in the object \(Y\) of \(E\) (i.e. of an endomorphism \(p\) such that \(p^2 = p\)), and if \(I\) is a filtered ordered set, then \(X\) is the limit that is inductive of the filtered inductive system \((Y_i)_{i\in I}\) defined by \(Y_i = Y\) for every \(i \in I\), \(p : Y_i \to Y_j\) if \(i < j\). Taking \(I\) large relative to \(\pi_0\) and card \(I \leq \pi\), one thus sees that if \(Y \in \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), then so is \(X\) by virtue of 9.12 b).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.17

Under the conditions of 9.16, for every cardinal \(c \geq \pi_1\), setting \(\pi = 2^c\), \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) is identical to the strictly full subcategory \(E_\pi\) of \(E\) consisting of the \(\pi\)-accessible objects.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.18

Let \(E\) be a category satisfying condition \(L_\pi\) (9.1), where \(\pi\) is a cardinal, and \(C\) a full subcategory of \(E\). We denote by \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)_\pi\) the full subcategory of the category \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)\) of ind-objects of \(C\) (8.2) consisting of the ind-objects of the form \((X_i)_{i\in I}\), where \(I\) is an ordered set large relative to \(\pi\). Consider the canonical functor \[ (X_i)_{i\in I} \mapsto \varinjlim_I X_i : \mathrm{Ind}(C)_\pi \to E . \tag{9.18.1} \]

a) For this functor to be fully faithful it is necessary and sufficient that every object \(X\) of \(C\) be a \(\pi\)-accessible object (9.3) of \(E\).

b) Let us place ourselves under the conditions of 9.17, in particular \(\pi = 2^c\), and take \(C = \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\). Then the functor (9.18.1) is an equivalence of categories.

Assertion a) is an immediate generalization of 8.7.5 a), and is proved in the same way. Then b) follows from 9.17 and from condition 9.12 c) of cardinal filtrations, which implies that the functor under consideration is essentially surjective.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.19

Under the conditions of 9.17, let \(C = \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), let \(F\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category, and consider the functor \[ \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F) \tag{9.19.1} \] induced by the "restriction to \(C\)" functor \(f \mapsto f|C\), where the source of (9.19.1) is the category of \(\pi\)-accessible functors from \(E\) to \(F\) (9.2). The preceding functor is fully faithful. If \(F\) satisfies condition \(L_\pi\) (9.1), then the functor (9.19.1) is an equivalence of categories.

The first assertion is proved as in 7.8, using 9.18 b). The second is obtained by constructing a quasi-inverse functor to (9.19.1), by associating to every functor \(f : C \to F\) the functor \((X_i)_{i\in I} \mapsto \varinjlim_i f(X_i)\) from \(\mathrm{Ind}(E_\pi)\) to \(F\), and using 9.18 b) to deduce from it a functor \(\overline{f} : E \to F\). Everything reduces to showing that the latter is \(\pi\)-accessible. But this is proved as the analogous assertion 8.7.3.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.20

Let \(E\) be a category admitting a cardinal filtration and such that every object of \(E\) is accessible (cf. 9.16), and let \(F\) be a category. Then:

a) The category \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_{\mathrm{acc}}\) of accessible functors from \(E\) to \(F\) (9.2) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. (NB we recall (9.0) that the given categories \(E, F\) are assumed to be \(\mathcal{U}\)-categories).

b) Suppose that \(F\) is stable under small filtered inductive limits. For every full subcategory \(C\) of \(E\) equivalent to a small category, with inclusion functor \(i : C \to E\), consider the corresponding functor \[ i_! : \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F) \] (5.1). For a functor \(f : E \to F\) to be accessible, it is necessary and sufficient that there exist a small subcategory \(C\) of \(E\), such that \(f\) lies in the essential image of the preceding functor \(i_!\).

Proof. a) It suffices to prove that for every cardinal \(\pi\) such that \(E\) satisfies \(L_\pi\), the full subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi\) of \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_{\mathrm{acc}}\) is a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category. It obviously suffices to verify this for cardinals of the form \(2^c\), with \(c\) large enough. But then this follows from 9.19, since (\(C = \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) being essentially small) \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,F)\) is obviously a \(\mathcal{U}\)-category.

b) By the transitivity of the formation of the functors \(i_!\), one may in the statement restrict to subcategories \(C\) of the form \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), where \(\pi\) is as in 9.17. One then sees easily that the composite functor \(\underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E),F) \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)_\pi \to \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(E,F)\), where the first arrow is quasi-inverse to (9.19.1), and the second is the inclusion, is none other than the functor \(i_!\), up to isomorphism. Hence assertion b) follows from 9.19.

blocks.title: Exercise
blocks.html:
Exercise 9.20.1

(The present exercise uses the notions of site and topos, developed in Exposés II and IV.) Let \(E\) be a \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos, \(\mathcal{V}\) a universe such that \(\mathcal{U}\in\mathcal{V}\), \(C\) a small full generating subcategory of the \(\mathcal{U}\)-topos \(E\), \(\pi_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) an infinite cardinal such that \(\pi_0 \geq \mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, C\). For every cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_0\), \(\pi \in \mathcal{U}\), let \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\) be the strictly full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the objects \(X\) such that there exists a strict epimorphic family \((X_i \to X)_{i\in I}\) with target \(X\), such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\) and \(X_i \in \mathrm{Ob}\, C\) for all \(i \in I\).

a) Show that \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E))_{\pi\geq\pi_0}\) is a cardinal filtration of the \(\mathcal{U}\)-category \(E\), and that one may choose \(\pi_0\) such that for every \(\pi \geq \pi_0\) one has the inclusions \[ E_\pi \subset \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E) \subset E_{\pi^{\pi_0}} , \] where, for every cardinal \(c\), \(E_c\) denotes the strictly full subcategory of \(E\) consisting of the \(c\)-accessible objects.

b) Choosing a cardinal \(\pi \geq \pi_0\) such that \(\pi = \pi^{\pi_0}\) (for example \(\pi\) of the form \(2^c\), with \(c > \pi_0\)), and setting \(C = \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E)\), show that one has an equivalence of categories \[ \mathrm{Ind}(C)_\pi \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } E , \] (notation \(\mathrm{Ind}(C)_\pi\) of 9.18).

c) Keeping the notations of b), let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a universe such that \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{V}\), and \(\widetilde{E}_{\mathcal{V}}\) the \(\mathcal{V}\)-topos of \(\mathcal{V}\)-sheaves on the site \(E\) (endowed with its canonical topology). Denote by \(\mathrm{Ind}(C,\mathcal{V})_\pi\) the category of \(\mathcal{V}\)-Ind-objects of \(C\) indexed by preordered index sets large with respect to \(\pi\). Show that one has an equivalence of categories \[ \mathrm{Ind}(C,\mathcal{V})_\pi \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } \widetilde{E}_{\mathcal{V}} . \]

d) Let \(c \in \mathcal{V}\) be a cardinal, and \(\mathrm{Ind}(E,\mathcal{V})'_c\) the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Ind}(E,\mathcal{V})\) consisting of the \(\mathcal{V}\)-ind-objects of \(E\) indexed by a preordered set that is large with respect to every cardinal \(< c\). Taking \(c = \mathrm{card}\, \mathcal{U}\), show that one has an equivalence of categories \[ \mathrm{Ind}(E,\mathcal{V})'_c \xrightarrow{\ \approx\ } \widetilde{E}_{\mathcal{V}} . \]

The present section 9.21 develops technical preliminaries for the proof of Theorem 9.22 below, which constitutes the main result of the present paragraph 9. Let \[ p : E \to B \tag{9.21.1} \] be a fibred functor, where \(B\) is a small category, and where the inverse image functors \[ f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha \] associated to the arrows \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\) are accessible (9.2). In particular, the fibre categories \(E_\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\)) satisfy condition L (9.1), so that, \(B\) being small, there exists a cardinal \(\pi'_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) such that all the categories \(E_\alpha\) satisfy condition \(L_{\pi'_0}\). Let \(\pi_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) be an infinite cardinal \(> \pi'_0\), so that one has \[ \pi_0 > \pi'_0 , \quad E_\alpha \text{ satisfies } L_{\pi'_0} \quad \text{for all } \alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B . \tag{9.21.2} \] Moreover, the hypotheses made immediately imply the existence of a cardinal \(c \in \mathcal{U}\) satisfying the following conditions: \[ \begin{cases} \text{a)} & c \text{ is infinite}, \\ \text{b)} & c \geq \mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, B, \\ \text{c)} & \text{for every arrow } f : \alpha \to \beta \text{ in } B, \text{ the functor } f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha \text{ is } c\text{-accessible}. \end{cases} \tag{9.21.3} \]

Suppose moreover that one can find, for each \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), a full subcategory \(C_\alpha\) of \(E_\alpha\), satisfying the following conditions: \[ \begin{cases} \text{a)} & \text{For all } X \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_\alpha,\ X \text{ is } c\text{-accessible in } E_\alpha\ (9.3). \\ \text{b)} & \text{For all } X \in \mathrm{ob}\, E_\alpha,\ \text{one can find an isomorphism } X \xrightarrow{\sim} \varinjlim_I X_i \text{ in } E_\alpha, \\ & \text{where the } X_i \text{ are in } C_\alpha \text{ and where } I \text{ is an ordered set large with respect to } c. \end{cases} \tag{9.21.4} \] Let \(\pi\) be a cardinal such that one has \[ \pi \geq \pi_0 , \quad \text{hence } \pi > \pi'_0 , \tag{9.21.5} \] and for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), let \[ C_\alpha^\pi \subset E_\alpha \tag{9.21.6} \] be the subcategory consisting of the objects that can be represented in the form \(\varinjlim_I X_i\), where \(I\) is an ordered set large with respect to \(\pi'_0\), with \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\), and where the \(X_i\) are in \(C_\alpha\). It is then clear, thanks to 7.5.2, that \(C_\alpha^\pi\) is essentially small, i.e. is equivalent to a small category.

Let \[ F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E) \tag{9.21.7} \] be the category of sections of \(E\) over \(B\), and let \[ F^\pi \subset F \tag{9.21.8} \] be the strictly full subcategory of \(F\) consisting of the sections \(X : \alpha \mapsto X(\alpha)\) such that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\) one has \[ X(\alpha) \in C_\alpha^\pi . \] It is clear, the \(C_\alpha^\pi\) being essentially small, that the same holds for the category \(F^\pi\). We shall show that this category is generating, and more precisely:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.9

Under the preceding conditions and with the preceding notations, the following holds:

(i) Every object of \(F\) is accessible (9.3). If \(d\) is a cardinal \(\geq \pi'_0\), and if \(\alpha \mapsto X(\alpha)\) is an element of \(F\) such that for every \(\alpha\), \(X(\alpha)\) is \(d\)-accessible in \(E_\alpha\), then \(X\) is \(d\)-accessible in \(F\).

(ii) Suppose \(\pi \leq c\), or that \(\pi'_0\) is finite (i.e. the \(E_\alpha\) stable under small filtered \(\varinjlim\)). Then every object \(X\) of \(F\) is isomorphic to an object of the form \(\varinjlim_I X_i\), where the \(X_i\) are in \(F^\pi\) and where \(I\) is large with respect to \(\pi\).
To prove (i), note that by virtue of (9.21.4) and of 9.9, every object of \(E_\alpha\) is accessible. On the other hand, \(F\) satisfies condition \(L_{\pi'_0}\), by virtue of the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.10

Let \(p : E \to B\) be a fibred functor, \(F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E)\), \(I\) a category, \(i \mapsto X_i\) a functor from \(I\) to \(F\). For \(\varinjlim_I X_i\) to be representable in \(F\), it suffices that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(\varinjlim_I X_i(\alpha)\) be representable in the fibre category \(E_\alpha\); when this is so, then \(\varinjlim_I X_i\) "is computed argument by argument". In particular, if the fibre categories satisfy condition \(L_{\pi'_0}\) (\(\pi'_0\) being a given cardinal), the same holds for \(F\).
We leave the details of the (easy) proof of 9.21.10 to the reader, contenting ourselves with remarking that it is convenient to use the following result, whose proof is immediate:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.21.10.1

With the hypotheses and notations of 9.21.10 for \(p : E \to B\), and for \(I\), for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), the inclusion functor \(E_\alpha \to E\) commutes with inductive limits of type \(I\).

Returning then to the general conditions of 9.21.9, let \(X\) be an object of \(F\). Since for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(X(\alpha)\) is accessible in \(E_\alpha\), there exists a cardinal \(d \in \mathcal{U}\) such that for every \(\alpha\), \(X(\alpha)\) is \(d\)-accessible in \(E_\alpha\). One may choose \(d \geq \pi'_0\), so that \(F\) satisfies \(L_d\) by virtue of 9.21.10. Using 9.21.10 again for the computation of the inductive limits \(\varinjlim_I Y_i\) in \(F\), with \(I\) large with respect to \(d\), one sees at once that \(X\) is \(d\)-accessible. This proves (i).
We shall now prove 9.21.9 (ii) in several steps ((9.21.11) to 9.21.16)).

Let then \[ X : \alpha \mapsto X(\alpha) \] be an object of \(F\). By virtue of (9.21.4 b)), one can, for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), find an ordered set \(I_\alpha\) large with respect to \(c\), and an isomorphism \(X(\alpha) = \varinjlim_{i\in I_\alpha} X(\alpha)_i\), where \(i \mapsto X(\alpha)_i\) is an inductive system of type \(I_\alpha\) in \(E_\alpha\), the \(X(\alpha)_i\) in \(C_\alpha\). Consider the product ordered set \(I = \prod_\alpha I_\alpha\); it is clear that it is large with respect to \(c\), and that the preceding inductive systems give rise to inductive systems in the \(E_\alpha\), \[ i \mapsto X(\alpha)_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_\alpha , \quad i \in \mathrm{ob}\, I , \tag{9.21.11} \] indexed by the same ordered set \(I\), and to isomorphisms \[ X(\alpha) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_I X(\alpha)_i \quad \text{in } E_\alpha , \tag{9.21.12} \] for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\). We assume the data (9.21.11) and (9.21.12) fixed in what follows.

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.13

Under the preceding conditions, one can find a map \(\varphi : I \to I\) such that \(\varphi(i) \geq i\) for all \(i \in I\), and a map \((i,f) \mapsto \lambda(i,f)\) from \(I\times\mathrm{Fl}\, B\) to \(\mathrm{Fl}\, E\), satisfying the following conditions:

a) For \(i \in I\), \((f : \alpha \to \beta) \in \mathrm{Fl}\, B\), \(\lambda(i,f)\) is an \(f\)-morphism from \(X(\alpha)_i\) to \(X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)}\), making the diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em@C=2em{ X(\alpha) \ar[rr]^-{X(f)} & & X(\beta) \\ & & X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[u] \\ X(\alpha)_i \ar[uu] \ar[urr]_(0.35){\lambda(i,f)} & & \\ \alpha \ar[rr]_-{f} & & \beta } \] commute, where the vertical arrows are the canonical morphisms deduced from (9.21.12).

b) For every \(i \in I\), and \((f : \alpha \to \beta) \in \mathrm{Fl}\, B\), one has commutativity in the diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em@C=2em{ & & X(\beta)_{\varphi^2(i)} \\ X(\alpha)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[urr]^-{\lambda(\varphi(i),f)} & & X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[u] \\ X(\alpha)_i \ar[u] \ar[urr]_(0.35){\lambda(i,f)} & & \\ \alpha \ar[rr]_-{f} & & \beta } \]

c) For every pair of consecutive arrows \(\alpha \xrightarrow{f} \beta \xrightarrow{g} \gamma\) of \(B\), one has commutativity in the following diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em@C=1.6em{ X(\alpha) \ar[r]^-{X(f)} & X(\beta) \ar[r]^-{X(g)} & X(\gamma) \\ & & X(\gamma)_{\varphi^2(i)} \ar[u] \\ & X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[ur]^-{\lambda(\varphi(i),g)} & X(\gamma)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[u] \\ X(\alpha)_i \ar[ur]^-{\lambda(i,f)} \ar[urr]_(0.3){\lambda(i,gf)} & & \\ \alpha \ar[r]_-{f} & \beta \ar[r]_-{g} & \gamma } \] where the vertical arrows are those deduced from (9.21.12).

Note moreover that the commutativity of the two upper trapezoids in b) is already contained in a), so that b) in fact asserts the commutativity of the lower triangle of the diagram under consideration.

Let us prove 9.21.13. Let \(i \in I\), and \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) an arrow in \(B\). Consider the composite \(X(\alpha)_i \to X(\alpha) \xrightarrow{\ X(f)\ } X(\beta) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_j X(\beta)_j\); it defines a morphism in \(E\): \[ X(\alpha)_i \to f^*(X(\beta)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } f^*(\varinjlim_j X(\beta)_j) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_j f^*(X(\beta)_j) , \] where the last equality comes from the fact that \(f^*\) is \(c\)-accessible (9.21.3 c)) and that \(I\) is large with respect to \(c\). By virtue of (9.21.4 a)), since \(X(\alpha)_i \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_\alpha\), the morphism under consideration factors through some \(f^*(X(\beta)_j)\), where \(j\) a priori depends on \(i\) and on \(f \in \mathrm{Fl}(B)\). But by virtue of (9.21.3 b)), and since \(I\) is large with respect to \(c\)), one may choose \(j\) independent of \(f\), say \(j = \varphi(i)\). Since \(I\) is filtered, one may assume \(\varphi(i) \geq i\). One thus finds, for \(i \in I\) and \(f \in \mathrm{Fl}\, F\), a morphism \[ X(\alpha)_i \to f^*(X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)}) , \] or what amounts to the same, an \(f\)-morphism \[ \lambda(i,f) : X(\alpha)_i \to X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} , \] which by construction makes the diagram \[ \xymatrix@R=1em@C=2em{ X(\alpha) \ar[rr]^-{X(f)} & & X(\beta) \\ & & X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[u] \\ X(\alpha)_i \ar[uu] \ar[urr]_(0.35){\lambda(i,f)} & & \\ \alpha \ar[rr]_-{f} & & \beta } \tag{D(f)} \] commute. Consider then, for given \(i, f, g\), the lower triangle of the diagram under consideration in 9.21.13 c); it is not clear that it commutes, but the two composites \(X(\alpha)_i \rightrightarrows X(\beta)_{\varphi^2(i)}\) become equal after composition with \(X(\beta)_{\varphi^2(i)} \to X(\beta)\), as follows from the commutativity of the two upper trapezoids, and of the overall boundary trapezoid, which are the diagrams \(D(f), D(g)\) and \(D(gf)\) respectively. Hence, since \(X(\alpha)_{\varphi^2(i)}\) is \(c\)-accessible (9.21.4 a)) and \(X(\alpha) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{j\in I} X(\alpha)_j\), with \(I\) large with respect to \(c\), it follows that one can find an element \(j \geq \varphi^2(i)\) of \(I\), such that the two arrows under consideration become equal after composition with \(X(\beta)_{\varphi^2(i)} \to X(\beta)_j\). A priori, \(j\) depends on \(i, f\) and \(g\). But for \(i\) fixed, the set of possible pairs \(f, g\) has cardinal \(\geq c^2 = c\), by virtue of (9.21.3 a) and b)), hence, \(I\) being large with respect to \(c\), one may choose \(j\) independent of \(f\) and of \(g\), say \(j = \varphi'(i) \geq \varphi^2(i) \geq \varphi(i)\). Let then, for every \(i \in I\) and \(f : \alpha \to \beta\), \[ \lambda'(i,f) : X(\alpha)_i \to X(\beta)_{\varphi'(i)} \] be the composite \(f\)-morphism \(X(\alpha)_i \to X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)} \to X(\beta)_{\varphi'(i)}\), where the second arrow is the transition morphism. It is then immediate, by construction, that \((\varphi', \lambda')\) satisfies conditions 9.21.13 a) and c), for \((\varphi,\lambda)\). Proceeding similarly for condition b), one sees that one can choose \(\varphi'\) in such a way that this condition is also satisfied for \((\varphi',\lambda')\). This completes the proof of 9.21.13).
Let now \[ J \subset I \] be a subset of \(I\) satisfying the following conditions:
a) \(J\) is filtered,
b) for every \(j \in J\), one has \(\varphi(j) \in J\),
c) for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(X_J(\alpha) = \varinjlim_{i\in J} X(\alpha)_i\) is representable in \(E_\alpha\).

Conditions a) and c) are satisfied in particular if \(J\) is large with respect to \(\pi'_0\) (9.21.2). It then follows from 9.21.10.1 that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(X_J(\alpha)\) is the inductive limit \(\varinjlim_{i\in J} X(\alpha)_i\) in \(E\). Now for an arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), the arrows \(\lambda(i,f)\), for \(i\) varying in \(J\), define thanks to 9.21.13 b) a morphism of ind-objects from \((X(\alpha)_i)_{i\in J}\) to \((X(\beta)_i)_{i\in J}\), whence a homomorphism \[ X_J(f) : X_J(\alpha) \to X_J(\beta) \] on the inductive limits, which is manifestly an \(f\)-homomorphism. Using 9.21.13 c), one finds that one has transitivity relations \[ X_J(gf) = X_J(g) X_J(f) , \] so that one has defined a section \(X_J \in \mathrm{ob}\, F\) of \(E\) over \(B\). Finally 9.21.13 a) shows us that the canonical homomorphisms \[ X_J(\alpha) \to X(\alpha) , \quad \alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B , \] are functorial in \(\alpha\), so that one has a canonical homomorphism \[ u_J : X_J \to X . \]

On the other hand, if \[ J' \supset J \] is another subset of \(I\) satisfying conditions a),b),c) above, one finds a canonical homomorphism \[ u_{J',J} : X_J \to X_{J'} , \] so that the \(X_J\) form an inductive system in \(F\), parametrized by the set (ordered by inclusion) of subsets \(J\) of \(I\) satisfying the conditions under consideration. Finally, the homomorphisms \(u_J\) above define a homomorphism of this inductive system into (the constant inductive system defined by) \(X\).

Let now \(K\) be a set of subsets \(J\) of \(I\), satisfying conditions a),b),c) considered in 9.21.14, and suppose that \(K\) is filtered, with union \(I\). Then it is clear that one has \[ \varinjlim_{J\in K} X_J \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } X , \] using 9.21.10.1, which reduces us to verifying that one has an isomorphism argument by argument.

Take for example for \(K\) the set of all subsets \(J\) of \(I\) that are large with respect to \(\pi'_0\), stable under \(\varphi\), and such that \(\mathrm{card}\, J \leq \pi\). Then by the definition (9.21.6) of \(C_\alpha^\pi\), one has, for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(X_J(\alpha) \in \mathrm{ob}\, C_\alpha^\pi\), hence \(X_J \in \mathrm{ob}\, F^\pi\). Consequently, 9.21.9 (ii) will be proved if we establish that \(K\) is large with respect to \(\pi\) (hence filtered) and has union \(I\). It will obviously suffice, for this, to prove that every subset \(S\) of \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, S \leq \pi\) is contained in some \(J \in K\). This will indeed follow from the hypothesis stated as a preliminary in 9.21.9 (ii), and from the

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.16

Let \(I\) be an ordered set, \(\pi\) an infinite cardinal, \(\varphi : I \to I\) a map from \(I\) to itself.

a) Suppose \(I\) filtered. Then for every subset \(S\) of \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, S \leq \pi\), there exists a filtered subset \(J \supset S\) of \(I\), such that \(\varphi(J) \subset J\) and \(\mathrm{card}(J) \leq \pi\).

b) Let \(\pi'_0\) be a cardinal \(< \pi\), and suppose \(I\) large with respect to \(\pi\). Then for every subset \(S\) of \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, S \leq \pi\), there exists a subset \(J \supset S\) of \(I\) large with respect to \(\pi'_0\), such that \(\varphi(J) \subset J\) and \(\mathrm{card}\, J \leq \pi\).

Let us prove, for example, b) (the proof of a) being analogous and simpler). Let \(P\) be the set of subsets of \(I\) of cardinal \(\leq \pi\), and let \(T \mapsto i_T : P \to I\) be a map such that for \(T \in P\), \(i_T\) is an upper bound of \(T\) in \(I\); the existence of this map simply expresses the hypothesis that \(I\) is large with respect to \(\pi\). Let \(A\) be a well-ordered set such that \(\mathrm{card}\, A = \pi\), and such that for every \(a \in A\), the set of \(a' \leq a\) has cardinal \(< \pi\). It follows in particular, since \(\pi'_0 < \pi\), that \(A\) is large with respect to \(\pi'_0\). Let us define by transfinite recursion maps \[ S \mapsto S_a : P \to P \quad (a \in A) , \] by the following formulas: \[ S_0 = S , \quad S_{a+1} = S_a \cup \varphi(S_a) \cup \{i_{S_a}\} , \quad S_a = \bigcup_{a'<a} S_{a'} \text{ if } a \text{ is a limit ordinal}. \] Let us then set, for \(S \in P\), \[ J(S) = \bigcup_{a\in A} S_a . \] It is then clear that \(J(S) \supset S\), that \(J(S)\) is stable under \(\varphi\), that \(\mathrm{card}\, J(S) \leq \pi\) (since \(\mathrm{card}\, A = \pi\)), and finally that \(J(S)\) is large with respect to \(\pi'_0\) (using the fact that \(A\) is large with respect to \(\pi'_0\)).
This proves 9.21.16 and completes the proof of 9.21.9.
Let us also point out a variant of 9.21.9:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.17

The notations are those of 9.21.9. We denote by \(F'\) the full subcategory \(\underline{\mathrm{Homcart}}_B(B,E)\) of \(F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E)\) consisting of the cartesian sections of \(E\) over \(F\). Then:

(i) Every object of \(F'\) is accessible. More precisely, let \(\alpha \mapsto X(\alpha)\) be an element of \(F'\), and let \(d\) be a cardinal such that \(d \geq \pi'_0\), \(d \geq c\), and such that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \(X(\alpha)\) is a \(d\)-accessible object of \(E\). Then \(X\) is a \(d\)-accessible object of \(F'\).

(ii) Suppose \(\pi \leq c\) and that the functors \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) are \(\pi'_0\)-accessible, or that the categories \(E_\alpha\) are stable under small filtered inductive limits, and that the functors \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) commute with the said inductive limits. Then every object \(X\) of \(F'\) is isomorphic to an object of the form \(\varinjlim_I X_i\), where for every \(i \in I\), \(X_i\) is an object of the full subcategory \(F'^\pi = F'\cap F^\pi\) of \(F'\), and where \(I\) is large with respect to \(\pi\).
Since the proof is entirely analogous to that of 9.21.9, we content ourselves with indicating the points where a modification of the latter is necessary. We first note:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.18

The statement 9.21.10 remains valid when one replaces \(F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E)\) by \(F' = \underline{\mathrm{Homcart}}_B(B,E)\), provided one assumes that the inverse image functors \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) commute with inductive limits of type \(I\).

If therefore under the conditions of 9.21.17, \(d\) is a cardinal such that \(d \geq c\) and \(d \geq \pi'_0\), it follows from the foregoing and from the hypothesis (9.21.3 c)) that for every ordered set \(I\) large with respect to \(d\), the inductive limits of type \(I\) are representable in \(F'\) and are computed argument by argument, whence the conclusion 9.21.17 (i) by an immediate argument.
To prove (ii), one must give a complement to 9.21.13:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 9.21.19

Under the conditions of 9.21.13, suppose that \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, F'\), i.e. that \(X\) is a cartesian section of \(E\) over \(B\). Then one can strengthen the conclusion by the assertion that there exists a function \(\mu\) which, to every \(i \in I\) and every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), associates a morphism \(\mu(i,f) : f^* X(\beta)_i \to X(\alpha)_{\varphi(i)}\) in \(E_\alpha\), in such a way that one has:

d) For every \(i \in I\) and every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), the two following diagrams are commutative: \[ \vcenter{\xymatrix@R=1.6em@C=1.4em{ X(\alpha)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[r]^-{\lambda(\varphi(i),f)} & f^*X(\beta)_{\varphi^2(i)} \\ f^*X(\beta)_i \ar[u]^-{\mu(i,f)} \ar[ur] & }} \qquad \vcenter{\xymatrix@R=1.6em@C=1.4em{ f^*X(\alpha)_{\varphi(i)} \ar[r]^-{\mu(\varphi(i),f)} & X(\alpha)_{\varphi^2(i)} \\ X(\alpha)_i \ar[u]^-{\lambda(i,f)} \ar[ur] & }} . \]

To prove it, one proceeds as in 9.21.3, considering the composite morphism \(f^*(X(\beta))_i \to f^*(X(\beta)) \xrightarrow{\ X(f)^{-1}\ } X(\alpha)\), where (as already in the writing of condition d)) one identifies in the notation an \(f\)-morphism \(R \to S\) of \(E\) with the morphism corresponding to it, \(R \to f^*(S)\) of \(E_\alpha\). Since \(X(\alpha) = \varinjlim_j X(\alpha)_j\), and \(I\) large with respect to \(c\), one can factor the preceding morphism through one of the \(X(\alpha)_j\), where \(j\) a priori depends on \(i\) and on \(f\), but can be chosen independent of \(f\), say \(\psi(i)\). Enlarging if necessary the function \(\varphi\) of 9.21.13, one may assume that \(\psi = \varphi\). Proceeding as for conditions b) and c) of 9.21.13, one sees that, enlarging further if necessary the map \(\varphi\), one may assume that the two diagrams of 9.21.19 d) are commutative.

The map \(\varphi\) being chosen as in 9.21.19, let us resume the argument of 9.21.14, where one must however assume that \(J\) satisfies, in addition to the stated conditions a) b) c), the condition:
d) For every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) in \(B\), the functor \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) commutes with inductive limits of type \(J\).

I claim that, by means of this additional condition, the section \(X_J\) of \(E\) over \(B\) is cartesian, i.e. for every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), the morphism \[ X_J(\alpha) \to f^*X_J(\beta) \tag{\(*\)} \] is an isomorphism. Indeed, by virtue of condition d) above, the target of the morphism under consideration is identified with \(\varinjlim_{i\in J} f^*(X(\beta)_i)\), and the morphism is obtained by passing to the \(\varinjlim_J\) from the morphism of ind-objects in \(E_\alpha\) \[ (X(\alpha)_i)_{i\in J} \to (f^*)(X(\beta)_i)_{i\in J} , \] deduced from the morphisms \(\lambda(i,f) : X(\alpha)_i \to f^*(X(\beta)_{\varphi(i)})\) for \(i \in J\). Now the conditions made explicit in 9.21.19 assure us that the preceding homomorphism of ind-objects is in fact an isomorphism, an inverse being obtained by the homomorphism deduced from the system of the \(\mu(i,f)\), for \(i \in J\). This proves our assertion that (*) is an isomorphism, hence that \(X \in \mathrm{ob}\, F'\).

We shall now suppose that the functors \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) are \(\pi'_0\)-accessible. Then the conditions on \(J\) considered in 9.21.20 are satisfied if \(J\) is large with respect to \(\pi'_0\), stable under \(\varphi\) and such that \(\mathrm{card}\, J \leq \pi\), and one completes the proof of 9.21.17 as in 9.21.15.

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 9.22

Let \(p : E \to B\) be a fibred functor, where \(B\) is a category essentially equivalent to a small category, and where for every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) in \(B\) the inverse image functor \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) is accessible (9.2). Suppose moreover that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), the fibre category \(E_\alpha\) admits a cardinal filtration (9.12) and that every object of \(E_\alpha\) is accessible (9.3). Then each of the categories \(F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E)\) and \(F' = \underline{\mathrm{Homcart}}_B(B,E)\) admits a small full subcategory generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1), and each of its objects is accessible.

It is immediate that the statement does not change essentially when one replaces \(B\) by a full subcategory \(B_0\) such that the inclusion functor \(B_0 \to B\) is an equivalence, and \(E\) by \(E_0 = E\times_B B_0\). This allows us to assume that \(B\) is a small category.

Let, for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), \((\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E_\alpha))_{\pi\geq\pi_\alpha}\) be a cardinal filtration of \(E_\alpha\). Let \(c_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) be a cardinal satisfying the following conditions: \[ \begin{cases} c_0 \geq \underset{\alpha\in\mathrm{ob}\, B}{\mathrm{Sup}}\, \pi_\alpha , \quad c_0 \geq \mathrm{card}\, \mathrm{Fl}\, B ; \\ \text{for every arrow } f : \alpha \to \beta \text{ of } B,\ f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha \text{ is } c_0\text{-accessible}; \\ \text{for every } \alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B,\ \text{the objects of } \mathrm{Filt}^{\pi_\alpha}(E_\alpha) \text{ are } c_0\text{-accessible}. \end{cases} \tag{9.22.1} \] Set \[ c = 2^{c_0} , \] so that \(c > c_0\), and for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), let \[ C_\alpha = \mathrm{Filt}^c(E_\alpha) . \] I claim that the preliminary conditions for 9.21.9 and 9.21.17 are verified, taking \(\pi = \pi_0 = c\). This is clear for (9.21.2) and (9.21.3). For (9.21.4 a)), this follows from 9.17, and (9.21.4 b)) follows from condition 9.12 c) for a cardinal filtration. Note moreover that condition 9.12 b) of cardinal filtrations implies that for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), one has \(C_\alpha^\pi = C_\alpha = \mathrm{Filt}^c(E_\alpha)\), where \(C_\alpha^\pi\) is defined in (9.21.6). Consequently, 9.22 follows from 9.21.9 and from 9.21.17, and more precisely, one has proved the

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.23

Under the conditions of 9.22, if \(c_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) is a cardinal satisfying conditions (9.22.1), and if \(c = 2^{c_0}\), then the subcategory \(F^c\) of \(F\) (resp. \(F'^c\) of \(F'\)) consisting of the \(X\) such that \(X(\alpha) \in \mathrm{ob}\, \mathrm{Filt}^c(E_\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\) is essentially small and generating by strict epimorphisms; more precisely, every object \(X\) of \(F\) (resp. \(F'\)) is isomorphic to an object of the form \(\varinjlim_I X_i\), where the \(X_i\) are in \(F^c\) (resp. in \(F'^c\)), and where \(I\) is an ordered set large with respect to \(c\).
By means of slightly stronger hypotheses in 9.22, one can moreover considerably sharpen 9.22 and 9.23:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.24

Under the conditions of 9.22, suppose that each of the categories \(E_\alpha\) (\(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, E\)) is stable under small filtered inductive limits, and that for every \(\pi \geq \pi_\alpha\), \(\mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E_\alpha)\) is stable under filtered inductive limits indexed by filtered ordered sets \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}\, I \leq \pi\) (which slightly strengthens the condition 9.12 b) of cardinal filtrations). In the case where it is \(F'\) that one considers, suppose moreover that for every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), the functor \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) commutes with small filtered inductive limits. Finally let \(c_0 \in \mathcal{U}\) be a cardinal satisfying conditions (9.22.1), and consider, for every cardinal \(\pi \geq c = 2^{c_0}\), the strictly full subcategory \(F^\pi\) (resp. \(F'^\pi\)) of \(F\) (resp. of \(F'\)) consisting of the \(X\) such that one has \(X(\alpha) \in \mathrm{Filt}^\pi(E_\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\). Then the subcategories under consideration define a cardinal filtration (9.12) of \(F\) (resp. of \(F'\)).

One must verify conditions a), b), c) of 9.12. Conditions a) and b) follow from the analogous conditions for the given cardinal filtrations of the \(E_\alpha\), and from 9.21.10 (resp. 9.21.18, taking into account the second of the conditions (9.22.1)). It remains to prove c), whose first part follows at once from 9.21.9 (resp. 9.21.17), taking \(\pi'_0 = 0\), \(\pi_0 = c\). It remains to prove that if one has two cardinals \(\pi' \geq \pi \geq c\), then for every \(X\) in \(F^{\pi'}\) (resp. \(F'^{\pi'}\)) one has \(X \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \varinjlim_{i\in K} X_i\), with the \(X_i\) in \(F^\pi\) (resp. \(F'^\pi\)), \(K\) large with respect to \(\pi\), and card \(K \leq \pi'^\pi\). For this, let us resume the proofs of 9.21.9 (ii) and of 9.21.17 (ii). One may assume that each \(I_\alpha\) has cardinal \(\leq \pi'\) by virtue of the condition 9.12 c) on the cardinal filtration of \(E_\alpha\), so that one will have \[ \mathrm{card}\, I \leq (\pi'^\pi)^{\mathrm{card}\,\mathrm{ob}\, B} \leq (\pi'^\pi)^c = \pi'^{\pi c} = \pi'^\pi . \] The index set \(K\) used in 9.21.15 resp. 9.21.21 is the set of subsets \(J\) of \(I\) that are filtered (i.e. large with respect to \(\pi'_0 = 0\)), stable under \(\varphi\) and such that card \(J \leq \pi\). It is then immediate that one has \[ \mathrm{card}\, K \leq (\mathrm{card}\, I)^\pi \leq (\pi'^\pi)^\pi = \pi'^{\pi^2} = \pi'^\pi , \] which completes the proof of 9.24.

To conclude, it is appropriate to give a statement freed from the somewhat technical hypotheses of 9.22, replacing them by the conjunction, for the \(E_\alpha\), of the hypotheses that intervene in 9.11 (which ensure the accessibility of the objects of the \(E\)) and in 9.13 (which ensure the existence of a cardinal filtration in \(E\)):

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.25

Let \(p : E \to B\) be a fibred functor, where \(B\) is a category equivalent to a small category, and where for every arrow \(f : \alpha \to \beta\) of \(B\), the functor \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) is accessible (9.2). Suppose moreover that, for every \(\alpha \in \mathrm{ob}\, B\), the fibre category \(E_\alpha\) satisfies the following conditions:

a) \(E_\alpha\) admits a small full subcategory, generating by strict epimorphisms (7.1).

b) \(E_\alpha\) is stable under fibre products, under kernels of double arrows, under sums of two objects and under cokernels of double arrows, and finally under small filtered inductive limits∗.

c) The functor \(\mathrm{Ker}(u,v)\) on the category of double arrows of \(E_\alpha\) is accessible (for example, commutes with small filtered inductive limits).

d) Every strict epimorphism of \(E_\alpha\) (10.2) is a universal strict epimorphism.

Under these conditions, each of the categories \(F = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}_B(B,E)\) and \(F' = \underline{\mathrm{Homcart}}_B(B,E)\) admits a small subcategory generating by strict epimorphisms, and all its objects are accessible (9.3).
Moreover, 9.24 gives us:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 9.26

Under the conditions of 9.25, and in the case where one considers \(F' = \underline{\mathrm{Homcart}}_B(B,E)\), suppose that the functors \(f^* : E_\beta \to E_\alpha\) commute with small filtered inductive limits. Then \(F\) (resp. \(F'\)) admits a cardinal filtration, which one can make explicit by the procedure of 9.24.

footnotes.html: (∗) This last condition being probably unnecessary, cf. 9.13.2.

blocks.html: 10. Glossary.
For the reader's convenience, we gather here the definitions of a few terms used in the preceding sections. We denote by \(C\) a category.
10.1. Cartesian, Cocartesian:

A diagram of \(C\) \[ \xymatrix{ A \ar[r] \ar[d] & B \ar[d] \\ C \ar[r] & D } \] is said to be cartesian if it is commutative and if the canonical morphism from \(A\) to the fibre product \(C\times_D B\) is an isomorphism. It is said to be cocartesian if the corresponding diagram of the category opposite to \(C\) is cartesian.
10.2. Epimorphism, strict epimorphism etc. Cf. 10.3.
10.3. Epimorphic family, strict epimorphic family etc.:

A family \[ f_i : A_i \to B , \quad i \in I , \] of arrows with the same target in \(C\) is called an epimorphic family if for every object \(C\) of \(C\), the map induced by the \(f_i\) \[ \mathrm{Hom}(B,C) \to \prod_i \mathrm{Hom}(A_i,C) \tag{10.3.1} \] is injective.

One says that the family under consideration is strict epimorphic if the image of the map (10.3.1) is formed of the families \((g_i)\) such that for every object \(R\) of \(C\), every pair of indices \(i, j \in I\) and every pair of arrows \(u : R \to A_i\), \(v : R \to A_j\) with \(f_i u = f_j v\), one also has \(g_i u = g_j v\). When the fibre products \(A_i \times_B A_j\) are representable for \(i, j \in I\), it amounts to the same to say that the essential image of (10.3.1) is formed of the \((g_i)\) such that for every pair of indices \(i, j \in I\), one has \(g_i \mathrm{pr}_1 = g_j \mathrm{pr}_2\), where \(\mathrm{pr}_1, \mathrm{pr}_2\) are the two projections of \(A_i \times_B A_j\). One says that the family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) is an effective epimorphic family if the preceding condition is satisfied, i.e. if it is strict epimorphic, and if the fibre products \(A_i \times_B A_j\) are representable.

One says that the family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) is a universal epimorphic family, (resp. universal effective epimorphic) if the morphisms \(f_i\) are squarable (10.3), and if for every arrow \(B' \to B\), the family of arrows \(f'_i : A'_i \to A_i\times_B B'\), \(i \in I\), deduced from the family \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) by base change \(B' \to B\), is epimorphic (resp. effective epimorphic).

The notion of universal strict epimorphic family will be defined in (II 2.5, 2.6). Note that when the morphisms \(f_i\) are squarable (for example if in \(C\) the fibre products are representable) this notion coincides with that of universal effective epimorphic family (use II 2.4). In the general case, one has among the six variants under consideration of the notion of epimorphicity the logical implications: \[ \xymatrix@R=1.8em@C=0.8em{ & & \text{universal effective epimorphic} \ar@{=>}[dll] \ar@{=>}[drr] & & \\ \text{effective epimorphic} \ar@{=>}[ddrrr] & & & & \text{universal strict epimorphic} \ar@{=>}[dll] \ar@{=>}[d] \\ & & \text{strict epimorphic} \ar@{=>}[dr] & & \text{universal epimorphic} \ar@{=>}[dl] \\ & & & \text{epimorphic} & } \] A morphism \(f : A \to B\) of \(C\) is called an epimorphism (resp. a strict epimorphism, resp. an effective epimorphism, resp. a universal epimorphism, resp. a universal effective epimorphism, resp. a universal strict epimorphism) if the family of morphisms reduced to the single element \(f\) is epimorphic (resp. ....).
10.4. Monomorphic family, strict monomorphic family etc.

A family of arrows \(f_i : A_i \to B\) of \(C\) is called monomorphic (resp. strict monomorphic, ....) if, as a family of arrows of the opposite category \(C^\circ\), it is epimorphic (resp. strict epimorphic, ...). An arrow \(f : A \to B\) of \(C\) is called a monomorphism (resp. a strict monomorphism, ...) if the family reduced to \(f\) is monomorphic (resp. strict monomorphic, ...), i.e. if \(f\), as an arrow of the opposite category \(C^\circ\), is an epimorphism (resp. a strict epimorphism, ....).
10.5. Monomorphism, strict monomorphism etc. Cf. 10.4.
10.6. Projector, image of a projector, direct summand of an object.

Let \(f : X \to X\) be an endomorphism of an object of \(C\). One says that \(f\) is a projector if one has \(f^2 = f\). Then the pair \((f, \mathrm{id}_X)\) admits a representable cokernel \(X'\) if and only if it admits a representable kernel \(X''\), and when this is so, there exists a unique isomorphism \(u : X' \to X''\) in \(C\) such that \(iup = f\), where \(p : X \to X'\) and \(i : X'' \to X\) are the morphisms canonical to it. One then generally identifies \(X'\) and \(X''\), and calls it the image of the projector \(f\); one says that the projector \(f\) admits an image if \(\mathrm{Ker}(f, \mathrm{id}_X)\) is representable, i.e. \(\mathrm{Coker}(f, \mathrm{id}_X)\) is representable. A subobject (resp. a quotient) \(Y\) of \(X\) is called a direct summand of \(X\) if one can find a projector \(f\) in \(X\) factoring through \(Y\), and admitting \(Y\) as image as a subobject (resp. as a quotient) of \(X\). One says sometimes, by abuse of language, that an object of \(C\) is a direct summand of \(X\), if it is isomorphic to the image of a projector in \(X\).
10.7. Squarable:
An arrow \(f : A \to B\) of \(C\) is called squarable if for every arrow \(B' \to B\) of \(C\), the fibre product \(A\times_B B'\) is representable in \(C\).
10.8. Quotient, strict quotient etc.

Let \(A\) be an object of \(C\). Two epimorphisms \(f : A \to B\), \(f' : A \to B'\) with source \(A\) are said to be equivalent if there exists an isomorphism \(u : B \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } B'\) such that \(uf = f'\). One obtains in this way an equivalence relation on the set of epimorphisms with source \(A\), whose classes are called the quotients, or quotient objects, of \(A\). For every quotient of \(A\), one generally assumes a chosen element of this class, say \(f : A \to B\), and one often speaks (by abuse of language) of the quotient \(B\) of \(A\) (or of the quotient \(f : A \to B\) of \(A\)). One says that \(B\) is a strict quotient (resp. an effective quotient, resp. a universal quotient, ....) if the morphism \(f : A \to B\) is a strict epimorphism (resp. an effective epimorphism, resp. a universal epimorphism, ...) (10.3).
10.9. Equivalence relations.

Let \(F, G\) be two presheaves of sets on \(C\). A diagram \(p_1, p_2 : F \rightrightarrows G\) is called an equivalence relation on \(G\) if for every object \(A\) of \(C\), the map \[ (p_1(A), p_2(A)) : F(A) \to G(A)\times G(A) \] induces a bijection of \(F(A)\) onto the graph of an equivalence relation on the set \(G(A)\).

A diagram \(p_1, p_2 : B \rightrightarrows C\) in \(C\) is called an equivalence relation on \(C\) if the corresponding diagram of presheaves is an equivalence relation. When in \(C\) the finite products and fibre products are representable, a functor \(\widehat{\varphi} : C \to C'\) commuting with finite products and fibre products transforms equivalence relations on \(C\) into equivalence relations on \(\widehat{\varphi}(C)\).

Let \(\pi : C \to D\) be a morphism of \(C\) such that the fibre product \(C\times_D C\) is representable. Then the diagram \(\mathrm{pr}_1, \mathrm{pr}_2 : C\times_D C \rightrightarrows C\) is an equivalence relation on \(C\).
10.10. Effective equivalence relation, effective universal.

An equivalence relation \(p_1, p_2 : R \rightrightarrows A\) on an object \(A\) of \(C\) is called an effective equivalence relation if there exists a morphism \(\pi : A \to B\) such that the square \[ \xymatrix{ R \ar[r]^-{p_2} \ar[d]_-{p_1} & A \ar[d]^-{\pi} \\ A \ar[r] & B } \] is cartesian and cocartesian. (The morphism \(\pi\) is the cokernel of the pair \((p_1, p_2)\), and is therefore determined up to unique isomorphism.) The morphism \(\pi\) is then an effective epimorphism; if it is a universal effective epimorphism (10.3) one says that the equivalence relation is effective universal.
10.11. Subobject, strict subobject etc.
These are the notions dual to those of quotient, strict quotient etc. (10.8).
BIBLIOGRAPHY
B. Mitchell, Theory of categories, Academic Press (1965).
Appendix: Universes (by N. Bourbaki∗)

footnotes.html: (∗) We reproduce here, with his agreement, secret papers of N. BOURBAKI. The references of this text refer to his learned work.

pages.title: 1. Definition and first properties of universes

blocks.html: 1. Definition and first properties of universes

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 1

A set \(\mathcal{U}\) is called a universe if it satisfies the conditions:

  1. (\(\mathcal{U}\).I)

    if \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) and if \(y \in x\), then \(y \in \mathcal{U}\);

  2. (\(\mathcal{U}\).II)

    if \(x, y \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(\{x,y\} \in \mathcal{U}\);

  3. (\(\mathcal{U}\).III)

    if \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}\);

  4. (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV)

    if \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), and if \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), then the union \(\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\);

  5. (\(\mathcal{U}\).?)

    if \(x, y \in \mathcal{U}\), then the pair \((x,y) \in \mathcal{U}\).

N.B. As has, I believe, been decided for the forthcoming editions, one defines the pair in the Kuratowski manner by \((x,y) = \{\{x,y\}, \{x\}\}\); condition (\(\mathcal{U}\).?) is unnecessary since it follows from (\(\mathcal{U}\).II).
Examples.
1) The empty set is a universe, denoted \(\mathcal{U}_0\).

2) Consider the non-empty finite words formed with the four symbols "\(\{\)", "\(\}\)", ",", and "\(\varnothing\)" (cf. Alg. I). Let us define, by recursion on the length \(n\) of such a word, the notion of meaningful word:
a) For \(n = 1\), only the word \(\varnothing\) is meaningful;

b) for a word \(A\) of length \(n\) to be meaningful, it is necessary and sufficient that there exist \(p\) distinct meaningful words \(A_1, \ldots, A_p\) (\(p \geq 1\)) of lengths \(< n\) such that \[ A = \{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_p\} . \] For example \(\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}, \{\{\varnothing\}\}, \{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}\) are meaningful words. It is clear, by recursion on the length, that every meaningful word denotes a term of Set Theory; for example, if \(A = \{A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_p\}\), \(A\) denotes the set whose elements are \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), and \(A_p\); these terms are obviously finite sets. Let \(\mathcal{U}_1\) be the set of the sets thus obtained. One verifies easily that \(\mathcal{U}_1\) satisfies the conditions (\(\mathcal{U}\).I), (\(\mathcal{U}\).II), (\(\mathcal{U}\).III) and (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV) of Def. 1 (but not that idiotic (\(\mathcal{U}\).?), which does not matter if one is willing to dispense with the pair). Hence \(\mathcal{U}_1\) is a universe. One will note that the elements of \(\mathcal{U}_1\) are finite, and that \(\mathcal{U}_1\) is countable.
In the statements that follow, \(\mathcal{U}\) denotes a universe.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 1

If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) and if \(y \subset x\), then \(y \in \mathcal{U}\).
Indeed, one has \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).III), whence \(y \in \mathfrak{P}(x)\) and \(y \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).I).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary

If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), every quotient set \(y\) of \(x\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).
Indeed \(y\) is a subset of \(\mathfrak{P}(x)\). Whence \(y \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).III) and Prop. 1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 2

If \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), one has \(\{x\} \in \mathcal{U}\).
This follows from (\(\mathcal{U}\).II) applied for \(y = x\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 3

Every pair, every triple, every quadruple of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).
This is true for pairs according to the N.B. or (\(\mathcal{U}\).?). One deduces from it the case of triples since \((x,y,z) = ((x,y),z)\), then that of quadruples since \((x,y,z,t) = ((x,y,z),t)\).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 4

If \(X, Y \in \mathcal{U}\), then \(X \times Y \in \mathcal{U}\).

Indeed, for \(x \in X\), \(\{x\} \times Y\) is the union of the family \(\{(x,y)\}_{y\in Y}\); since one has \(\{(x,y)\} \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).I), (\(\mathcal{U}\).II) and Prop. 3, one has \(\{x\} \times Y \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV). Finally \(X \times Y\) is the union of the family \((\{x\} \times Y)_{x\in X}\); it is therefore an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV) again.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1

If \(X, Y, Z, \ldots\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), all the sets of the scale built on \(X, Y, Z, \ldots\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (cf. chap. IV, § ).
This follows indeed from successive applications of Prop. 4 and of (\(\mathcal{U}\).III).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2

If \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) and if \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), the sum set \(\sum_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Indeed, this sum set is a subset of the product \((\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha) \times I\) (chap. II), a product whose two factors are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (by (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV) and the hypothesis). One then applies Prop. 4 and 1.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 5

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), every correspondence between \(X\) and \(Y\) (in particular every map from \(X\) to \(Y\)) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Indeed, such a correspondence \(C\) is a triple \((X, Y, \Gamma)\) where \(\Gamma\) is a subset of \(X \times Y\) (the graph of \(C\)) (chap. II, § ). One has \(\Gamma \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 4 and 1. Whence \(C \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 3.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 6

If \(X, Y \in \mathcal{U}\), every set \(Z\) of correspondences between \(X\) and \(Y\) (in particular of maps from \(X\) to \(Y\)) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Indeed, \(Z\) is a subset of \(\{X\} \times \{Y\} \times \mathfrak{P}(X \times Y)\). Now this product is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 2 and the Cor. to Prop. 4. One therefore has \(Z \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 1.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary

If \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), and if \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), one has \(\prod_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha \in \mathcal{U}\).
Indeed, this product is a set of maps from \(I\) to \(\bigcup_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha\), and this union is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV).

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 7

If \(X\) is a subset of \(\mathcal{U}\) whose cardinal is at most that of an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), then \(X\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Let \(I\) be an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(\mathrm{card}(X) \leq \mathrm{card}(I)\). One has a surjection \(i \mapsto x_i\) from a subset \(I'\) of \(I\) onto \(X\). Then \(X\) is the union of the family \((\{x_i\})_{i\in I'}\); now this union is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 1, Prop. 2 and (\(\mathcal{U}\).IV).

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary

If \(\mathcal{U}\) is non-empty, every finite subset of \(\mathcal{U}\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), and \(\mathcal{U}\) has elements of arbitrary finite cardinal.
On the other hand, if \(\mathcal{U} = \varnothing\), \(\varnothing\) is a finite subset of \(\varnothing\) but not an element of \(\varnothing\).

Indeed, if \(\mathcal{U}\) is non-empty, Prop. 2 shows that a one-element set \(x_0\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\). By recursion on \(n\), set \(x_{n+1} = \mathfrak{P}(x_n)\). One has \(x_n \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).III), and \(\mathrm{card}(x_{n+1}) = 2^{\mathrm{card}(x_n)}\), so that \(\mathcal{U}\) has elements of arbitrarily large finite cardinal.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

It follows from Prop. 2 and the Cor. to Prop. 7 that every non-empty universe \(\mathcal{U}\) contains the universe \(\mathcal{U}_1\) of Ex. 2; indeed one has \(\varnothing \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 1 . Thus \(\mathcal{U}_1\) is the intersection of all non-empty universes. More generally:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 8

If \((\mathcal{U}_\lambda)_{\lambda\in L}\) is a non-empty family of universes, then \(\mathcal{U} = \bigcap_{\lambda\in L} \mathcal{U}_\lambda\) is a universe.
This follows at once from Def. 1.
2. Universes and species of structures

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a species of structure; suppose, to fix ideas and lighten the exposition, that each structure of species \(\mathcal{E}\) is defined on a base set. Let \((X,S)\) be a structure of species \(\mathcal{E}\) (\(X\) being the base set, and \(S\) the structure), and let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. If \(X \in \mathcal{U}\), then all the constitutive objects of the structure \(S\) on \(X\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (by Cor. 1 to Prop. 4, no. 1 and by (\(\mathcal{U}\).I)) so that the structure \((X,S)\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Suppose now that \(\mathcal{E}\) is a species of structure with morphisms. If \(X\) and \(X'\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) equipped with structures of species \(\mathcal{E}\), then the set of morphisms from \(X\) to \(X'\) is again an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) (no. 1, Prop. 6).

Consider then the category \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) defined in § 1, no. 2, ex. c). Since the objects and the arrows of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\), \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) is a pair of subsets of \(\mathcal{U}\), equipped with a quadruple of maps; it is not, in general, an element of \(\mathcal{U}\). The notation \(X \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) will mean that \(X\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) equipped with a structure of species \(\mathcal{E}\).
The category \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) is stable under numerous operations:
a) If \(X \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\), and if \(X'\) is a subset of \(X\) that admits an induced structure, then \(X' \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\). This follows from Prop. 1, no. 1.
b) If \(X \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\), and if \(X''\) is a quotient set of \(X\) that admits a quotient structure, then \(X'' \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) (Cor. to Prop. 1, no. 1).

c) If \(X, Y \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\), and if \(X \times Y\) admits a product structure, then \(X \times Y \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) (Prop. 4, no. 1). More generally, if \((X_i)_{i\in I}\) is a family of elements of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\), if one has \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), and if \(\prod_{i\in I} X_i\) admits a product structure, then \(\prod_{i\in I} X_i \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) (Cor. to Prop. 6). Analogous assertions for sum structures (Cor. 2 to Prop. 4).

d) Let \(I\) be a preordered set, and \((X_i, f_{ij})_{i,j\in I}\) a projective system (resp. inductive) of sets equipped with structures of species \(\mathcal{E}\) and with morphisms; let \(L\) be the limit of this system, in the sense of chap. III . If \(X_i \in \mathcal{U}\) for all \(i\), if \(I \in \mathcal{U}\), and if \(L\) admits a projective (resp. inductive) limit structure, then one has \(L \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\): indeed \(L\) is a subset of \(\prod_{i\in I} X_i\) (resp. a quotient set of \(\sum_{i\in I} X_i\)), and is therefore an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by no. 1.
Let us give a few more particular examples:

1) Let \(X, Y \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Top})\) be two locally compact spaces. Then the set \(\mathcal{C}(X,Y)\) of continuous maps from \(X\) to \(Y\), equipped with the topology of compact convergence (Top. Géné. X), is an element of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Top})\). Indeed one has \(\mathcal{C}(X,Y) \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 6 of no. 1.

2) Let \(X, Y \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Ab})\). Then the group \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}}(X,Y)\) is an element of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Ab})\) by Prop. 6 of no. 1. If one supposes moreover that one has \(\mathbb{Z} \in \mathcal{U}\), the tensor product \(X \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}} Y\) is an element of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Ab})\); indeed this tensor product is a quotient of \(\mathbb{Z}^{(X \times Y)}\), which is a subset of \(\mathbb{Z}^{X \times Y}\), which itself is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 4 and 6 of no. 1.

3) Let \(X \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Unif})\) be a uniform space. Then its completion \(\widehat{X}\) is an element of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Unif})\). Indeed \(\widehat{X}\) is a set of equivalence classes of Cauchy filters on \(X\); now a filter on \(X\) is an element of \(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(X))\), so an equivalence class of filters is an element of \(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(X)))\), so that \(\widehat{X}\) is an element of \(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(X))))\), hence an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).III) and (\(\mathcal{U}\).I).

N.B. Moral: Bourbaki will have to take care to properly "canonify" his constructions. For example, in those where one adjoins an element \(\infty\) (Alexandroff compactification, projective field), it will be advantageous to take \(\infty = \varnothing\) (since \(\varnothing\) is an element of every non-empty universe) and to form the sum set of \(\{\varnothing\}\) and the given set. Of course one would also have to "canonify" the two-element set serving to construct the sum sets; thus \(\{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}\) seems to me a good candidate since it belongs to every non-empty universe.
3. Universes and categories

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(C\) a category. We write \(C \in \mathcal{U}\) if one has \(\mathrm{Ob}(C) \in \mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}(C) \in \mathcal{U}\). This writing is justified by the fact that \(C\) is the sextuple formed of \(\mathrm{Ob}(C)\), of \(\mathrm{Fl}(C)\) and of the four structural maps; hence if \(\mathrm{Ob}(C) \in \mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}(C) \in \mathcal{U}\), these four maps are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (no. 1, Cor. 1 to Prop. 4), hence so is the sextuple \(C\) (no. 1, Prop. 3, cum grano salis). This is moreover a particular case of no. 2, if one considers the species of structure "cat" of category. With the notations of no. 2, the relation \(C \in \mathcal{U}\) is also written \(C \in (\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{cat})\).

One will note that a category such as \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Ens})\), \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Ord})\), \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Top})\) or \((\mathcal{U} - \mathrm{Gr})\) is not, in general, an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Let \(C, D\) be two categories and \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe such that \(C, D \in \mathcal{U}\). If \(C'\) is a subcategory of \(C\), one has \(C' \in \mathcal{U}\); the product category \(C \times D\), the sum category of \(C\) and \(D\), the opposite categories \(C^\circ\) and \(D^\circ\) are also elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) (cf. no. 2). The functor category \(E = \underline{\mathrm{Hom}}(C,D)\) is likewise an element of \(\mathcal{U}\): indeed \(\mathrm{Ob}(E)\) is a set of pairs of maps \(\mathrm{Ob}(C) \to \mathrm{Ob}(D)\), \(\mathrm{Fl}(C) \to \mathrm{Fl}(D)\), hence \(\mathrm{Ob}(E) \in \mathcal{U}\) by no. 1; as for \(\mathrm{Fl}(E)\), it is a set of functorial morphisms, that is to say of maps \(\mathrm{Ob}(C) \to \mathrm{Fl}(D)\), whence \(\mathrm{Fl}(E) \in \mathcal{U}\) by Prop. 6 of no. 1 .

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 9

Let \(\mathcal{E}\) be a species of structure with morphisms, and \(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{U}'\) two universes such that \(\mathcal{U}' \subset \mathcal{U}\). Then \((\mathcal{U}' - \mathcal{E})\) is a full subcategory of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\).

Indeed, if \(x\) and \(y\) are objects of \((\mathcal{U}' - \mathcal{E})\), they are by definition objects of \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\). As for \(\mathrm{Hom}(x,y)\), it is the same set in both categories (cf. §1, no. 2, ex. c)).

N.B. One will note that the hypothesis that \(\mathcal{U}\) and \(\mathcal{U}'\) are universes is unnecessary, so that Prop. 9 would advantageously move up to § 1, no. 4. But the Tribe requested that it be here.

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

It happens that the axioms of the species of structure \(\mathcal{E}\) imply that the cardinals of the sets equipped with structures of species \(\mathcal{E}\) are bounded by a fixed cardinal, say \(c\) (for example the species of structure of finite group, of group of finite type, of module of finite type over a fixed ring \(A\), or of algebra of finite type over \(A\)). Suppose then that there exists an element \(z\) of \(\mathcal{U}'\) such that \(c \leq \mathrm{card}(z)\). Then, for every set \(x\) equipped with a structure of species \(\mathcal{E}\), there exists an element \(x'\) of \(\mathcal{U}'\) equipotent to \(x\), for example a subset of \(z\); let us equip \(x'\) with the structure deduced from that of \(x\) by transport of structure; one obtains in this way an element of \((\mathcal{U}' - \mathcal{E})\).
