It follows that the inclusion functor from \((\mathcal{U}' - \mathcal{E})\) to \((\mathcal{U} - \mathcal{E})\) is then essentially surjective (§4, no. 2, Def. 2) and is therefore an equivalence of categories (§4, no. 3, Th. 1).
4. The axiom of universes

The most agreeable stability results of no. 2 are of interest only if one can apply them to something other than the two small universes \(\mathcal{U}_0\) and \(\mathcal{U}_1\) described in no. 1. We shall therefore add to the axioms of Set Theory the following axiom:
(A.6) For every set \(x\), there exists a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(x \in \mathcal{U}\).

This axiom implies that, if \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is a family of sets, there exists a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(x_\alpha \in \mathcal{U}\) for all \(\alpha \in I\): it suffices, indeed, to apply (A.6) to \(x = \bigcup_{\alpha\in I} x_\alpha\) and to apply Prop. 1 of no. 1.

In particular, given a category \(C\), there exists a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(C \in \mathcal{U}\) in the sense of no. 3: one applies the foregoing to the family \((\mathrm{Ob}(C), \mathrm{Fl}(C))\). This applies to categories of the form \((V - \mathcal{E})\) where \(\mathcal{E}\) is a species of structure with morphisms and \(V\) a set, a universe for example; in general one has \(V \neq \mathcal{U}\).

For example, if \(V\) is a universe, one has \(\mathrm{Ob}(V - \mathrm{Ens}) = V\) and \(\mathrm{Fl}(V - \mathrm{Ens}) \subset V\) (no. 1, Prop. 5). The universes \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \((V - \mathrm{Ens}) \in \mathcal{U}\) are therefore those such that \(V \in \mathcal{U}\). Now the relation \(V \in V\) is impossible for a universe: indeed, for every subset \(A\) of \(V\), one would have \(A \in V\) (no. 1, Prop. 1), whence \(\mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{P}(V)) \leq \mathrm{card}(V)\), which is impossible.
5. Universes and strongly inaccessible cardinals

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe. By condition (\(\mathcal{U}\).I) of Def. 1, every element \(x\) of \(\mathcal{U}\) is a subset of \(\mathcal{U}\); one therefore has \(\mathrm{card}(x) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\). Since the cardinals of the subsets of \(\mathcal{U}\) form a well-ordered set, the cardinal \[ \underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) = \sup_{x\in\mathcal{U}} \mathrm{card}(x) \tag{1} \] exists. Note that, for every cardinal \(\underline{c} < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\), there exists an element \(x\) of \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(\mathrm{card}(x) = \underline{c}\); indeed, there exists by definition \(y \in \mathcal{U}\) such that \(\underline{c} \leq \mathrm{card}(y) \leq \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\), and one takes for \(x\) a suitable subset of \(y\). Conversely, if \(x \in \mathcal{U}\), one has \(\mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\); indeed one has \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}\) by (\(\mathcal{U}\).III), whence \(2^{\mathrm{card}(x)} \leq \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\). The cardinal \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) therefore has the following properties:

1) If \(\underline{c}\) is a cardinal \(< \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\), one has \(2^{\underline{c}} < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\); indeed, if \(x\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) of cardinal \(\underline{c}\), one has \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}\) by application of (\(\mathcal{U}\).III), whence \(2^{\underline{c}} < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\).

2) If \((\underline{c}_\lambda)_{\lambda\in I}\) is a family of cardinals such that \(\underline{c}_\lambda < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) for all \(\lambda \in I\) and such that \(\mathrm{card}(I) < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\), then the sum cardinal \(\sum_{\lambda\in I} \underline{c}_\lambda\) is \(< \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\). Indeed let \(x_\lambda \in \mathcal{U}\) be such that \(\mathrm{card}(x_\lambda) = \underline{c}_\lambda\); replacing if necessary \(I\) by an equipotent index set, one may assume that one has \(I \in \mathcal{U}\); then the sum set of the \(x_\lambda\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) (Cor. 2 to Prop. 4 of no. 1), which proves our assertion.
Let us lay down the following definition:

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 2

A cardinal \(\underline{d}\) is said to be strongly inaccessible if:

(FI.1) If \(\underline{c}\) is a cardinal such that \(\underline{c} < \underline{d}\), one has \(2^{\underline{c}} < \underline{d}\).

(FI.2) If \((\underline{c}_\lambda)_{\lambda\in I}\) is a family of cardinals such that \(\underline{c}_\lambda < \underline{d}\) for all \(\lambda \in I\) and if \(\mathrm{card}(I) < \underline{d}\), then \(\sum_{\lambda\in I} \underline{c}_\lambda < \underline{d}\).

Examples. The cardinal 0 and the countably infinite cardinal are strongly inaccessible. No non-zero finite cardinal is strongly inaccessible. Thus we have just shown that the axiom (A.6) of universes implies the relation:
(A'.6) Every cardinal is strictly bounded above by a strongly inaccessible cardinal.
Conversely:

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 1

The relation (A'.6) implies the axiom (A.6) of universes.

Indeed let \(A\) be a set. The task is to construct a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) of which \(A\) is an element. Let us define by recursion a sequence \((A_n)_{n\geq 0}\) of sets by means of: \[ A_0 = A , \quad A_{n+1} = \text{union of the elements of } A_n = \text{set of the elements of } A_n . \tag{2} \] Set \(B = \bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} A_n\). Let, by (A'.6), \(\underline{c}\) be a strongly inaccessible cardinal such that \(\mathrm{card}(B) < \underline{c}\).

There exists a well-ordered set \(I\) such that \(\mathrm{card}(I) = \underline{c}\). Replacing if necessary \(I\) by its smallest segment of cardinal \(\underline{c}\), one may assume that every segment of \(I\) distinct from \(I\) has a cardinal \(< \underline{c}\).

We shall denote by \(\varepsilon\) the smallest element of \(I\). It follows from the hypothesis on the segments that \(I\) has no greatest element (otherwise one would remove it), hence that every element of \(I\) admits a successor; for \(\alpha \in I\), we shall denote by \(s(\alpha)\) the successor of \(\alpha\).

This being so, let us define, by transfinite recursion, a family \((B_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) of sets by means of: \[ \begin{cases} B_\varepsilon = B \\ B_{s(\alpha)} = B_\alpha \cup \mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha) \\ B_\alpha = \bigcup_{\beta<\alpha} B_\beta \text{ if } \alpha \text{ has no predecessor}. \end{cases} \tag{3} \] Set \(\mathcal{U} = \bigcup_{\alpha\in I} B_\alpha\). We shall show that \(\mathcal{U}\) is the sought-for universe.
First one has \(A \in \mathcal{U}\), since \(A = A_0\) is a subset of \(B = B_\varepsilon\), hence an element of \(\mathfrak{P}(B_\varepsilon) \subset B_{s(\varepsilon)}\).

Note next that, for every \(\alpha \in I\), one has: \[ \mathrm{card}(B_\alpha) < \underline{c} . \tag{4} \] Let us proceed indeed by transfinite recursion on \(\alpha\). It is true for \(\alpha = \varepsilon\) by hypothesis. From (4) one deduces \(\mathrm{card}(B_{s(\alpha)}) \leq \mathrm{card}(B_\alpha) + 2^{\mathrm{card}(B_\alpha)} \leq \underline{c} + \underline{c}\) (by (FI.1)) \(= \underline{c}\) (since \(\underline{c}\) is infinite). Finally, if \(\alpha\) has no predecessor, the set \(I'\) of the \(\beta < \alpha\) has cardinal \(< \underline{c}\); whence (if \(\mathrm{card}(B_\beta) < \underline{c}\) for all \(\beta < \alpha\)), \(\mathrm{card}(B_\alpha) = \mathrm{card}(\bigcup_{\beta\in I'} B_\beta) \leq \sum_{\beta\in I'} \mathrm{card}(B_\beta) < \underline{c}\) (by (FI.2)). This proves (4).

Let us now show that one has \[ \mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c} \text{ for all } x \in \mathcal{U} . \tag{5} \] Indeed, it suffices to show that, for every \(\alpha \in I\), one has "\(\mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c}\) for all \(x \in B_\alpha\)". Let us proceed again by transfinite recursion on \(\alpha\). It is true for \(\alpha = \varepsilon\), since, if \(x \in B_\varepsilon = B\), there exists \(n \geq 0\) such that \(x \in A_n\); whence \(x \subset A_{n+1}\) by (2), \(x \subset B\) and \(\mathrm{card}(x) \leq \mathrm{card}(B) < \underline{c}\). The case where \(\alpha\) has no predecessor is obvious. Finally, if \(x \in B_\alpha\) and if \(\alpha = s(\beta)\), one has either \(x \in B_\beta\) and the assertion "\(\mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c}\)" is true by recursion, or \(x \in \mathfrak{P}(B_\beta)\), whence \(x \subset B_\beta\) and the assertion "\(\mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c}\)" is true by (4).
We are now in a position to show that \(\mathcal{U}\) is indeed a universe:

(\(\mathcal{U}\).I) Let \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) and \(y \in x\). The task is to show that \(y \in \mathcal{U}\). In other words the task is to show that, for every \(\alpha \in I\), one has the relation: \[ \text{"}\, x \in B_\alpha \text{ and } y \in x \implies y \in B_\alpha \,\text{"} . \] One proceeds again by transfinite recursion on \(\alpha\). It is true for \(\alpha = \varepsilon\) since \(x \in B_\varepsilon = B\) implies \(x \in A_n\) for some \(n\); hence, if \(y \in x\), one has \(y \in A_{n+1}\), whence \(y \in B = B_\varepsilon\). The passage to an element \(\alpha\) without predecessor is obvious. Let us finally pass from \(\alpha\) to \(s(\alpha)\): if \(x \in B_{s(\alpha)}\) and if \(y \in x\), one has, either \(x \in B_\alpha\), whence \(y \in B_\alpha \subset B_{s(\alpha)}\) by recursion, or \(x \in \mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha)\), whence again \(y \in B_\alpha \subset B_{s(\alpha)}\).

(\(\mathcal{U}\).II) Let \(x, y \in \mathcal{U}\). Since the family \((B_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is increasing by (3), there exists \(\alpha \in I\) such that \(x, y \in B_\alpha\). Then \(\{x, y\} \in \mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha) \subset B_{s(\alpha)} \subset \mathcal{U}\).

(\(\mathcal{U}\).III) Let \(x \in \mathcal{U}\). There then exists \(\alpha \in I\) such that \(x \in B_\alpha\). It therefore suffices to show that, for every \(\alpha \in I\), one has the relation: \[ \text{"}\, x \in B_\alpha \implies \mathfrak{P}(x) \in B_{s(s(\alpha))} \,\text{"} . \] One proceeds again by transfinite recursion on \(\alpha\). If \(\alpha = \varepsilon\), one has \(x \in A_n\) for some \(n\), whence \(y \in A_{n+1} \subset B = B_\varepsilon\) for every subset \(y\) of \(x\); thus one has \(y \in \mathfrak{P}(B_\varepsilon) \subset B_{s(\varepsilon)}\) for all \(y \in \mathfrak{P}(x)\), whence \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \subset B_{s(\varepsilon)}\) and \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathfrak{P}(B_{s(\varepsilon)}) \subset B_{s(s(\varepsilon))}\), so that our assertion is true for \(\alpha = \varepsilon\). The passage to an element \(\alpha\) without predecessor is immediate, since \(\beta < \alpha\) then implies \(s(s(\beta)) < \alpha\). Let us finally pass from \(\alpha\) to \(s(\alpha)\); let \(x \in B_{s(\alpha)}\); if \(x \in B_\alpha\), one has \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in B_{s(s(\alpha))} \subset B_{s(s(s(\alpha)))}\) by recursion; if \(x \in \mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha)\), one has \(x \subset B_\alpha\), whence \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \subset \mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha)\) and \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathfrak{P}(\mathfrak{P}(B_\alpha)) \subset B_{s(s(s(\alpha)))}\).

(\(\mathcal{U}\).IV) Let \((x_\lambda)_{\lambda\in K}\) be a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(K \in \mathcal{U}\). The task is to show that the union \(x = \bigcup_{\lambda\in K} x_\lambda\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\). For every \(\lambda \in K\), let us choose an \(\alpha(\lambda) \in I\) such that \(x_\lambda \in B_{\alpha(\lambda)}\). Let us show that the set \(\alpha(K)\) of the \(\alpha(\lambda)\) is bounded above in \(I\): indeed, if it were not, one would have \[ I = \bigcup_{\lambda\in K} [\varepsilon, \alpha(\lambda)] , \] which would contradict (FI.2) since \(\mathrm{card}(K) < \underline{c}\) and \(\mathrm{card}([\varepsilon, \alpha(\lambda)]) < \underline{c}\) for all \(\lambda \in K\). Let then \(\beta\) be an upper bound of \(\alpha(K)\); one has \(x_\lambda \in B_\beta\) for all \(\lambda \in K\) since the family \((B_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is increasing. One therefore has \(x_\lambda \subset B_\beta\) by what we saw in the proof of (\(\mathcal{U}\).I), whence \(x = \bigcup_{\lambda\in K} x_\lambda \subset B_\beta\). By (3) it follows that one has \(x \in B_{s(\beta)}\), whence \(x \in \mathcal{U}\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 3

Let \(x, y\) be two sets and \(n\) an integer \(\geq 0\). One says that \(y\) is a component of order \(n\) of \(x\) if there exists a sequence \((x_j)_{j=0,\ldots,n}\) such that \(x_0 = x\), \(x_n = y\), and \(x_{j+1} \in x_j\) for \(j = 0, \ldots, n-1\).

Thus \(x\) is the only component of order 0 of \(x\). The components of order 1 (resp. 2) of \(x\) are the elements of \(x\) (resp. the elements of the elements of \(x\)). One says that \(y\) is a component of \(x\) if there exists \(n \geq 0\) such that \(y\) is a component of order \(n\) of \(x\). The relation "\(y\) is a component of \(x\)" is a preorder relation. By the selection-and-union scheme (chap. II, ...) the relation "\(y\) is a component of \(x\)" is collectivizing with respect to \(y\), so that the components of \(x\) form a set.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 4

Let \(\underline{c}\) be a cardinal. One says that a set \(x\) is of type \(\underline{c}\) (resp. of strict type \(\underline{c}\), of finite type) if all the components of \(x\) have cardinals \(\leq \underline{c}\) (resp. \(< \underline{c}\), finite).

Examples. The elements of the universe \(\mathcal{U}_1\) (no. 1, ex. 2) are all of finite type. If \(\underline{c}\) is a cardinal, and if \(x\) is of type \(\underline{c}\) (resp. strict type \(\underline{c}\), finite type), then every component of \(x\) and every subset of \(x\) are of type \(\underline{c}\) (resp. strict type \(\underline{c}\), finite type); likewise \(\mathfrak{P}(x)\) is of type \(2^{\underline{c}}\) (resp. of strict type \(2^{\underline{c}}\), of finite type). If \(x\) is of type \(\underline{c}\) and if \(\underline{c} \leq \underline{c}'\), then \(x\) is of type \(\underline{c}'\).

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma

Let \(\underline{c}\) be an uncountable strongly inaccessible cardinal, and \(X\) a set of strict type \(\underline{c}\). Then there exists a cardinal \(\underline{d} < \underline{c}\) such that \(X\) is of type \(\underline{d}\).

Indeed, for every integer \(n\), denote by \(\underline{d}_n\) the cardinal of the set \(X_n\) of the components of order \(n\) of \(X\). One has \(\underline{d}_0 = 1\), \(\underline{d}_1 = \mathrm{card}(X) < \underline{c}\), and, since \(X_n = \bigcup_{y\in X_{n-1}} y\), one deduces from it, by recursion on \(n\) and use of (FI.2), that one has \(\underline{d}_n < \underline{c}\) for all \(n\). Then the \(\underline{d}_n\) are bounded above by the cardinal \(\underline{d} = \sum_{j\geq 0} \underline{d}_j\), which is \(< \underline{c}\) by (FI.2) and the hypothesis of uncountability of \(\underline{c}\). Then, if \(Y\) is a component of order \(n\) of \(X\), one has \(\mathrm{card}(Y) \leq \mathrm{card}(X_{n+1}) \leq \underline{d}\). Q.E.D.

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 10

Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(\underline{c}\) a strongly inaccessible cardinal. Then the set \(\mathcal{U}'\) of the \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) that are of strict type \(\underline{c}\) is a universe.

Indeed, if \(x, y \in \mathcal{U}'\) and if \(z \in x\), one obviously has \(z \in \mathcal{U}'\) and \(\{x, y\} \in \mathcal{U}'\). If \(x \in \mathcal{U}'\), one has \(\mathrm{card}(x) < \underline{c}\), whence \(\mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{P}(x)) < \underline{c}\) by (FI.1); since a component of \(\mathfrak{P}(x)\) is either \(\mathfrak{P}(x)\), or a subset of \(x\), or a component of \(x\), one has \(\mathfrak{P}(x) \in \mathcal{U}'\). Finally if \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) is a family of elements of \(\mathcal{U}'\) such that \(I \in \mathcal{U}'\), one has \(\mathrm{card}(\bigcup_\alpha x_\alpha) < \underline{c}\) by (FI.2); since every component of order \(> 0\) of \(\bigcup_\alpha x_\alpha\) is a component of some \(x_\alpha\), one indeed has \(\bigcup_\alpha x_\alpha \in \mathcal{U}'\). Q.E.D.

Remark on the cardinal \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\). Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe and \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) the cardinal defined by (1), i.e. \[ \underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) = \sup_{x\in\mathcal{U}} \mathrm{card}(x) . \] One obviously has \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\), since, let us recall, \(x \in \mathcal{U}\) implies \(x \subset \mathcal{U}\). But the equality \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) = \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\) is not always true. For example let \((x_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) be an uncountable family of symbols with the axioms: \[ \text{"}\, x_\alpha = \{x_\alpha\} \text{ for all } \alpha \in I \,\text{"} , \quad \text{"}\, x_\alpha \neq x_\beta \text{ if } \alpha \neq \beta \,\text{"} \] (in other words \(x_\alpha\) is a set with a single element, namely itself). Let us form, as in ex. 2 of no. 1, the "meaningful words" formed with the symbols \(\varnothing, x_\alpha, \{, \}\) and , . Each denotes a finite set. Let \(\mathcal{U}\) be the set of these. One verifies easily that the conditions of Def. 1 are satisfied, so that \(\mathcal{U}\) is a universe. Since the meaningful words are finite sequences of elements of a set of cardinal \(\mathrm{card}(I) + 4 = \mathrm{card}(I)\); one has \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}) = \mathrm{card}(I)\) (chap. III; in fact \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}) \geq \mathrm{card}(I)\) suffices, and it is obvious). On the other hand, \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) is the countable cardinal, whence \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) < \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\).

The strict inequality \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) < \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\) is due to the fact that we have introduced here sets \(x_\alpha\) such that \(x_\alpha \in x_\alpha\). If one forbids horrors of this kind, one obtains \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}) = \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) for every universe \(\mathcal{U}\), as well as other very pretty results "of no possible use". This is what we shall do in the following section.
6. Artinian sets and universes

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.html:
Definition 5

One says that a set \(x\) is artinian if there exists no infinite sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) such that \(x_0 = x\) and \(x_{n+1} \in x_n\) for all \(n \geq 0\).
Examples. The sets \(\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}, \{\varnothing, \{\varnothing\}\}\), more generally the elements of the universe \(\mathcal{U}_1\) of no. 1, are artinian.

In pictorial terms, if \(x\) is artinian, and if one takes an element \(x_1\) of \(x\), then an element \(x_2\) of \(x_1\), etc., the process must stop, and one arrives at a component \(x_n\) of \(x\) that is empty. In other words the artinian sets are "built starting from \(\varnothing\)"; this will be made precise later (cf. (*) in the proof of Th. 2).
The artinian sets obviously enjoy the following properties:
(AR.I) If \(x\) is artinian, every subset of \(x\) and every component of \(x\) are artinian. For \(x\) to be artinian, it is necessary and sufficient that every element of \(x\) be artinian.
(AR.II) If \(x\) and \(y\) are artinian, then \(\{x,y\}\) is artinian.
(AR.III) If \(x\) is artinian, \(\mathfrak{P}(x)\) is artinian.
(AR.IV) Every union of artinian sets is an artinian set.
These properties show at once that one has the

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 11

If \(\mathcal{U}\) is a universe, the set of the artinian elements of \(\mathcal{U}\) is a universe, necessarily artinian.

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary

If \(x\) is an artinian set, there exists an artinian universe \(\mathcal{U}\) such that \(x \in \mathcal{U}\).
Indeed, by the axiom (A.6), \(x\) is an element of a universe \(V\); one takes for \(\mathcal{U}\) the set of the artinian elements of \(V\).
The following proposition is even less useful than the rest of the section:

blocks.title: Proposition
blocks.html:
Proposition 12

Let \(A\) be an artinian set. Then:

a) For every \(x \in A\), one has \(x \notin x\);

b) If \(x, y \in A\), one cannot have both \(x \in y\) and \(y \in x\);

c) For every \(x \in A\), the relation "\(y\) is a component of \(z\)" between components \(y, z\) of \(x\) is an order relation;

d) For every non-empty element \(x\) of \(A\), there exists \(y \in x\) such that \(x \cap y = \varnothing\).

Indeed the negation of a) (resp. of b)) entails the existence of an infinite sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) contradicting Def. 5, namely \((x, x, x, \ldots)\) (resp. \((x, y, x, y, x, y, \ldots)\)). The negation of c) means that there exist \(x \in A\), distinct components \(y, z\) of \(x\), and chains of memberships: \[ y \in y_1 \in \ldots \in y_q \in z , \quad z \in z_1 \in \ldots \in z_r \in y ; \] whence, as in b), an infinite sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) contradicting Def. 5 . Finally, if d) is false, there exists a non-empty element \(x\) of \(A\) such that \(x \cap y \neq \varnothing\) for all \(y \in x\); one sets \(x_0 = x\), and takes for \(x_1\) an element of \(x\); since \(x \cap x_1 \neq \varnothing\), one takes for \(x_2\) an element of \(x \cap x_1\) and so on; more formally one defines by recursion a sequence infinite \((x_n)_{n\geq 1}\) of elements of \(x\) by means of \(x_1 \in x\), \(x_{n+1} \in x_n \cap x\) for \(n \geq 1\); then the sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) contradicts Def. 5 .

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

Let \(B\) be a set. For \(B\) to be artinian, it is necessary and sufficient that every set \(A\) of sets of components of \(B\) satisfy condition d) of Prop. 12. Indeed the necessity follows from (AR.I) and from Prop. 12. Conversely, if \(B\) is not artinian, there exists an infinite sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 0}\) with \(x_0 = B\) and \(x_{n+1} \in x_n\) for all \(n \geq 0\); one then takes for \(A\) the subset reduced to the set \(X\) of the \(x_n\); thus \(A\) contains an element non-empty \(X\) such that, for every element \(y\) of \(X\), one has \(y \cap X \neq \varnothing\) (indeed \(y\) is of the form \(x_n\), and one has \(x_{n+1} \in y \cap X\)).

blocks.title: Theorem
blocks.html:
Theorem 2

Let \(\underline{c}\) be an infinite cardinal. Then:

a) The relation "\(x\) is an artinian set of type \(\underline{c}\) (resp. of strict type \(\underline{c}\))" is collectivizing with respect to \(x\); the set \(A_{\underline{c}}\) of the artinian sets of type \(\underline{c}\) has cardinal \(2^{\underline{c}}\).

b) If \(\underline{c}\) is strongly inaccessible, the set \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) of the artinian sets of strict type \(\underline{c}\) is a universe of cardinal \(\underline{c}\); the cardinal \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}) = \sup_{x\in\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}} \mathrm{card}(x)\) is \(\underline{c}\).

c) If a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) admits an element of cardinal \(\underline{c}\), every artinian set of type \(\underline{c}\) belongs to \(\mathcal{U}\) (in other words \(A_{\underline{c}} \subset \mathcal{U}\)).

c') If a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) is non-empty, every artinian set of finite type is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\).
Before proving Th. 2, let us deduce from it some illuminating corollaries:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 1

If a universe \(\mathcal{U}\) is artinian, then \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\) is strongly inaccessible, and \(\mathcal{U}\) is the set of the artinian sets of strict type \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\).

Indeed set \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) = \sup_{x\in\mathcal{U}} \mathrm{card}(x)\). It is a strongly inaccessible cardinal (beginning of no. 5). Suppose it first uncountable; then, for every infinite cardinal \(\underline{c} < \underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\), every artinian set of type \(\underline{c}\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by c); hence every artinian set of strict type \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) is an element of \(\mathcal{U}\) by the lemma of no. 5 . This last assertion remains valid if \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\) is countable by c'). Conversely, by (\(\mathcal{U}\).I), every element of \(\mathcal{U}\) is of strict type \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})\). Hence \(\mathcal{U}\) is the universe \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}(\mathcal{U})}\) of b), whence \(\underline{c}(\mathcal{U}) = \mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U})\) by b).

It follows from Cor. 1 that an artinian universe is determined uniquely by its cardinal (which is moreover strongly inaccessible). One therefore has a "one-to-one correspondence" between universes artinian and strongly inaccessible cardinals. In particular:

blocks.title: Corollary
blocks.html:
Corollary 2

The inclusion relation \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{U}'\) between artinian universes is a well-ordering relation.

Indeed the relation \(\underline{c} \leq \underline{c}'\) between cardinals is a well-ordering relation (chap. III) and, with the notations of b) of Th. 2, the relations \(\underline{c} \leq \underline{c}'\) and \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}} \subset \mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}'}\) are equivalent.
Note that Th. 2, b) gives a second proof of Th. 1 (no. 5).

Let us turn to the proof of Th. 2 . Given a set \(A\), we shall call a chain of \(A\) any finite sequence \((x_j)_{j=0,\ldots,n}\) such that \(x_0 = A\) and \(x_{j+1} \in x_j\) for \(j = 0, \ldots, n-1\). The chains of \(A\) form a set, by the selection-and-union scheme; denote it by \(G(A)\). Given a chain \(X = (x_j)_{j=0,\ldots,n}\), the chains of the form \((x_i)_{i=0,\ldots,q}\) with \(q \leq n\) will be said to be smaller than \(X\); one obtains in this way, on \(G(A)\), a structure of ordered set. For \(A\) to be artinian, it is necessary and sufficient that \(G(A)\) be a "noetherian" ordered set (i.e. satisfying the equivalent conditions of chap. III, § 6, no. 5).
We shall show that:
(*) If \(A\) is artinian, it is determined uniquely by the isomorphism class of the ordered set \(G(A)\).

Indeed, given an ordered set \(G\) and an element \(g \in G\), we shall denote by \(S(g)\) the set of the \(g' \in G\) such that \(g < g'\) and such that \(g \leq h \leq g'\) implies \(h = g\) or \(h = g'\) (in other words the set of the "immediate successors" of \(g\)). Consider the map \(\theta\) which, to every chain \(X = (x_0, \ldots, x_n)\) of \(G(A)\) associates the set \(x_n\); one then has, for every \(X \in G(A)\): \[ \theta(X) = \{ \theta(X') \mid X' \in S(X) \} . \] Since \(A\) is the image under \(\theta\) of the smallest element \(X_0 = (A)\) of \(G(A)\), it will suffice for us to show that \(\theta\) is uniquely determined by the isomorphism class of the ordered set \(G(A)\). Now this follows from the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 1

Let \(G\) be a noetherian ordered set and \(\varphi\) a map of \(G\) such that, for every \(g \in G\), one has: \[ \varphi(g) = \{ \varphi(g') \mid g' \in S(g) \} . \tag{1} \] Then \(\varphi\) is uniquely determined. Moreover, if \(\mathcal{U}\) is a universe containing an element equipotent to \(G\), \(\varphi\) takes its values in \(\mathcal{U}\).
The hypothesis implies that one has \(\varphi(g) = \varnothing\) if \(g\) is a maximal element of \(G\).

Let, indeed, \(\varphi\) and \(\varphi'\) be two maps such that (1) is true; if \(\varphi \neq \varphi'\), the set of the \(g \in G\) such that \(\varphi(g) \neq \varphi'(g)\) is non-empty, hence admits a maximal element \(h\) since \(G\) is noetherian; one then has \(\varphi(g) = \varphi'(g)\) for all \(g > h\), in particular for every "successor" \(g \in S(h)\); whence \(\varphi(h) = \varphi'(h)\) by (1), which is a contradiction; one therefore indeed has \(\varphi = \varphi'\). Let now \(\mathcal{U}\) be a universe containing an element \(x\) equipotent to \(G\); let us show that \(\varphi\) takes its values in \(\mathcal{U}\); otherwise let \(h\) be an element maximal among the \(g \in G\) such that \(\varphi(g) \notin \mathcal{U}\); one has \(\varphi(g') \in \mathcal{U}\) for all \(g' \in S(h)\) so that \[ \varphi(h) = \{ \varphi(g') \mid g' \in S(h) \} \] is a subset of \(\mathcal{U}\); now, since its cardinal is less than \(\mathrm{card}(G)\), hence than the cardinal of an element of \(\mathcal{U}\), one has \(\varphi(h) \in \mathcal{U}\) (no. 1, Prop. 7); this contradiction shows that \(\varphi\) takes its values in \(\mathcal{U}\).

This being so, let us prove a) of Th. 2. One may restrict to the non-resp. assertion, since the other follows from it at once. Let \(\underline{c}\) be an infinite cardinal. If \(A\) is a set of type \(\underline{c}\) one has: \[ \mathrm{card}(G(A)) \leq \underline{c} . \tag{2} \] Indeed, if one denotes by \(A_n\) the set of the components of order \(n\) of \(A\), one has \(\mathrm{card}(A_1) \leq \underline{c}\) and \(\mathrm{card}(A_{n+1}) \leq \underline{c} \cdot \mathrm{card}(A_n)\), whence \(\mathrm{card}(A_n) \leq \underline{c}^n\) by recursion; now \(\underline{c}^n = \underline{c}\) since \(\underline{c}\) is infinite (chap. III); whence \(\mathrm{card}(\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty} A_n) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathbb{N})\cdot\underline{c} = \underline{c}\) (chap. III); now \(G(A)\) is a set of finite sequences of elements of \(\bigcup_n A_n\), so that one indeed has the inequality (2) (chap. III). This being so, if \(E\) is a set of cardinal \(\underline{c}\), the datum of an order structure on a subset \(E'\) of \(E\) is equivalent to the datum of the subset of \(E \times E\) formed of the \((x,y)\) such that \(x \in E'\), \(y \in E'\) and \(x \leq y\). Hence, by virtue of (2), the classes of isomorphism of the ordered sets \(G(A)\) (where \(A\) is of type \(\underline{c}\)) form a set \(\mathfrak{G}_{\underline{c}}\), and one has \(\mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{G}_{\underline{c}}) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{P}(E \times E)) = 2^{\underline{c}}\). Let \(\mathfrak{G}'_{\underline{c}}\) be the subset of \(\mathfrak{G}_{\underline{c}}\) formed of the classes of noetherian ordered sets having a smallest element; if, to every \(G \in \mathfrak{G}'_{\underline{c}}\), one associates the value of the function \(\varphi\) of Lemma 1 at the smallest element of \(G\), one obtains a map \(\theta\) of \(\mathfrak{G}'_{\underline{c}}\) whose image contains all the artinian sets of type \(\underline{c}\). The latter therefore indeed form a set \(A_{\underline{c}}\), and one has \(\mathrm{card}(A_{\underline{c}}) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{G}'_{\underline{c}}) \leq \mathrm{card}(\mathfrak{G}_{\underline{c}}) \leq 2^{\underline{c}}\).

It remains to see that one has \(\mathrm{card}(A_{\underline{c}}) = 2^{\underline{c}}\). For this it suffices to see that there exists an artinian set \(B\) of type \(\underline{c}\) and of cardinal \(\underline{c}\), since the subsets of \(B\) will then be elements of \(A_{\underline{c}}\). This existence follows from the following lemma:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 2

For every cardinal \(\underline{c}\), there exists an artinian set \(B\) of type \(\underline{c}\) and of cardinal \(\underline{c}\).

We proceed by transfinite induction on \(\underline{c}\). For \(\underline{c} = 0\) there is no choice, and we take \(B = \varnothing\). If \(\underline{c}\) has a predecessor \(\underline{c}'\), let \(B'\) be an artinian set of type \(\underline{c}'\) and of cardinality \(\underline{c}'\); we then have \(\underline{c} \leq 2^{\underline{c}'}\), so that there exists a subset \(B\) of \(\mathfrak{P}(B')\) of cardinality \(\underline{c}\); the elements of \(B\) are subsets of \(B'\) and therefore have cardinalities \(\leq \underline{c}' \leq \underline{c}\); the higher-order components of \(B\) are components of \(B'\), and therefore also have cardinalities \(\leq \underline{c}' \leq \underline{c}\). Finally, if \(\underline{c}\) has no predecessor, then for every cardinal \(\underline{c}_\lambda < \underline{c}\) we choose an artinian set \(B_\lambda\) of type \(\underline{c}_\lambda\) and of cardinality \(\underline{c}_\lambda\); then \(B = \bigcup_\lambda B_\lambda\) answers the question. This proves Lemma 2, and completes the proof of part a).

We turn to b). Let \(\underline{c}\) be a strongly inaccessible cardinal. We already know, by a), that the artinian sets of strict type \(\underline{c}\) form a set \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\). The fact that \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) is a universe follows at once from the properties (AR.I) to (AR.IV) of artinian sets (beginning of the n°), and from bounds on cardinals analogous to those of Prop. 10 of n° 5. The relation \(\sup_{x\in\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}} \mathrm{card}(x) = \underline{c}\) follows from Lemma 2, applied to the cardinals \(< \underline{c}\). Finally, to show that \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}) = \underline{c}\), let us first suppose \(\underline{c}\) uncountable; by the lemma of n° 5, \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) is the union \(\bigcup_{\underline{d}<\underline{c}} A_{\underline{d}}\), where \(A_{\underline{d}}\) denotes the set of artinian sets of type \(\underline{d}\); now \(\mathrm{card}(A_{\underline{d}}) = 2^{\underline{d}} < \underline{c}\) (by a)); on the other hand the set of cardinals \(\underline{d} < \underline{c}\) has cardinality \(\leq \underline{c}\) (chap. III); whence \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}) \leq \underline{c} \cdot \underline{c} = \underline{c}\), and also \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}) \geq \underline{c}\) since \(\mathrm{card}(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}) \geq \mathrm{card}(A_{\underline{d}}) = 2^{\underline{d}}\) for all \(\underline{d} < \underline{c}\).

The case \(\underline{c} = 0\) being trivial, there remains the case where \(\underline{c}\) is the countably infinite cardinal. In this case \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) is the set of artinian sets of finite type (i.e. finite together with all their components), and we use a pretty result of a combinatorial nature:

blocks.title: Lemma
blocks.html:
Lemma 3

(D. König?). Consider two infinite sequences \((E_n)_{n\geq 1}\), \((\varphi_n)_{n\geq 1}\) of finite sets \(E_n\) and maps \(f_n : E_{n+1} \to E_n\). If there exists no infinite sequence \((x_n)_{n\geq 1}\) such that \(x_n \in E_n\) and \(f_n(x_{n+1}) = x_n\) for all \(n\), then \(E_n\) is empty for \(n\) large enough.

In other words, if all the sequences \((x_n)\) such that \(f_n(x_{n+1}) = x_n\) are finite, their lengths are bounded. This can be expressed in terms of projective limits: a projective limit of non-empty finite sets is non-empty (cf. Top. Géné., Chap. I, 2e éd. §9, n°6, prop.8, 2°)).

We argue, indeed, by contradiction. If there exist non-empty \(E_n\) for arbitrarily large \(n\), then no \(E_n\) is empty (for \(E_n = \varnothing\) entails \(E_{n+1} = \varnothing\) in view of the existence of \(f_n : E_{n+1} \to E_n\)). Let us call "coherent" the finite sequences \((x_j)_{1\leq j\leq n}\) such that \(f_j(x_{j+1}) = x_j\) for \(j = 1, \ldots, n-1\). Let us prove, by induction on \(n\), the existence of a coherent sequence \((a_1, \ldots, a_n)\) (\(a_i \in E_i\)) which, for every \(q \geq n\), can be extended to a coherent sequence \((a_1, \ldots, a_n, x_{n+1}, \ldots, x_q)\) of length \(q\). This is obvious for \(n = 0\), since no \(E_q\) is empty. Let us pass from \(n\) to \(n + 1\). If, for every \(x \in f_n^{-1}(\{a_n\}) \subset E_{n+1}\), all coherent sequences extending \((a_1, \ldots, a_n, x)\) had lengths bounded by an integer \(q(x)\), then all coherent sequences extending \((a_1, \ldots, a_n)\) would be of bounded length (by \(\sup_x q(x)\)) since \(E_{n+1}\) is finite; there exists therefore \(a_{n+1} \in f_n^{-1}(\{a_n\})\) such that the coherent sequence \((a_1, \ldots, a_n, a_{n+1})\) admits extensions of arbitrary length. This being so, we have an infinite sequence \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) which contradicts the hypothesis.

It follows from Lemma 3 that if \(A\) is an artinian set of finite type, then the ordered set \(G(A)\) of its chains is finite: indeed, one takes for \(E_n\) the set of chains \((x_n \in x_{n-1} \in \ldots \in x_1 \in A)\) with \(n + 1\) terms (which is finite, since the components of \(A\) of order \(\leq n + 1\) are finite in number and are all finite), and for \(f_n\) the map \((x_{n+1} \in x_n \in x_{n+1} \ldots) \mapsto (x_n \in x_{n-1} \in \ldots)\). Now the set of isomorphism classes of finite ordered sets is countable: indeed, giving an order structure on a finite subset of \(\mathbb{N}\) amounts to giving its graph, which is a subset finite of \(\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}\); on the other hand the set of finite subsets of a countable set is countable (chap. III). It follows from (*) and Lemma 1 that the set \(G\) of artinian sets of finite type is countable. It is infinite by Lemma 2 (or, more simply, by use of the sequence \((z_n)_{n\geq 0}\) defined by means of \(z_0 = \varnothing\), \(z_{n+1} = \{z_n\}\)). This completes the proof of b).

blocks.title: Remark
blocks.html:
Remark

We have just proved that, if \(A\) is an artinian set of finite type, it has only a finite number of components. There therefore exists an integer \(n\) such that \(A\) is of type \(n\).

We turn to the proof of c). Let \(\underline{c}\) be an infinite cardinal, \(\mathcal{U}\) a universe admitting an element of cardinality \(\underline{c}\), and \(A\) an artinian set of type \(\underline{c}\). Then the ordered set \(G(A)\) has cardinality \(\leq \underline{c}\) (formula (2) above). The second assertion of Lemma 1, applied to \(G(A)\), shows that the map \((x_0, \ldots, x_n) \mapsto x_n\) from \(G(A)\) takes its values in \(\mathcal{U}\). In other words, all the components of \(A\) are elements of \(\mathcal{U}\). This proves c). The proof of c') is analogous: if \(A\) is an artinian set of finite type, we have just seen that \(G(A)\) is finite; since \(\mathcal{U}\) is non-empty, it contains an element equipotent to \(G(A)\) by the cor. to Prop. 7 (n° 1). Q.E.D.
7. Woolly metamathematical remarks
a) The axiom "every set is artinian" is harmless. Indeed, if we have a model \(M\) of Set Theory, the set \(M'\) of artinian elements of \(M\) is also a model (cf. Prop. 11).

b) The axiom (A.6) of universes (and the equivalent axiom (A'.6) of strongly inaccessible cardinals) is independent of the rest of Set Theory. Indeed, let \(\underline{c}\) be the first uncountable strongly inaccessible cardinal. The universe \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) of artinian sets of strict type \(\underline{c}\) (Th. 2, b)) is a model of Set Theory without (A.6): we call "sets" the elements of \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\), the "membership relation" is the restriction to \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) of the ordinary one, etc. The "universes" of the model are thus the ordinary universes that are elements of \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\). Now we have seen that the only universes that are elements of \(\mathcal{U}_{\underline{c}}\) are the two small ones \(\mathcal{U}_0 = \varnothing\) and \(\mathcal{U}_1\). Thus \(\mathcal{U}_1\) is a "set" which is an element of no "universe". We therefore have a model of Set Theory in which (A.6) is false.

c) Bourbaki was too cautious in being content to "presume" that the axiom of infinity (A.5) is independent of the preceding axioms and schemes. It is indeed so, for the countable universe \(\mathcal{U}_1\) of artinian sets of finite type is a model in which (A.5) is false, and in which the preceding axioms and schemes are true.
d) It would be very interesting to prove that the axiom (A.6) of universes is harmless. This seems difficult, and it is even unprovable, says Paul Cohen.

The adjective "woolly" in the title means that, in constructing models, we have not taken the trouble to doctor the symbol \(\tau\) so that it does not lead out of it. The key to this, if one considers a model \(M\), is to replace the ordinary \(\tau_x(R(x))\) by: \[ \tau_x(R(x) \text{ and } x \in M) . \] It still remains to check that this indeed transforms the ordinary quantifiers into the quantifiers formerly called "typical": \[ (\forall x \in M) \text{ and } (\exists x \in M) . \]
Exercises
1) Let \(n\) be an integer \(\geq 1\). Show that the set of artinian sets of type \(n\) is infinite (the sets \(z_0 = \varnothing\), \(z_1 = \{\varnothing\}\), \(z_{q+1} = \{z_q\}\) are of type 1).

2) Let us call the height of a set \(A\) the least upper bound (finite or infinite) of the integers \(n\) such that there exists a sequence \(x_n \in x_{n-1} \in \ldots \in x_0 = A\). Show that the sets of height \(\leq n\) are finite and form a finite set, whose cardinality \(p_n\) is computed by means of \(p_0 = 1\), \(p_{n+1} = 2^{p_n}\) (proceed by induction on \(n\), noting that the elements of a set \(A\) of height \(\leq n\) are sets of height \(\leq n - 1\)).
3) Let \(G\) be a noetherian ordered set admitting a smallest element \(g_0\) and such that for every \(h \in G\), the set of \(g \leq h\) is finite and totally ordered.
a) Show that every element \(h \neq g_0\) of \(G\) admits one and only one predecessor.

b) Let \(\varphi\) be the map on \(G\) defined in Lemma 1 (i.e. \(\varphi(g)\) is the set of the \(\varphi(g')\) where \(g'\) runs through the set of successors of \(g\)). We set \(A = \varphi(g_0)\). Show that \(A\) is an artinian set. For \(g \in G\), let \(g_0 < g_1 < \ldots < g_n = g\) be the sequence of elements \(\leq g\); set \(f(g) = (\varphi(g_0), \varphi(g_1), \ldots, \varphi(g_n))\); show that \(f\) is an increasing surjective map from \(G\) onto the ordered set \(G(A)\) of the text. Show that, if \(f\) is injective, it is an isomorphism from \(G\) onto \(G(A)\).

c) For \(g \in G\), let \(M_g\) be the set of upper bounds of \(g\). Suppose that, for every pair of distinct elements \(g, g'\) having the same predecessor \(p\), the ordered sets \(M_g\) and \(M_{g'}\) are non-isomorphic. Show that the map \(f\) of b) is then an isomorphism from \(G\) onto \(G(A)\).

[If \(f(g) = f(g')\) with \(g \neq g'\) and if \(g_0 < g_1 < \ldots < g_n = g\) and \(g'_0 < g'_1 < \ldots < g'_{n'} = g'\) are the sequence of elements \(\leq g\) and that of elements \(\leq g'\), show that \(n = n'\), and that one may assume that \(g\) and \(g'\) have the same predecessor \(p\); then consider the set of \(p \in G\) such that there exist two distinct successors \(g, g'\) of \(p\) such that \(f(g) = f(g')\), a maximal element \(q\) of this set, and two distinct successors \(h, h'\) of \(q\) such that \(f(h) = f(h')\); note that the restrictions of \(f\) to \(M_h\) and to \(M_{h'}\) are injective, hence (by b)) are isomorphisms from \(M_h\) onto \(G(\varphi(h))\) and from \(M_{h'}\) onto \(G(\varphi(h'))\); deduce from the hypothesis of non-isomorphism of \(M_h\) and \(M_{h'}\) that one has \(\varphi(h) \neq \varphi(h')\), which contradicts \(f(h) = f(h')\)].

N.B. Exercise 3) gives very precise information on the way in which artinian sets are "manufactured". We already knew that such a set \(A\) is determined by the isomorphism class of the ordered set \(G(A)\) (Lemma 1). We now know how to characterize the ordered sets \(G\) isomorphic to some \(G(A)\):
α) \(G\) is noetherian and admits a smallest element;
β) For every \(g \in G\), the set of \(h \leq g\) is totally ordered and finite (whence the existence and uniqueness of the predecessor of \(g\));
γ) If \(g, g'\) are distinct elements having the same predecessor, the set \(M_g\) of upper bounds of \(g\) and the set \(M_{g'}\) of upper bounds of \(g'\) are not isomorphic.

4) Let \((A_n)_{n\geq 0}\) be the sequence of finite ordinals, defined by \(A_0 = \varnothing\), \(A_{n+1} = A_n \cup \{A_n\}\). Show that the ordered set \(G(A_n)\) has \(2^n\) elements, and that the number of its elements of height \(q\) (in the sense of Exerc. 2)) is \(\binom{n}{q}\).
BIBLIOGRAPHY
